Q2 Cross-Service Invariants Review — June 4, 2025
One-Page Preparation Brief

Circulated by: Alex Valdez · Requested by: Hema · Drafted: 2025-06-02

1. Purpose (and what this review does NOT do)

The June 4 review is a check that current owner-map provenance has named mapped owners and explicit exception routes. It is scoped to the three lanes below.

Out of scope — explicit boundaries:
- Does not create a centralized release-approval gate.
- Does not change service ownership or backup designations.
- Does not authorize Lantern beyond June 30, 2025.
- Does not add accounts, data sources, or tenants.
- Does not begin a new metrics-pipeline scale-response cycle.
- Alex is not the catch-all owner for implementation, telemetry, operations, or release readiness in any lane.

2. Lane A — Owner-Map Provenance

What we are checking: every cross-service invariant in scope has a named mapped implementation owner, a rollback owner, and a boundary-specific exception owner, each on the record (runbook entry field or forum readout).

Invariant | Mapped impl owner | Rollback owner | Exception owner | Provenance on record?
Cardinality Guardrails: label-cardinality preflight | (see §4 — open) | (see §4) | Nadia — alert semantics; Cyrus — cost/cardinality angle | rb_1789206351936 under metrics-router, review-path language named
Cardinality Guardrails: alert-source classification | Nadia | (see §4) | Nadia — alert semantics | rb_1789206351936, Dec-12-2023 required-operating-rule block
Cardinality Guardrails: parity check (label-name) | Nadia (alerting/dashboards); Cyrus team (rollup-service) | per service owner | routes back to mapped service owner, not a generic reviewer | rb_shard_keeper_label_parity; pre-push sync rule post-May-18
metrics-router canary alert response | (see §4 — canary owner field) | deploy-pipeline rollback | per service owner | rb_metrics_router_canary
Lantern two-account read-only boundary | Iris — customer interp; Alex — fresh-data, tenant, denials, latency, errors | n/a (read-only) | Iris is NOT the exception owner for Lantern data-contract questions | Lantern stop-contract ownership split

Exception route rule (from Hema's infra cross-service proposal): an ownership exception routes back to the mapped service owner, not to a generic reviewer. An exception owner is not a stand-in for the mapped release owner. The April engineering-forum readout will demonstrate the rule using mapped-owner examples; the review should hold any drift against this.

3. Lane B — Lantern Two-Account Read-Only Boundary Through June 30, 2025

- Boundary is read-only across two accounts, in force through 2025-06-30. The review does not extend, narrow, or re-authorize it.
- Ownership split on the active stop-contract:
  - Alex: fresh-data, tenant, denials, latency, errors.
  - Iris: customer interpretation.
  - Iris is not the exception owner for Lantern data-contract questions; those route to the mapped service owner.
- Harbor Health used the published ownership card twice during the extension period (2025-05-22, 2025-05-29) to route follow-ups without requesting raw incident text — relayed by Iris as the third concrete observation from the extension. (Confirmed in scope as evidence the boundary is operating as designed.)
- Out of scope for June 4: whether the boundary extends past June 30. That decision is separate and does not get pre-decided here.

4. Lane C — Cardinality Guardrails Checks

The signed-off preflight covers both router and shard-keeper paths (rb_1789206351936). The Dec-12-2023 required operating rule names three checks:

1. Label-cardinality preflight. Identifies new/changed label keys and value-shape behavior. Must classify the changed value set as bounded, expected high-cardinality with an owner and budget, or effectively unbounded. Live-path label changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture; replay/mirror validation alone is not enough.

2. Alert-source classification check. Classifies whether the relevant panel or alert signal is live-path, replay-source, mirror-source, or other validation-source evidence. Replay/mirror movement remains visible as investigation evidence but is not rollback criteria by itself. Reviewers must not let validation-source panels read like live rollback triggers.

3. Parity check. Cross-service label-name or meaning changes require rollup-service parity before promotion. A green metrics-router canary does not substitute for downstream consumers expecting the same name and semantics. The pre-push sync rule for shard-keeper (Nadia + Cyrus team) is the on-the-record instance.

Non-goals the entry is explicit about: not a mature/complete Cardinality Guardrails program, not a general telemetry rewrite, does not move enforcement ownership to data platform, does not make Wes (or any practical backup) the default enforcement owner.

5. Open question for the room — is anything missing from the owner-map?

I want to surface this before the meeting rather than assume the answer:

- rb_1789206351936 (the canonical Cardinality Guardrails entry) does not currently carry an owner/backup field — it has service, title, body, and timestamps only. The mapped implementation owner is named inside the body (Nadia for alert semantics; Cyrus for cost/cardinality), but the entry header itself does not surface that through the runbook store the way rb_ingest_edge_cutover (alex / yuki) or rb_shard_keeper_label_parity (alex / nadia) do. - A green metrics-router canary on route_pattern-class changes does not substitute for rollup-service parity — that boundary is named in the body but the corresponding rollback owner for a failed parity check is not separately mapped in the entry. The exception route points at "mapped service owner," but the cross-service case (who actually pulls the change back when both sides are involved) is not explicitly named.

- The "is validation-only evidence rollback-worthy?" question is named as an open question in the first-cut body itself (Nov-2023) and was reaffirmed in the 2023-10-30 incident-scope patch. It has not been closed; the review should not assume it has.

If any of those turns into a missing provenance cell, the right outcome on June 4 is to name the gap and route the fix back to the relevant mapped owner — not to absorb it into the review itself.

6. Where the boundaries bite me personally

I want this on the record before the meeting so it does not become a side conversation:

- I am not the catch-all owner for implementation, telemetry, operations, or release readiness in any of these lanes. Each lane routes to its named mapped owner; the review's job is to confirm the names exist and the routes point at them, not to consolidate them under me.

- I do not own Cardinality Guardrails enforcement, do not own the rollup-service, do not own the metrics-router canary response as primary, and do not own the Lantern boundary's interpretation. I do own the surfaces named in §3 for the active stop-contract; that does not extend.

- If the review needs an owner-map cell filled in, the request goes to the mapped service owner for that cell, not to me as a fallback.

— end of brief —

## Canary note — 2023-08-16 (scheduled load-test label noise)

Context: Severity-3 cardinality canary fired while Cyrus was running a scheduled load test against metrics-router. Wes isolated the spike to an unbounded `experiment_id` label coming only from the load-test traffic, checked the deploy path, and confirmed the service itself was not regressing. Cyrus stopped the load test and the canary cleared without escalation or rollback. This note is for the next responder.

- **A cardinality canary during a known scheduled load test is expected to trip, not a service regression.** Before treating the alert as a metrics-router regression, confirm whether a scheduled load test is in progress (check #ops-loadtests / ask Cyrus / check the load-test calendar). If yes, do not rollback.
- **Isolate the label to the load-test traffic first.** Check whether the unbounded labels (`experiment_id`, `user_id`, `request_id`, anything tenant/key-shaped) are present only on load-test traffic or also on production traffic. If load-test-only, the spike is from the load generator, not from metrics-router.
- **Check the deploy path, but do not assume deploy is the cause.** A green canary + a recent config-only change + a load test in flight usually means the load test is the source. Wes's 2023-08-16 investigation pattern is the reference: isolate label → rule out deploy → rule out downstream → confirm load-test scope → ask the load-test owner to stop.
- **Coordinate with the load-test owner before stopping or rolling back.** Cyrus stops the load test on confirmation; do not rollback metrics-router without that conversation. Rollback during a load-test-driven alert is the wrong action and creates a second incident.
- **No cardinality-control project, no ownership change.** This is a documentation note so the next responder does the same fast isolation rather than treating noise as a regression. Cardinality controls on load-test labels are tracked separately and are not owned by the canary response.

---

## Canary note — 2023-09-07 (post-canary CPU-only warmup, not a rollback)

Context: Second day of metrics-router data after the config-checksum cleanup canary. The affected AZ's CPU uplift has settled to ~2–3%, checksum-cache invalidations are back near baseline, cache-cardinality stayed flat, p99 stayed inside the normal 182–188 ms band, error rate stayed at 0.02%, dropped writes stayed clean, and rollup-service lag stayed flat. No user-visible signal moved. Closing as checksum-cache warmup after the config-checksum cleanup, not a rollback case.

- **A small residual CPU uplift in one AZ on the first 1–2 days after a config-checksum cleanup is warmup, not a regression.** Cache entries rehydrate under the new checksum regime; CPU cost comes back to baseline as the cache refills. Do not rollback on CPU alone if p99, error rate, dropped writes, cache-cardinality, and downstream lag are all flat.
- **Re-check the four user-visible signals before any rollback action.** p99 (must stay in the 182–188 ms band), error rate (~0.02% baseline), dropped writes (clean), and rollup-service lag (flat). If all four are flat, the rollout is fine and the residual CPU is warmup.
- **Checksum-cache invalidations returning near baseline is the confirming signal.** Elevated invalidations dominated by `checksum-mismatch-on-read` would be a different problem (would reconsider the rollout). Invalidations back near baseline + cache-cardinality flat means the cache is settling, not churning.
- **Triggers that WOULD change the call:** cache-hit ratio in the affected AZ dropping materially; checksum-cache invalidations dominated by `checksum-mismatch-on-read`; any of the four user-visible signals (p99 / error rate / dropped writes / rollup-service lag) moving off baseline. None of these fired on 2023-09-07.
- **No second-day page expected.** This note exists so the next on-call does not treat CPU-only post-canary warmup as an automatic rollback. If the four user-visible signals stay flat, leave the rollout in place and let the cache finish warming.

---

## Canary note — 2023-09-27 (parser-cache warmup during canary, not a rollback)

Context: Tiny metrics-router parser cleanup canary warmup ran on 2023-09-26; full rollout through the deploy pipeline finished on 2023-09-27 and stayed quiet. p99 stayed in the normal band, error rate held at 0.02%, dropped writes stayed clean, rollup-service lag stayed flat, and parser-cache misses did not repeat on full rollout. Closing as a parser-cache warmup that the canary allowed to hold, not a rollback case. This note is for the next responder who sees parser-cache misses during a future parser-cleanup canary.

- **A short burst of parser-cache misses during a parser-cleanup canary is warmup, not a regression.** The parser cache rehydrates against the new parser path while the canary holds. Treat parser-cache misses during canary the same way as the 2023-09-07 checksum-cache warmup: hold the rollout and verify on the four user-visible signals before any rollback action.
- **Hold and verify on the four user-visible signals.** p99 must return to baseline, and error rate (~0.02%), dropped writes (clean), and rollup-service lag (flat) must stay flat. If all four hold, the warmup is settling and the rollout can proceed.
- **Parser-cache misses stopping on their own is the confirming signal.** Parser-cache misses that recede as the cache fills under the new parser path means the cache is settling, not churning. Continued parser-cache misses at canary traffic level with any of the four user-visible signals moving off baseline is a different problem.
- **Triggers that WOULD change the call:** any of the four user-visible signals (p99 / error rate / dropped writes / rollup-service lag) moving off baseline during the warmup window; parser-cache misses that do not recede as the canary holds; a parser-cache miss rate that grows against steady canary traffic instead of decaying. None of these fired on 2023-09-27.
- **Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged.** The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) and the canary gating criteria still apply. This note only describes how to interpret a parser-cache warmup within those requirements; it does not relax any of them.

## Canary note — 2024-05-30 (generation and cleanup-pause guidance during canary)

Context: The existing canary response covered CPU, memory, queue depth, route-delivery divergence, dropped series, and restarts. It did not cover active-versus-retired generation counts, epoch drain, matcher cleanup, or stop-the-world cleanup pauses. This note adds the missing generation and cleanup evidence without changing the three-step canary response, the four user-visible signals, or any prior warmup-vs-rollback call. - **Compare p99 by pod alongside active and retired generation counts and cleanup-pause duration.** p99 by pod is the diagnostic; the active-generation count and the retired-generation count describe whether the router has finished draining the previous generation, and the cleanup-pause duration describes whether the stop-the-world matcher cleanup is staying cheap. A transient p99 spike that recovers while active and retired generation counts stay consistent and cleanup pauses stay bounded is warmup-style movement, not a regression. The pre-existing four user-visible signals (p99 in the 182–188 ms band, error rate ~0.02%, dropped writes clean, rollup-service lag flat) still gate the call.
- **Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 ms.** Retired-object accumulation above four means the previous generation has not drained into the active set; cleanup pauses above 100 ms mean the stop-the-world matcher cleanup is no longer cheap enough to ride alongside canary traffic. In either case, hold the rollout pipeline, do not push the next config change, and verify before resuming pushes. This is a pause on pushes, not a rollback — the existing rollback criteria below still decide whether a rollback is warranted.
- **Verify before resuming pushes.** With pushes paused, verify all of the following, in this order: active-generation consistency (every pod reports the same active generation, no mixed-generation pods), route parity (router deliveries match the previous-generation route table for the same label set), dropped series (clean, no new series dropped against the pre-canary baseline), reload failures (none, or back inside the pre-canary rate), and restarts (none, or back inside the pre-canary rate). Treat it the same way as the 2023-09-07 checksum-cache warmup and the 2023-09-27 parser-cache warmup: hold, verify on the signals above, do not rollback on p99 alone.

## Canary note — 2024-07-25 (owner-led window rule: fresh opening decision per window, bounded single-push execution, threshold stops, rollback set unchanged)

Context: The 2024-05-30 note established the pause-on-pushes rule and the five-signal verify-before-resume set, and the 2024-06-18 note encoded the stop / bounded single-push resume / immediate re-pause / rollback boundary that infra review accepted. The 2024-06-18 wording framed each push as if it carried its own per-push approval. That per-push framing is superseded by the owner-led window rule below: windows, not individual pushes, are the unit Alex opens. Each window still permits a sequence of single-file pushes while the threshold conditions hold, but a fresh opening decision from Alex is required for every window — including any window opened after recovery from a threshold stop, and any window opened after a fully observed push closes. The rollback set is unchanged and the three-step canary response, the four user-visible signals, the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and the deploy-pipeline-only rule remain in force. This note supersedes the per-push-approval framing in the 2024-06-18 note; it does not relax canary gating, does not authorize laptop deploys, does not change the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision.

- **Window is the unit Alex opens.** Each configuration-push window requires a fresh opening decision from Alex. A fresh opening decision is required (a) to start the first window after this note, (b) to start any window after a threshold stop, and (c) to start any window after a previous window's fully observed push closes. No window is implicit and no window carries forward from a prior approval. Wes, as practical backup, may open a window only when Alex is unreachable, and Alex remains the primary owner of the opening decision in all other cases. Wes is not becoming the primary owner; Alex remains primary and Wes remains the practical backup.
- **Inside a window, mapped operators may make single-file pushes while the threshold conditions hold.** Mapped operators are the engineers and service owners already assigned to the affected files. While a window is open, those mapped operators may push single-file changes through the deploy pipeline, one at a time, provided every push returns the full health set to baseline before the next push lands. "Full health set to baseline" means: retired-generation count at or below four, cleanup-pause p99 at or below 100 ms, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity against the previous-generation table, dropped series clean against the pre-canary baseline, reload failures at or below the pre-canary rate, and restarts at or below the pre-canary rate. The full health set is the per-push gate inside the window; it is not a substitute for Alex's window-opening decision.
- **Exceeding either threshold stops the window immediately.** The window stops the moment retired generations accumulate above four, or the moment a cleanup pause above 100 ms is observed. "Stop" means no further pushes land via the deploy pipeline for the remainder of that window, no matter how clean the rest of the health set looks. Stop is automatic, not a judgement call; the next push requires a fresh opening decision from Alex and a new window. A threshold stop does not escalate to rollback on its own — rollback is decided by the rollback set at the end of this note — but a threshold stop ends the window unconditionally.
- **After recovery, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed push.** Once the threshold conditions have cleared (retired generations drained back to four or fewer, cleanup pauses back at or below 100 ms, and the full health set returned to baseline), Alex may open a new window. That fresh window, by rule, permits exactly one fully observed push. "Fully observed" means p99, heap, active-generation count, retired-generation count, cleanup-pause duration, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts are all monitored across the entire push window and the post-push drain. No second push may be launched inside that window until the observation window closes cleanly.
- **Another window requires a separate fresh decision after that push returns the full health set to baseline.** The one fully observed push permitted under the fresh window does not authorize a return to steady-state cadence, and it does not roll over into a second push on its own. They are not pause-class signals and they are not warmup-style signals; on any one of them the call is rollback, not hold-and-verify, not bounded single-push resume, and not a fresh window. The rollback set in this note is the same set as the 2024-05-30 note and the 2024-06-18 note; this note only restates it alongside the window rule.

Do not collapse the two: a window stop does not escalate to rollback unless one of the rollback conditions fires, and a single rollback-class signal does not get treated as a window stop.
- **Ownership boundary is unchanged.** Alex remains the primary owner of the window-opening decision. Wes remains the practical backup and may open a window only when Alex is unreachable. Mapped operators remain the ones who execute single-file pushes inside an open window; they do not open windows and they do not make rollback calls. Infra review's accepted boundary on 2024-06-17 (resume prerequisites holding continuously for 10 minutes, identical active-generation sets across all canary pods, cleanup-pause p99 strictly below 100 ms before resuming pushes) still gates entry into a fresh window; the window rule above describes what happens inside a window once those prerequisites are satisfied, and it does not relax them.
- **Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged.** The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) still applies. This note supersedes the per-push-approval framing in the 2024-06-18 note and replaces it with the owner-led window rule; it does not relax canary gating, does not authorize laptop deploys, does not change the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision.

## Canary note — 2024-10-07 (aligned thresholds, recovery-push rule, and the 103 ms stopped-window example) — REFERENCE ACCEPTED 2024-10-08

Context: On 2024-10-07 Alex and Wes re-ran the canary reference session and re-stated the aligned thresholds and the recovery sequence that have been in force under the 2024-05-30 and 2024-07-25 notes. Wes and Alex walked through a real recorded case from the second September push that surfaced the boundary on cleanup-pause duration, and that case is recorded below as the canonical stopped-window example. The 94 ms recovery-push exercise scheduled for 2024-10-08 has been completed; Hema accepted the exercised canary-response reference for future use by Wes and other mapped operators, and that exercise and acceptance are recorded in the 2024-10-08 sub-note below.

**Aligned thresholds (re-stated, unchanged from 2024-05-30 / 2024-07-25):**

- **Retired generations must remain at four or fewer.** Anything above four means the previous generation has not drained into the active set; pushes pause, do not escalate to rollback on this signal alone.
- **Cleanup pauses must remain at or below 100 ms.** Anything above 100 ms means the stop-the-world matcher cleanup is no longer cheap enough to ride alongside canary traffic; pushes pause, do not escalate to rollback on this signal alone.
- **The full health set must return to baseline after every push.** Between pushes inside a window, retired-generation count, cleanup-pause p99, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts must all be back at baseline. A push that returns the full health set to baseline is what permits the next push; a push that does not return the full health set to baseline ends the window.
- **Exceeding either ceiling stops the window.** The window stops the moment retired generations accumulate above four, or the moment a cleanup pause above 100 ms is observed. Stop is automatic; no further pushes land for the remainder of that window, no matter how clean the rest of the health set looks. Stop does not escalate to rollback on its own — rollback is decided by the rollback set below.

**Recovery sequence (re-stated, unchanged from 2024-07-25):**

- After a threshold stop, retired generations drain back to four or fewer, cleanup pauses come back at or below 100 ms, and the full health set returns to baseline. Only then does a fresh opening decision become available.
- A fresh opening decision permits exactly one fully observed recovery push. "Fully observed" means p99, heap, active-generation count, retired-generation count, cleanup-pause duration, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts are all monitored across the entire push window and the post-push drain.
- The recovery push does not reopen a multi-push window. No second push may be launched inside that fresh window until the observation window closes cleanly and the full health set returns to baseline again. A subsequent window requires a separate fresh opening decision after that recovery push's observation window closes.

**Rollback set (unchanged):** Active-generation inconsistency across pods, route divergence from the previous-generation table, dropped series off baseline, reload failure, or restart — on any one, the call is rollback via the deploy pipeline. Pause and rollback remain different actions; do not collapse the two.

**Recorded example — second September push (correctly classified as a stopped window):**

- The push changed the intended single file (single-file push inside an open window).
- Retired generations peaked at four. (At the ceiling, not above it.)
- Cleanup pause was 103 ms. (Above the 100 ms ceiling by 3 ms.)
- The window stopped immediately on the cleanup-pause observation.
- Full health returned seven minutes later: retired generations back at four or fewer, cleanup pauses back at or below 100 ms, the rest of the full health set (active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, restarts) back at baseline.
- No additional push occurred inside that window. The next push required a fresh opening decision and a new window.

Wes classified this case as a **stopped window**, not a completed safe push and not a reopened window. The classification is the point: a push that returns the full health set to baseline is a completed safe push, a push that ends with a threshold stop is a stopped window, and a stopped window does not authorize further pushes inside the same window even after recovery. The recovery sequence above is what governs what comes next.

**103 ms stopped-window classification rules (for the next responder):**

- A push is a **completed safe push** only if every signal in the full health set — retired-generation count ≤ 4, cleanup-pause p99 ≤ 100 ms, active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, restarts — returns to baseline. The 103 ms observation alone disqualifies the September push from this classification regardless of how clean the rest of the health set looked.
- A push is a **stopped window** if either ceiling was exceeded during the push, even by a small margin and even if everything else in the health set returned to baseline. 103 ms vs the 100 ms ceiling is a stopped window, not a near-miss safe push.
- A stopped window is **not** automatically a reopened window after recovery. Recovery makes a fresh opening decision available; it does not carry the prior window forward, and it does not authorize further pushes inside the prior window. The next push requires a fresh decision and a new window.
- The seven-minute full-health recovery time on this case is descriptive, not prescriptive. A future stopped window may take longer or shorter to drain; the rule is full-health-return-to-baseline, not a fixed recovery duration.

**Triggers that WOULD change the call (none fired on the September case):**

- A cleanup-pause observation at or below 100 ms while retired generations stayed at or below four: would have been a completed safe push, not a stopped window.
- An active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped-series movement, reload failure, or restart during the push: would have been rollback, not stop.
- A cleanup pause above 100 ms accompanied by retired-generation accumulation above four: still a stopped window, not a more severe classification.

**2024-10-08 — completed 94 ms recovery-push exercise and Hema's acceptance (closes the prior pending-validation marker):**

- Alex and Wes ran the metrics-router reference exercise on the recorded 94 ms recovery push. Wes identified this push as the one fully observed push authorized by Alex's fresh post-recovery decision, verified that retired generations stayed at four or fewer and that the full health set returned to baseline, and did not describe it as a reopened window. The classification matches the 103 ms rule above: the 94 ms observation is at or below the 100 ms cleanup-pause ceiling, the prior window did not roll forward, and the fresh window contained exactly one fully observed push.
- Hema accepted the exercised canary-response reference for future use by Wes and other mapped operators. The reference is now part of the canary-response record; no change is proposed to the aligned thresholds, the recovery sequence, or the rollback set, and Hema's acceptance does not move ownership of any rollback decision.
- Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged. The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) still applies. ## Canary note — 2023-08-16 (scheduled load-test label noise)

Context: Severity-3 cardinality canary fired while Cyrus was running a scheduled load test against metrics-router. Wes isolated the spike to an unbounded `experiment_id` label coming only from the load-test traffic, checked the deploy path, and confirmed the service itself was not regressing. Cyrus stopped the load test and the canary cleared without escalation or rollback. This note is for the next responder.

- **A cardinality canary during a known scheduled load test is expected to trip, not a service regression.** Before treating the alert as a metrics-router regression, confirm whether a scheduled load test is in progress (check #ops-loadtests / ask Cyrus / check the load-test calendar). If yes, do not rollback.
- **Isolate the label to the load-test traffic first.** Check whether the unbounded labels (`experiment_id`, `user_id`, `request_id`, anything tenant/key-shaped) are present only on load-test traffic or also on production traffic. If load-test-only, the spike is from the load generator, not from metrics-router.
- **Check the deploy path, but do not assume deploy is the cause.** A green canary + a recent config-only change + a load test in flight usually means the load test is the source. Wes's 2023-08-16 investigation pattern is the reference: isolate label → rule out deploy → rule out downstream → confirm load-test scope → ask the load-test owner to stop.
- **Coordinate with the load-test owner before stopping or rolling back.** Cyrus stops the load test on confirmation; do not rollback metrics-router without that conversation. Rollback during a load-test-driven alert is the wrong action and creates a second incident.
- **No cardinality-control project, no ownership change.** This is a documentation note so the next responder does the same fast isolation rather than treating noise as a regression. Cardinality controls on load-test labels are tracked separately and are not owned by the canary response.

## Canary note — 2023-09-07 (post-canary CPU-only warmup, not a rollback)

Context: Second day of metrics-router data after the config-checksum cleanup canary. The affected AZ's CPU uplift has settled to ~2–3%, checksum-cache invalidations are back near baseline, cache-cardinality stayed flat, p99 stayed inside the normal 182–188 ms band, error rate stayed at 0.02%, dropped writes stayed clean, and rollup-service lag stayed flat. No user-visible signal moved. Closing as checksum-cache warmup after the config-checksum cleanup, not a rollback case.

- **A small residual CPU uplift in one AZ on the first 1–2 days after a config-checksum cleanup is warmup, not a regression.** Cache entries rehydrate under the new checksum regime; CPU cost comes back to baseline as the cache refills. Do not rollback on CPU alone if p99, error rate, dropped writes, cache-cardinality, and downstream lag are all flat.
- **Re-check the four user-visible signals before any rollback action.** p99 (must stay in the 182–188 ms band), error rate (~0.02% baseline), dropped writes (clean), and rollup-service lag (flat). If all four are flat, the rollout is fine and the residual CPU is warmup.
- **Checksum-cache invalidations returning near baseline is the confirming signal.** Elevated invalidations dominated by `checksum-mismatch-on-read` would be a different problem (would reconsider the rollout). Invalidations back near baseline + cache-cardinality flat means the cache is settling, not churning.
- **Triggers that WOULD change the call:** cache-hit ratio in the affected AZ dropping materially; checksum-cache invalidations dominated by `checksum-mismatch-on-read`; any of the four user-visible signals (p99 / error rate / dropped writes / rollup-service lag) moving off baseline. None of these fired on 2023-09-07.
- **No second-day page expected.** This note exists so the next on-call does not treat CPU-only post-canary warmup as an automatic rollback. If the four user-visible signals stay flat, leave the rollout in place and let the cache finish warming.

## Canary note — 2023-09-27 (parser-cache warmup during canary, not a rollback)

Context: Tiny metrics-router parser cleanup canary warmup ran on 2023-09-26; full rollout through the deploy pipeline finished on 2023-09-27 and stayed quiet. p99 stayed in the normal band, error rate held at 0.02%, dropped writes stayed clean, rollup-service lag stayed flat, and parser-cache misses did not repeat on full rollout. - **Parser-cache misses stopping on their own is the confirming signal.** Parser-cache misses that recede as the cache fills under the new parser path means the cache is settling, not churning. Continued parser-cache misses at canary traffic level with any of the four user-visible signals moving off baseline is a different problem.
- **Triggers that WOULD change the call:** any of the four user-visible signals (p99 / error rate / dropped writes / rollup-service lag) moving off baseline during the warmup window; parser-cache misses that do not recede as the canary holds; a parser-cache miss rate that grows against steady canary traffic instead of decaying. None of these fired on 2023-09-27.
- **Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged.** The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) and the canary gating criteria still apply. This note only describes how to interpret a parser-cache warmup within those requirements; it does not relax any of them.
- **No parser-cache warmup page expected for a future parser-cleanup canary.** If the four user-visible signals stay flat, hold the rollout through the warmup and let the parser cache finish warming.

"Stop" means no further pushes land via the deploy pipeline for the remainder of that window, no matter how clean the rest of the health set looks. Stop is automatic, not a judgement call; the next push requires a fresh opening decision from Alex and a new window. A threshold stop does not escalate to rollback on its own — rollback is decided by the rollback set at the end of this note — but a threshold stop ends the window unconditionally.
- **After recovery, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed push.** Once the threshold conditions have cleared (retired generations drained back to four or fewer, cleanup pauses back at or below 100 ms, and the full health set returned to baseline), Alex may open a new window. That fresh window, by rule, permits exactly one fully observed push. "Fully observed" means p99, heap, active-generation count, retired-generation count, cleanup-pause duration, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts are all monitored across the entire push window and the post-push drain. No second push may be launched inside that window until the observation window closes cleanly.
- **Another window requires a separate fresh decision after that push returns the full health set to baseline.** The one fully observed push permitted under the fresh window does not authorize a return to steady-state cadence, and it does not roll over into a second push on its own. A second window requires a separate fresh opening decision from Alex, and that decision is only available after the first push's full observation window has closed and the full health set has returned to baseline. The cycle (threshold stop → recovery → fresh decision → exactly one fully observed push → full health set back to baseline → fresh decision → next window) is the only path forward; the cycle does not compress into a single decision and the cycle does not skip steps.
- **Consistency, parity, dropped-series, reload, and restart failures remain rollback conditions.** Rollback via the deploy pipeline is required on any of: active-generation inconsistency across pods, route divergence from the previous-generation table, dropped series off baseline, reload failure, or restart. These five are rollback-class signals. They are not pause-class signals and they are not warmup-style signals; on any one of them the call is rollback, not hold-and-verify, not bounded single-push resume, and not a fresh window. The rollback set in this note is the same set as the 2024-05-30 note and the 2024-06-18 note; this note only restates it alongside the window rule.
- **Pause and rollback are different actions.** A window stop (retired gens > 4 or cleanup pause > 100 ms) ends the window and requires a fresh opening decision from Alex before pushes resume. A rollback condition (active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped series, reload failure, restart) routes through the deploy pipeline to revert. Do not collapse the two: a window stop does not escalate to rollback unless one of the rollback conditions fires, and a single rollback-class signal does not get treated as a window stop.
- **Ownership boundary is unchanged.** Alex remains the primary owner of the window-opening decision. Wes remains the practical backup and may open a window only when Alex is unreachable. Mapped operators remain the ones who execute single-file pushes inside an open window; they do not open windows and they do not make rollback calls. Infra review's accepted boundary on 2024-06-17 (resume prerequisites holding continuously for 10 minutes, identical active-generation sets across all canary pods, cleanup-pause p99 strictly below 100 ms before resuming pushes) still gates entry into a fresh window; the window rule above describes what happens inside a window once those prerequisites are satisfied, and it does not relax them.
- **Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged.** The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) still applies. This note supersedes the per-push-approval framing in the 2024-06-18 note and replaces it with the owner-led window rule; it does not relax canary gating, does not authorize laptop deploys, does not change the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision.

## Canary note — 2024-10-07 (aligned thresholds, recovery-push rule, and the 103 ms stopped-window example) — REFERENCE ACCEPTED 2024-10-08

Context: On 2024-10-07 Alex and Wes re-ran the canary reference session and re-stated the aligned thresholds and the recovery sequence that have been in force under the 2024-05-30 and 2024-07-25 notes. Wes and Alex walked through a real recorded case from the second September push that surfaced the boundary on cleanup-pause duration, and that case is recorded below as the canonical stopped-window example. The 94 ms recovery-push exercise scheduled for 2024-10-08 has been completed; Hema accepted the exercised canary-response reference for future use by Wes and other mapped operators, and that exercise and acceptance are recorded in the 2024-10-08 sub-note below.

**Aligned thresholds (re-stated, unchanged from 2024-05-30 / 2024-07-25):**

- **Retired generations must remain at four or fewer.** Anything above four means the previous generation has not drained into the active set; pushes pause, do not escalate to rollback on this signal alone.
- **Cleanup pauses must remain at or below 100 ms.** Anything above 100 ms means the stop-the-world matcher cleanup is no longer cheap enough to ride alongside canary traffic; pushes pause, do not escalate to rollback on this signal alone.
- **The full health set must return to baseline after every push.** Between pushes inside a window, retired-generation count, cleanup-pause p99, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts must all be back at baseline. A push that returns the full health set to baseline is what permits the next push; a push that does not return the full health set to baseline ends the window.
- **Exceeding either ceiling stops the window.** The window stops the moment retired generations accumulate above four, or the moment a cleanup pause above 100 ms is observed. Stop is automatic; no further pushes land for the remainder of that window, no matter how clean the rest of the health set looks. Stop does not escalate to rollback on its own — rollback is decided by the rollback set below.

**Recovery sequence (re-stated, unchanged from 2024-07-25):**

- After a threshold stop, retired generations drain back to four or fewer, cleanup pauses come back at or below 100 ms, and the full health set returns to baseline. Only then does a fresh opening decision become available.
- A fresh opening decision permits exactly one fully observed recovery push. "Fully observed" means p99, heap, active-generation count, retired-generation count, cleanup-pause duration, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts are all monitored across the entire push window and the post-push drain.
- The recovery push does not reopen a multi-push window. No second push may be launched inside that fresh window until the observation window closes cleanly and the full health set returns to baseline again. A subsequent window requires a separate fresh opening decision after that recovery push's observation window closes.

**Rollback set (unchanged):** Active-generation inconsistency across pods, route divergence from the previous-generation table, dropped series off baseline, reload failure, or restart — on any one, the call is rollback via the deploy pipeline. Pause and rollback remain different actions; do not collapse the two.

**Recorded example — second September push (correctly classified as a stopped window):**

- The push changed the intended single file (single-file push inside an open window).
- Retired generations peaked at four. (At the ceiling, not above it.)
- Cleanup pause was 103 ms. (Above the 100 ms ceiling by 3 ms.)
- The window stopped immediately on the cleanup-pause observation.
- Full health returned seven minutes later: retired generations back at four or fewer, cleanup pauses back at or below 100 ms, the rest of the full health set (active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, restarts) back at baseline.
- No additional push occurred inside that window. The next push required a fresh opening decision and a new window.

Wes classified this case as a **stopped window**, not a completed safe push and not a reopened window. The classification is the point: a push that returns the full health set to baseline is a completed safe push, a push that ends with a threshold stop is a stopped window, and a stopped window does not authorize further pushes inside the same window even after recovery. The recovery sequence above is what governs what comes next.

**103 ms stopped-window classification rules (for the next responder):**

- A push is a **completed safe push** only if every signal in the full health set — retired-generation count ≤ 4, cleanup-pause p99 ≤ 100 ms, active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, restarts — returns to baseline. The 103 ms observation alone disqualifies the September push from this classification regardless of how clean the rest of the health set looked.
- A push is a **stopped window** if either ceiling was exceeded during the push, even by a small margin and even if everything else in the health set returned to baseline. 103 ms vs the 100 ms ceiling is a stopped window, not a near-miss safe push.
- A stopped window is **not** automatically a reopened window after recovery. Recovery makes a fresh opening decision available; it does not carry the prior window forward, and it does not authorize further pushes inside the prior window. The next push requires a fresh decision and a new window.
- The seven-minute full-health recovery time on this case is descriptive, not prescriptive. A future stopped window may take longer or shorter to drain; the rule is full-health-return-to-baseline, not a fixed recovery duration.

**Triggers that WOULD change the call (none fired on the September case):**

- A cleanup-pause observation at or below 100 ms while retired generations stayed at or below four: would have been a completed safe push, not a stopped window.
- An active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped-series movement, reload failure, or restart during the push: would have been rollback, not stop.
- A cleanup pause above 100 ms accompanied by retired-generation accumulation above four: still a stopped window, not a more severe classification.

**2024-10-08 — completed 94 ms recovery-push exercise and Hema's acceptance (closes the prior pending-validation marker):**

- Alex and Wes ran the metrics-router reference exercise on the recorded 94 ms recovery push. Wes identified this push as the one fully observed push authorized by Alex's fresh post-recovery decision, verified that retired generations stayed at four or fewer and that the full health set returned to baseline, and did not describe it as a reopened window. The classification matches the 103 ms rule above: the 94 ms observation is at or below the 100 ms cleanup-pause ceiling, the prior window did not roll forward, and the fresh window contained exactly one fully observed push.
- Hema accepted the exercised canary-response reference for future use by Wes and other mapped operators. The reference is now part of the canary-response record; no change is proposed to the aligned thresholds, the recovery sequence, or the rollback set, and Hema's acceptance does not move ownership of any rollback decision.
- Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged. The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) still applies. This 2024-10-08 sub-note closes the prior pending-validation marker; it does not relax canary gating, does not authorize laptop deploys, does not change the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision.

## Canary note — 2025-04-15 (host-maintenance rejoin gate, durable rule for rejoining instances)

Context: The 2025-04-12 response to a stale-generation alert on metrics-router is closed and was correct. The stale-generation debrief confirmed that the alert fired correctly and that the response actions were the right ones. The debrief surfaced one missing piece in the canary-response runbook: an explicit rule for what happens when an instance rejoins after host maintenance. Alex, Hema, and Nadia agreed that a rejoining instance must remain isolated until it reports the current active generation, and that a missing generation report does not count as healthy. Once the rejoining instance reports the current generation, the ordinary consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health checks must all pass before isolation is released. This note adds that durable rejoin gate. It does not change ownership, does not create or open an owner-led window, and does not authorize a configuration push.

- **A rejoining instance is isolated until it reports the current active generation.** "Rejoining" covers any instance coming back into the fleet after host maintenance, host reboot, OS patching, hypervisor migration, or any other event that takes the instance out of steady-state and then returns it. While the instance is rejoining, treat it as not part of the active fleet for consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health decisions. Isolation ends only when the instance reports the current active generation on its own. A missing generation report — no report at all, an empty report, a stale generation, or a generation that does not match the active set — does not count as reporting the current active generation and the instance stays isolated.
- **A missing generation report is not healthy.** Do not infer health from the absence of a generation report, do not infer health from "the instance is up" alone, and do not infer health from liveness or readiness probes that do not include the active generation. Treat the missing report as the same class of failure as a stale generation report: the instance has not rejoined the active set and the isolation holds. The next on-call does not need a new decision to keep the instance isolated; the rule above is the default.
- **After the rejoining instance reports the current active generation, the ordinary checks gate isolation release.** Only after the rejoining instance reports the current active generation do consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health checks run against it. Isolation release requires all of the following, in this order: active-generation consistency (the rejoining instance reports the same active generation as the rest of the fleet, no mixed-generation state across pods), route parity (deliveries from the rejoining instance match the previous-generation route table for the same label set), dropped series (clean against the pre-canary baseline, no new series dropped because of the rejoining instance), route delivery (the rejoining instance routes the same way as the rest of the fleet on a held label set), and the rest of the health set (cleanup-pause p99 at or below 100 ms, retired-generation count at or below four, reload failures at or below the pre-canary rate, restarts at or below the pre-canary rate). If any of those is off, isolation stays in place; resolve the off-state first, then re-run the gate.
- **The rejoin gate is independent of the canary gating, the window rule, and the rollback set.** The rejoin gate above governs when a single rejoining instance leaves isolation; it is not a canary-response decision and it does not interact with the three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed). It does not open an owner-led window, does not authorize a single-file configuration push, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision. Active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped-series movement, reload failure, or restart during a rejoin still routes through the deploy pipeline on the rollback criteria from the prior notes.
- **Ownership boundary is unchanged.** Alex remains the primary owner of the canary response and the window-opening decision. Wes remains the practical backup. Mapped operators remain the ones who execute single-file pushes inside an open window. Host-maintenance rejoins are not configuration pushes; the deploy-pipeline-only rule, the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and the laptop-deploy prohibition all remain in force. The rejoin gate is a read-and-isolate rule, not a write-side rule.
- **Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged.** The three-step canary response, the aligned thresholds (retired-generation count ≤ 4, cleanup-pause p99 ≤ 100 ms), the recovery sequence, the owner-led window rule, the rollback set, the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, the replay-mirror separation, and the deploy-pipeline-only rule all stay as written. This note only adds the durable rejoin gate for rejoining instances after host maintenance; it does not relax canary gating, does not authorize laptop deploys, does not create or open an owner-led window, does not authorize a configuration push, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision.

Oncall can read "rejected" as a hard failure and page/escalate when the correct posture is "no action, retries will succeed." Either say "rejected with retryable backpressure (queue-full)" or lead with "retryable queue-full."

Got the seed. It already defines the four bullet categories (new label keys, risky families, sample distinct counts, alert-source semantics) plus the live/validation boundary and explicit non-goals — that's the basis for the checklist. Drafting now as plain text.

Title: Cardinality Guardrails — first control slice: PR/review checklist

Use this on any metrics-router or shard-keeper change that adds label keys, modifies a relabel rule, or changes the cardinality shape of an existing label family. Pass = the reviewer can tick every numbered item. Fail = any single item untickable; the change does not get the cardinality preflight green check, regardless of code-side LGTM.

PREFLIGHT TRIGGER (one of these is true; otherwise this checklist does not apply)

[ ] The change introduces a label key not already in the router's known label inventory for the affected metric path.
[ ] The change modifies a relabel rule, label family, or label-schema map in metrics-router or shard-keeper.
[ ] The change touches rollup-service label handling in a way that could shift the cardinality shape seen by the consumer side.

If none apply, do not run this checklist; this is not a generic review template.

A. NEW LABEL KEYS (treated as additive cardinality risk until bounded)

[ ] PASS — Every new label key is listed in the PR description with: name, intended value space, who owns the value set (service / tenant / request / external), and the metric path it appears on.
[ ] PASS — Distinct-value counts are attached for each new key from a short-window sample of the path the change touches. A "will be bounded in practice" claim without a sample is a fail.
[ ] FAIL if — A new key is added with no sample, no owner, or an external/unowned value set and no bounded-cardinality argument.

B. RISKY LABEL FAMILIES

[ ] PASS — The PR has been scanned against the known risky-family list: request-scoped IDs, user/path/email-derived fields, free-form tag values, raw URLs, and any label whose value set is not owned by the service emitting it. Each hit is either removed, justified with a bounded-cardinality argument, or explicitly called out as out-of-scope-but-tracked.
[ ] PASS — If a risky-family label survives, the PR names where the sample distinct-count threshold lives for "risky" and who owns tuning it (current open question per the seed; until resolved, surface the open question in the PR, do not bury it).
[ ] FAIL if — A request-scoped ID, raw URL, or external/unowned value set is added without a bounded-cardinality argument. This is the most common reject path.

C. SAMPLE DISTINCT COUNTS

[ ] PASS — A short-window distinct-count sample is attached for the affected path, per new or modified key. The window, source path, and tenant mix are named.
[ ] PASS — Any sample whose distinct count is unbounded in practice (grows with traffic or tenants) is flagged in the PR, not only in the preflight output. Flagged = labeled as risky + an explicit bounded-or-not call from the owner.
[ ] FAIL if — Distinct-count sample is missing for any new or modified key, OR a flagged unbounded sample ships without an owner call.

D. ALERT-SOURCE SEMANTICS (the validation-only rule)

[ ] PASS — Any cardinality finding the preflight emits is classified at the source as either live or validation-only. The classification lives on the finding itself, not in a separate doc.
[ ] PASS — Validation-only findings are routed to the mismatch-investigation queue — the same queue as live findings. They are not dropped, not hidden, and not auto-resolved.
[ ] PASS — The replay/mirror validation panel remains visible on the on-call landing page. This PR does not propose hiding it, suppressing it, or de-emphasizing it. Subtitle convention is preserved: "Source: replay validation — not a live-path rollback signal."
[ ] FAIL if — A validation-only finding is treated as "safe to ignore," discarded, or auto-resolved without investigation. Validation-only is scope (no live rollback off it), not permissi…

shard-keeper runbook index entry for the April 18, 2023 outage (canonical incident ID INC-2023-04-18-001).

What happened.
- Trigger: a label-name change originating from an earlier Nadia dashboard work landed in shard-keeper without the matching rollup-service consumer picking up the new name.
- Effect: every shard-keeper-backed alert that keyed off the new label went silent on the cause side while every symptom alert that did not key off it fired normally. Symptom alerts loud, cause alerts silent — the alert-source split is the primary diagnostic signature.
- Investigation: initial hours chased a network-layer red herring before the label-name diff inside shard-keeper was identified as the cause.
- Impact: ingestion was impaired for approximately the entire incident window. No data loss.
- Recovery: shard-keeper was rolled back. The rollback path was shakier than it should have been; this is recorded as a follow-up, not as part of normal rollback behavior.
- Severity and duration: sev2, ~5h45m total window.
- Responder: Alex (primary on-call); Hema was not paged during the active window (a judgment call that was later questioned in the postmortem review); Cyrus paged at the right hour.

Why this entry exists.
- The label-parity gap between shard-keeper and rollup-service is the durable lesson. A green metrics-router canary on a label-name change does not substitute for downstream consumer parity.
- The symptom-alert-loud / cause-alert-silent failure mode is the signature to recognize in any future label-parity regression, including replay/mirror validation cases.
- The network-layer red herring is recorded so the next on-call does not lose the first few hours to the same misdiagnosis.

Durable follow-ups (closed).
- Label-name parity rule encoded in the shard-keeper runbook: shard-keeper label-name changes require rollup-service parity before promotion. Pre-push sync: Nadia (alerting / dashboards) + Cyrus team (rollup-service). Recorded in rb_shard_keeper_label_parity.
- 5/22 audit closed the parity gap.
- 6/6 cutover push (11:00) cleared the residual parity debt.
- 6/27 verification at 85% clean (labels + restart path).

Durable follow-ups (open).
- Cross-service parity rollback owner for the case where both shard-keeper and rollup-service are involved in a single label-name change: not separately mapped at the runbook-header level. Exception route currently points at "mapped service owner" but the cross-service case routes back through the label-parity pre-push sync.
- Postmortem authorship split intact (Nadia = postmortem process; Alex = cross-service failure-case reviewer; Wes = responder paths).

Pointers.
- shard-keeper rollback procedure: rb_shard_keeper_rollback.
- Label-parity rule and pre-push sync: rb_shard_keeper_label_parity.
- Cardinality Guardrails preflight (live vs validation source classification, parity check): rb_1789206351936 (under metrics-router; cross-service, not ownable to a single service header).

Resonates with.
- Apr 14, 2026 shard-keeper / rollup-service outage (postmortem doc_postmortem_apr14_outage, dated 2026-04-21): same failure-mode family, different year, different service header.
- 2023-10-30 incident-scope patch and the related validation-only-evidence question; first-cut Cardinality Guardrails preflight codified the live/validation source distinction partly in response to the kind of symptom/cause split observed here.

Owner and standing.
- shard-keeper primary: alex. shard-keeper backup: nadia.
- This index entry is informational; the operational responses live in rb_shard_keeper_rollback and rb_shard_keeper_label_parity. Do not edit those entries from this one — append a dated note and route the change through the entry that owns the procedure.

messages.content:
[2026-03-26T12:08:00-04:00] The Lantern strategy meeting is complete. After reviewing the frozen operating evidence and the divergent Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce requests, Hema and Theo decided that Lantern will become a Sphere product-platform line effective April 1, 2026 rather than remain only a narrow add-on. Through March 31, the existing authorization and operating terms remain unchanged.

Effective April 1, Iris owns the customer promise, adoption criteria, and UI interpretation. I retain freshness, tenant-isolation, authorization-denial, latency, and error monitoring plus the shared data contract, source-registration safety gates, and failure-mode review. Product Engineering owns implementation. Lantern explains provenance-backed service and system state, Cardinality Guardrails owns pipeline limits and cost signals, and the owner map remains the source of published responsibility. Lantern will not produce release-readiness judgments or employee-performance interpretations. Any new source type must enter through shared registration with tenant-scoped authorization before source access, required provenance and source timestamps, explicit unknown for stale or missing input, excluded-field checks, and a successful safety rerun before customer use.

From April 1 through September 30, Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce—and no other accounts—are authorized for continued read-only access through the shared authorization wrapper, limited to provenance-backed deploy movement, published service ownership, timestamped incident-load summaries, and explicit unknown states. No additional account, cost data, CSV export, raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifier or comparison, inferred or unpublished ownership, internal-only fallback data, or write capability is authorized.

An authorization-wrapper bypass, adapter call after denial, cross-tenant material, stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown, deploy event without required provenance, unpublished ownership, incident-load summary without its source timestamp, exposure of any excluded field, or loss of read-only enforcement immediately suspends both accounts pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check. Latency and other errors do not independently suspend access unless they cause one of those violations.

Convert “Lantern platform boundary proposal — March 26 strategy review” into the final decision record, including the frozen evidence reviewed, and append the transition decision to “Lantern October 8 final-review decision record,” clearly preserving the current terms through March 31 and dating the new direction, role split, and access terms to April 1.

arguments.body:
Mosaic capacity response — final decision record

Last refreshed: 2026-01-08 (qualifying 19.78M / 90-minute staged replay result; prior refresh 2025-12-11 forecast update)
Document role: single current record of the Mosaic scale-response cycle — prior still-true evidence, current ownership split, the new forecast, the replay requirement, the qualified accepted-batch diagnostic, and the still-open production-evidence condition.

================================================================
1. STATUS
================================================================

- The broader Mosaic scale-response cycle REMAINS OPEN.
- NO capacity-related production window is open or authorized.
- The 19.78M / 90-minute staged replay HAS BEEN EXECUTED and QUALIFIED as the binding precondition for any capacity-related production window above 16.0M pts/min — see Section 11 below.
- Qualifying the replay supplies the required STAGED EVIDENCE. It does NOT itself open or authorize a capacity-related production window.
- DIRECT PRODUCTION EVIDENCE and a later CLOSEOUT DECISION are still pending.

================================================================
2. OWNERSHIP (CURRENT)
================================================================

- Metrics-router PRIMARY: Wes
    - Owns implementation.
    - Owns load-test evidence.
    - Owns any later opening decision for any capacity-related production window.
- Metrics-router BACKUP: Alex
    - Covers the opening decision ONLY if Wes is unavailable.
    - Remains responsible, in every case, for the cross-service invariant and the failure-mode boundary.
- Rollup-service capacity and parity evidence: Cyrus and Roman (retained).
- Queue and refusal alert semantics: Nadia (retained).

Note on the ownership flip: prior to the 2025-12-05 metrics-router ownership review, Alex was primary and Wes was backup. As of the 2025-12-11 refresh, ownership is Wes-primary / Alex-backup as set out above. The role boundaries above are the operative ones from this date forward; any prior block in this record that described an earlier ownership state is preserved below for the historical record but does not govern going forward.

================================================================
3. NEW FORECAST (2025-12-11, from Mosaic Commerce account team)
================================================================

- Effective January 20, 2026, the expected Mosaic Commerce peak rises from 16.0M to 17.2M data points per minute.
- This triggered a fresh 90-MINUTE STAGED REPLAY at 19.78M data points per minute — 15% above the new 17.2M peak — using the FORECAST tenant distribution, batch-size distribution, and burst pattern.
- The replay was scheduled for Thursday, January 8, 2026, 10:00–11:30 AM ET (Wes, Cyrus, Roman, Nadia, Alex).

================================================================
4. REPLAY REQUIREMENT (BINDING FOR THE 19.78M REPLAY)
================================================================

The 19.78M replay qualified only if it satisfied EVERY one of the following conditions throughout the full 90-minute window. Any single failure would have disqualified the replay.

(A) Numeric 5-minute stops — must NOT trip for 5 consecutive minutes:
    - q_wait_p99 > 400 ms
    - retry_q_full > 0.005  (i.e., 0.5%)

(B) Tenant limit:
    - No tenant exceeds 64 pending batches at any time.

(C) Accepted-batch:
    - Every accepted batch reconciles to exactly one terminal result.
    - No accepted batch is lost.

(D) Cross-service invariants — must each remain at baseline:
    - Consistency
    - Parity
    - Dropped-series
    - Route
    - Shard-keeper lease
    - Rollup-service
    - Full-health

================================================================
5. QUALIFIED ACCEPTED-BATCH DIAGNOSTIC (PROSPECTIVE)
================================================================

- As of 2025-11-17, the metrics-router accepted-batch diagnostic is QUALIFIED for prospective production observation.
    - Supplied by: Wes (implementation + executed evidence) and Nadia (reconciliation evidence + diagnostic design).
    - Scope: 25,000 injected crash-and-restart runs, including the previously missing case (process exit AFTER requeue intent was durably recorded but BEFORE the replacement transport attempt was linked); coverage included both one consecutive requeue and two consecutive requeues.
    - Result: recovery retained the same durable accepted_batch_id across the crash-and-restart boundary; every replacement transport attempt was linked to the original accepted-batch identity BEFORE dispatch; each accepted batch reconciled to exactly one terminal result; pre-acceptance refusals stayed outside the accepted-batch population; raw accepted_batch_id and transport-attempt identities stayed OUT of metric labels; the permissioned diagnostic performed the reconciliation.
- The diagnostic was used during the 19.78M replay to observe the accepted-batch condition (Section 4C).
- The qualification is PROSPECTIVE ONLY. It does not retroactively establish whether any accepted batch was lost on 2025-10-06.

================================================================
6. PRODUCTION CONTROL (UNCHANGED)
================================================================

- Global queue: 2,048 batches.
- Per-tenant pending-batch limit: 64.
- Backpressure model: retryable pre-acceptance refusal for excess work.
- Raw accepted_batch_id and transport-attempt identities stay out of metric labels; pre-acceptance refusals stay outside the accepted-batch population.

================================================================
7. ALERTING (CARRIED FORWARD)
================================================================

- Nadia's alert v2 — q_wait_p99{src}>400 cause, retry_q_full{src}>0.005 symptom; 5-min window; src ∈ {live_prod, staged, replay}; halts active stage; live_prod pages — remains NOT LIVE in prod.
- Until alert v2 is live, the 5-min stop conditions in Section 4A remain the operative gates.
- Owner: Nadia. Scope unchanged.

================================================================
8. PRIOR EVIDENCE STILL BINDING (HISTORICAL, RESTATED)
================================================================

The following prior evidence remains true and is restated here as the operative baseline that the cycle continues to hold against:

- 2025-09-09 — Nadia alert v2 semantics defined (see Section 7).
- 2025-09-12..15 — Baselines held; owner-led production window planned.
- 2025-09-22..26 — Owner-led production window (Wes-implemented, Alex-reviewed): stepped 10% → 50% Wednesday, 100% health Thursday, monitor-only Friday. Production held clean ONLY through 14.2M pts/min. Mosaic ramp requires DIRECT PRODUCTION OBSERVATION ≥ 16.0M pts/min before any capacity increase can be claimed on production data.
- 2025-09-29 — Pre-event PE = no. Owner map at that time: Alex primary, Wes backup (subsequently flipped on 2025-12-05; see Section 2).
- 2025-09-24..26 — Mosaic ramp precondition stated: prod ≥ 16M direct observation needed before any further capacity step.
- 2025-10-06 — Production observation day. Accepted-batch loss condition remains UNESTABLISHED (no Oct 6 artifact was retroactively re-examined; the now-qualified diagnostic is designed for prospective observation, not retroactive proof).
- 2025-10-07 — Evidence review: did NOT close the broader scale-response cycle; no new production window opened; no owner-map change at that time.
- 2025-10-20 — PR #1988 (Wes) metrics-router accepted-batch evidence: race condition found in ~4/10,000 events between enqueue and ledger append; not lost at the time, but the reconcile invariant was broken; production unchanged. This is the failure mode the now-qualified diagnostic is designed to observe going forward.
- 2025-10-30 — Accepted-batch evidence checkpoint (Wes + Nadia): revised evidence passed the injected restart-between-acceptance-and-ledger case and the immediate-dispatch race; the remaining gap was the restart-during-requeue case, which 2025-11-17 then closed.
- 2025-11-17 — Restart-during-requeue evidence (Wes + Nadia): see Section 5. Qualified the diagnostic for prospective production observation.
- 2025-12-05 — Metrics-router ownership review: ownership flipped to Wes-primary / Alex-backup per Section 2. Other boundaries unchanged.
- 2025-12-11 — Forecast update from Mosaic Commerce account team (see Section 3) and the resulting 19.78M replay requirement.
- 2025-12-18 — Confirmation of the 19.78M / 90-min replay date: Thursday, January 8, 2026, 10:00–11:30 AM ET (Wes, Cyrus, Roman, Nadia, Alex).
- 18.4M staged above-forecast — had been exercised prior to 2025-10-06; staging is not a substitute for the production direct-observation requirement.

================================================================
9. WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS AND IS NOT
================================================================

- IS: the single current record of (a) prior still-true evidence, (b) the current Wes-primary / Alex-backup ownership split, (c) the new Mosaic Commerce forecast and the resulting 19.78M replay requirement, (d) the qualified accepted-batch diagnostic, (e) the qualifying 19.78M replay result of 2026-01-08 (see Section 11), and (f) the still-open production-evidence condition that gates any capacity-related production window.
- IS NOT: a closure of the scale-response cycle, an authorization of any production window, or any retroactive confirmation that production behaved correctly on 2025-10-06.

================================================================
10. NEXT PERMITTED MOVEMENT
================================================================

- The 19.78M / 90-min staged replay has now been executed and qualified — see Section 11. That supplies the required STAGED EVIDENCE.
- The qualifying replay does NOT itself open or authorize any capacity-related production window.
- Direct production evidence at ≥ 16.0M pts/min and a later closeout decision are still pending.
- On a qualifying production observation (every condition in Section 4 holds in live production at ≥ 16.0M pts/min), Wes — as metrics-router primary — may open any later capacity-related production window.
- The broader scale-response cycle closes only when a qualifying production observation is followed by group review of the staged + production evidence together, with all 5-min stops and cross-service invariants intact.
- Until that closure, this document and the #infra bounded summary are the operative references.

================================================================
11. 19.78M / 90-MINUTE STAGED REPLAY — RESULT (2026-01-08)
================================================================

Executed Thursday, January 8, 2026, 10:00–11:30 AM ET.

(A) Configuration
    - Target load: 19.78M data points per minute (15% above the new 17.2M forecast peak).
    - Duration: 90 minutes.
    - Workload: new forecast's tenant distribution, batch-size distribution, and burst pattern.

(B) Observed measurements (entire 90-minute window)
    - Queue-wait p99: 319 ms  (Section 4A limit: ≤ 400 ms — PASS)
    - Retryable queue-full responses: 0.17%  (Section 4A limit: ≤ 0.5% — PASS)
    - Highest tenant pending-batch count: 62  (Section 4B limit: ≤ 64 — PASS)

(C) Accepted-batch outcome (observed via the qualified accepted-batch diagnostic — Section 5)
    - Every accepted batch reconciled to exactly one terminal result.
    - No accepted batch was lost.  (Section 4C — PASS)

(D) Cross-service invariants — remained at baseline throughout the full 90 minutes:
    - Consistency — PASS
    - Parity — PASS
    - Dropped-series — PASS
    - Route — PASS
    - Shard-keeper lease — PASS
    - Rollup-service — PASS
    - Full-health — PASS

(E) Owner verifications
    - Cyrus and Roman verified rollup-service capacity and parity.
    - Nadia verified queue and refusal alert semantics.
    - Alex reviewed cross-service invariant and failure-mode boundaries; found no exception.

(F) Overall result
    - QUALIFYING REPLAY. Every condition in Section 4 held for the full 90 minutes.
    - The replay supplies the required STAGED EVIDENCE for the 19.78M / 90-minute precondition.
    - The qualifying replay does NOT itself open or authorize any capacity-related production window. Direct production evidence at ≥ 16.0M pts/min and a later closeout decision are still pending.
