## OTel collector 0.91 — production rollout note (2023-07-25 / 2023-07-27)

Closed out after the heightened watch ended. Final note from Yuki on 2023-07-27.

- **Outcome: production-clean.** Error rate stayed flat across the rollout
  and through the >72h follow-up window. CPU stayed flat. Heightened watch
  was closed on 2023-07-25 with no rollback needed.
- **Memory delta to record:** p95 memory settled ~5% above the pre-bump
  collector baseline. This is inside normal headroom and is not an alert
  threshold, but it is the new steady-state — record it so future bumps
  don't get re-litigated from scratch.
- **Future collector bumps still require:**
  1. A staging replay against representative prod-shaped load before any
     production push.
  2. An explicit memory watch during the production rollout window —
     p95 memory vs. the post-0.91 baseline (~5% above pre-0.91), not vs.
     the original pre-bump line.
  "Approved before" is not sufficient justification on its own; each bump
  must clear both gates above.

## OTel exporter retry — retry-only patch note (sha:0a91b7c, 2023-10-09)

Narrow note covering only the retry-only exporter change that has been quiet
in prod since 2023-10-09. Not a collector-wide tuning reference.

- **Scope:** OTLP HTTP exporter retry settings only. The `memory_limiter`
  configuration was deliberately left out of this patch and is tracked
  separately; do not conflate the two.
- **Exporter retry values applied:**
  - `retry_on_failure.max_interval` = 15s
  - `retry_on_failure.max_elapsed_time` = 5m
- **Post-deploy checks (run during the rollout window):**
  1. Dropped-writes counter — must remain flat vs. pre-patch baseline.
  2. Backpressure counters — must remain flat vs. pre-patch baseline.
  3. Retry log volume — observed lower ~24h into the prod deployment
     (2023-10-26); treat lower retry log volume as the expected steady
     state, not as an anomaly.
- **What this note does NOT cover:** batch processor sizing, queue tuning,
  `memory_limiter` thresholds, or any other collector-wide knobs. Those
  remain out of scope for this entry.

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the
operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without
hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real
  backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that
as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

Owner: alex. Backup: yuki.

## 2024-01-04 — ingest-edge staging rollback-drill hygiene

After-action from the 2024-01-03 ingest-edge staging rollback drill
(posted by Wes on 2024-01-04). Capturing while the gap is fresh. This
section covers staging-drill hygiene only and does not change production
ownership, the owner map, or anything in the cutover checklist above.

**Scope and boundaries (unchanged from the 2023-12-22 handoff):**
- Deploy-pipeline path only. Laptop deploys are out of scope for this
  drill class and bypass the canary path; do not generalize drill
  findings to laptop deploys.
- Wes can run daylight first-pass for the ingest-edge staging rollback
  drill solo. Production ownership stays with alex; the owner map is
  unchanged.
- shard-keeper is out of scope for this drill unless explicitly paired
  with the shard-keeper on-call. Do not touch shard-keeper state from a
  solo staging rollback drill.
- Unsafe or ambiguous signals escalate; do not interpret them in-place.

**The gap (only one, mundane but real):**
- The drill checklist did not explicitly call out verifying the
  load-test tag TTL and cleanup owner *before* the rollback-drill staging
  lane was opened. The drill still proceeded, but the omission is the
  kind of thing that ages into a real-world surprise, so it's worth
  capturing.

**Add to the staging rollback-drill checklist (before opening the lane):**
1. Confirm the load-test tag TTL in use and record it on the drill card.
   - If TTL is unknown, treat that as an unsafe signal and escalate
     before opening the staging lane.
2. Confirm the named cleanup owner for the load-test tag and record it
   on the drill card.
   - If no cleanup owner is identified, treat that as an unsafe signal
     and escalate before opening the staging lane.
3. Only after both are recorded should the rollback-drill staging lane
  be opened.

**What this does NOT change:**
- The Mar 17 prod cutover checklist above.
- The label-name / label-map alerting path (still tracked against Nadia's
  parity doc and written sign-off).
- The OTel collector 0.91 and OTel exporter retry-only sections.
- Production ownership, the owner map, or the backup designation.

## ingest-edge v2.19.4 — randomized Retry-After (1–3s) is now production behavior

**Status as of 2024-04-02:** ingest-edge v2.19.4 is at 100% in production.
Randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` is the production behavior;
this is not a temporary tuning knob and the service is not expected to
return to the baseline behavior.

**Production gates passed at full production (2024-04-02):**
- Peak retry rate: 129,000 attempts/sec
- p99 latency peak: 188 ms
- Queue depth peak: 75%
- Accepted throughput: 2.9% below baseline (within accepted envelope)
- 5xx rate: no increase vs. pre-rollout baseline

**Stop boundaries (treat any one of these as a stop-and-roll-back signal):**
- p99 latency ≥ 190 ms (in-body threshold; matches the gating language
  carried through the rollout). 188 ms at full prod was inside this.
- 5xx rate increase vs. pre-rollout baseline (none observed).
- Accepted throughput drop exceeding the accepted envelope (2.9% below
  baseline at full prod was inside this).
- Queue depth sustained above the operational ceiling (75% peak at full
  prod was inside this).

A stop boundary being hit is not a tuning exercise — it is a rollback
signal. Do not negotiate the threshold in the middle of an incident.

**Observed maxima from the rollout gates:**

| Gate  | Peak retries (attempts/sec) | p99 peak (ms) | Queue depth peak | Accepted throughput vs. baseline | 5xx change |
|-------|-----------------------------|---------------|------------------|----------------------------------|------------|
| 10%   | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update |
| 50%   | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update |
| 100%  | 129,000                     | 188           | 75%              | -2.9%                            | no increase |

The 10% and 50% gate maxima were not captured here because only the
full-production observation was supplied for this update. Do not back-fill
those rows from memory — pull the per-gate metrics from the rollout card
or the metrics-router export before relying on them.

**Formal 48-hour production check:** still due 2024-04-04. Do not close
out the v2.19.4 rollout until that check has run and the result is
recorded against this entry.

**Out of scope for this section (unchanged):**
- The label-name / label-map alerting path above (still DRAFT, still
  blocked on Nadia's written sign-off and the parity doc).
- Production ownership, the owner map, and the backup designation.
- The OTel collector 0.91 and OTel exporter retry-only sections above.

## 2024-07-05 — tenant-fair queue is now production behavior

The mapped owner completed the remaining ingest-edge rollout on 2024-07-05.
Tenant-fair queue behavior is now production behavior; this is not a
temporary tuning knob and the service is not expected to return to the
prior queue shape.

**Observed at 50% and full production:**

- Noisy-tenant tests preserved the eight-waiting cap — a single noisy
  tenant could not push other tenants past the cap.
- Newly queued low-volume tenants entered the ring immediately —
  small or bursty tenants were not stranded behind a dominant noisy
  tenant.
- Work-conserving dispatch used each eligible slot — when eligible
  work existed, slots were not left idle.
- Empty tenants disappeared from the ring after cancellation — the
  ring shed vacated slots rather than holding dead entries.
- Every queue-cap response retained `Retry-After` — clients continued
  to receive a usable back-off signal at the cap.

**Existing requirements preserved alongside the new tenant-fair queue
behavior (do not relax; do not roll a queue change forward without
re-checking each of these against the proposed change):**

- Four-active-per-pod limit.
- Two-active-per-tenant limit.
- Bounded-decompression requirement.
- Retry requirements (incl. the v2.19.4 randomized 1–3s `Retry-After`
  documented in the section above).

**Existing rollout checks that remained clean at 50% and full production:**

- Active-work check.
- Accepted-point check.
- Dropped-point check.
- Restart check.

**Out of scope for this section (unchanged):**

- The label-name / label-map alerting path above (still DRAFT, still
  blocked on Nadia's written sign-off and the parity doc).
- The OTel collector 0.91 and OTel exporter retry-only sections above.
- The v2.19.4 randomized Retry-After section above (separate concern;
  its 48-hour production check and gate-maxima backfill remain tracked
  there).
- Production ownership, the owner map, and the backup designation.

## 2027-05-28 — bounded service-discovery membership check (follow-up to the May 24 zone imbalance)

Follow-up to the May 24 zone imbalance. This section is a single,
bounded operational follow-up: verify service-discovery membership
matches the ready-endpoint set by zone, confirm that load-balancer
traffic distribution has returned to baseline after a refresh, and
close out the imbalance only after caller-visible accounting reconciles
cleanly. It is *not* a new routine, *not* a shift in the operator
rotation, and *not* a change to the owner map.

**Scope and boundaries (explicit):**
- One bounded service-discovery membership check tied to the May 24
  zone imbalance. No change to alerting, no change to the LB
  configuration outside the refresh required to reconcile membership
  with the ready-endpoint set, and no change to any other runbook
  section above.
- The May 24 zone imbalance was an operational event; this section
  records the close-out procedure for that event, not a standing
  check. Do not generalize this procedure into a recurring task.
- Production ownership stays with alex (primary) and yuki (backup).
  The owner map is unchanged. Alex is not becoming the routine
  operator of any new ingest-edge surface as a result of this check;
  alex's role on this section is bounded to the close-out of the
  May 24 imbalance only.

**Step 1 — Compare ready endpoints with load-balancer membership by zone.**
1. Pull the current ready-endpoint set from ingest-edge's readiness
   surface, grouped by zone.
2. Pull the current load-balancer membership (i.e. the endpoints the
   LB is actively routing to), grouped by zone.
3. For each zone, diff the two sets:
   - Endpoints that are ready but not in LB membership → candidates
     to add on refresh.
   - Endpoints that are in LB membership but not ready → candidates
     to remove on refresh.
   - Endpoints present in both → unchanged.
4. Record the diff by zone on the incident card before any refresh.
   If any diff cannot be reconciled to a single, named endpoint
   (e.g. a duplicate or an unidentifiable ID), stop and escalate —
   do not proceed with a refresh against an unreconciled diff.

**Step 2 — Refresh load-balancer membership to match the ready set.**
1. Apply the diff from Step 1 in a single bounded refresh action.
   Do not perform a full LB reset; only add the missing ready
   endpoints and remove the not-ready LB entries.
2. After the refresh, re-pull the LB membership by zone and confirm
   it now equals the ready-endpoint set per zone (Step 1's diff is
   empty).

**Step 3 — Verify traffic distribution has returned to baseline.**
1. Compare per-zone traffic share against the pre-May-24 baseline.
   Use the same metric definition as the May 24 imbalance response
   (do not introduce a new metric).
2. Pass criterion: every zone's traffic share is within the accepted
   envelope of the pre-May-24 baseline. If any zone is outside the
   envelope, do not proceed to Step 4 — re-open the imbalance and
   re-diff ready vs. LB membership before any further refresh.

**Step 4 — Confirm queue occupancy and caller errors remain at baseline.**
1. Queue occupancy: compare against the pre-May-24 baseline. Pass
   criterion is that occupancy is at or below baseline; do not
   accept a transient overshoot as "settled" without an explicit
   observation window (default: 15 minutes of flat-or-declining
   occupancy after the refresh).
2. Caller errors (5xx rate, rejected-for-overload responses, dropped
   points): compare against the pre-May-24 baseline. Pass criterion
   is no increase vs. baseline. Any increase is a stop signal — do
   not declare the imbalance closed while caller errors are elevated.
3. If either check fails, do not proceed to Step 5.

**Step 5 — Reconcile every accepted request to exactly one caller-visible terminal result before closure.**
This is the accounting gate. Before declaring the May 24 zone
imbalance closed, reconcile accepted work end-to-end:

1. For the imbalance window (May 24 → refresh-complete), enumerate
   every request that the platform marked as **accepted**.
2. For each accepted request, identify exactly one
   caller-visible terminal result:
   - Success (200 / accepted points written), OR
   - Explicit client-recoverable failure surfaced to the caller
     (e.g. 4xx with reason, OTLP partial success with a rejected
     count and reason, HTTP 413 oversized_batch with accepted=0 /
     rejected=submitted count), OR
   - An explicit retryable terminal (e.g. a `Retry-After` cap
     response that the caller can act on).
3. Pass criteria for closure — all three must hold:
   - **No duplicated accepted work.** Each accepted request maps to
     exactly one terminal result; no accepted request produced two
     or more distinct terminal results surfaced to the caller
     (e.g. a 200 from one path plus a 200 from a replay path for
     the same accepted request is a duplicate and a fail).
   - **No unaccounted accepted work.** Every accepted request has a
     mapped terminal result; none are missing.
   - **No leaked queue occupancy.** After the reconciliation, queue
     occupancy attributable to the imbalance window is at zero. Any
     residual queue occupancy tied to the imbalance window is a
     fail — it means accepted work has not reached a
     caller-visible terminal and is still being held internally.
4. If any of the three pass criteria fails, do not declare closure.
   Re-open the imbalance, return to Step 1, and surface the specific
   accounting failure on the incident card.

**Step 6 — Close-out only after Steps 1–5 all pass.**
1. Record the per-zone diff, the refresh action, the
   traffic-share comparison, the queue/error comparison, and the
   accounting reconciliation on the incident card.
2. Update last_updated against this entry only when all five steps
   have passed and the accounting reconciliation is signed off.
3. Do not roll any change forward (no new alerting, no new check,
  no LB-config change outside the bounded refresh) as part of
  closure.

**What this section does NOT change (explicit):**
- Production ownership of ingest-edge stays with alex (primary) and
  yuki (backup). The owner map is unchanged.
- Alex is **not** the routine operator of this check. This section
  is a single bounded close-out of the May 24 zone imbalance; it
  does not establish a recurring task, an on-call rotation slot,
  or a standing operator assignment for alex on any new
  ingest-edge surface.
- The label-name / label-map alerting path above (still DRAFT,
  still blocked on Nadia's written sign-off and the parity doc).
- The OTel collector 0.91, OTel exporter retry-only,
  2024-01-04 staging rollback-drill hygiene, v2.19.4 randomized
  Retry-After, tenant-fair queue, and PR 2519 sections above.
- The memory-slope canary stop rule (rb_1789250051828), the OTLP
  partial-success entry (rb_1789273768109), and the HTTP 413
  oversized-batch entry (rb_1789412825310).
- The Mar 17 prod cutover checklist above and the
  "avoid Friday afternoons" rule.

## 2027-09-02 — tenant-burst operating check

A bounded operating check for tenant-burst behavior. The eight-waiting
cap and the retryable-overflow posture are already production behavior
under the 2024-07-05 tenant-fair queue section above; this entry records
the operating check that verifies the cap holds end-to-end under burst
load, that accepted work still reconciles to exactly one terminal
result, and that the burst does not bleed into other tenants or into
caller errors. This entry is a verification record; it does not roll
any change forward, does not adjust the cap, and does not move the
implementation, release, or rollback path.

**Operating rules under tenant burst (all six must hold during the
check):**

1. **Per-tenant waiting cap.** A tenant may have at most eight waiting
   requests at any point during the burst. Requests beyond the eighth
   must not be accepted; they must remain retryable and must fail
   before acceptance (e.g. a queue-cap response with `Retry-After`,
   per the 2024-07-05 tenant-fair queue section above). The cap is
   per tenant, not global.
2. **Retryable overflow.** Excess requests from a capped tenant
   remain retryable — the caller can act on the failure (e.g. back
   off on the returned `Retry-After`) and resubmit. The overflow must
   not be silently dropped, must not be coalesced with a distinct
   request, and must not be accepted-then-failed after acceptance.
3. **Acceptance reconciliation.** Every request that ingest-edge
   marks as accepted must reconcile to exactly one caller-visible
   terminal result: success, explicit client-recoverable failure
   surfaced to the caller, or an explicit retryable terminal (e.g.
   a `Retry-After` cap response). No accepted request may produce
   two or more distinct terminal results surfaced to the caller
   (no duplicated accepted work), and no accepted request may be
   missing a terminal result (no unaccounted accepted work).
4. **Other tenants remain at baseline.** Tenants other than the
   bursting tenant must remain at their pre-burst baseline for
   waiting count, accepted throughput, and queue depth. A burst on
   one tenant must not push a neighbor over the cap, must not starve
   a neighbor of dispatch, and must not increase a neighbor's
   `Retry-After` rate vs. the pre-burst baseline.
5. **Caller errors remain at baseline.** The 5xx rate, the
   rejected-for-overload response rate, and the dropped-point count
   must remain flat vs. the pre-burst baseline for the duration of
   the check. Any increase in any of these during a burst is a stop
   signal, not a successful isolation result.
6. **Queue drains to zero.** After the burst subsides and the
   tenant's queue is emptied, queue occupancy attributable to the
   burst window must end at zero. Any residual queue occupancy tied
   to the burst window is a fail — it means accepted work has not
   reached a caller-visible terminal and is still being held
   internally.

**How to run the check (bounded; not a standing routine):**

1. Confirm the bursting tenant and the burst window on the incident
   card. The check is run against an observed tenant burst, not
   synthesized.
2. Capture the pre-burst baseline for: per-tenant waiting count
   (`waiting_count{tenant}`), accepted throughput, queue depth,
   5xx rate, rejected-for-overload rate, and dropped-point count.
3. During the burst window, observe each of the six operating rules
   above. Record any violation on the incident card with the time,
   the rule that was violated, and the specific metric reading.
4. After the burst subsides, reconcile accepted work end-to-end
   (the accounting gate from Step 5 of the 2027-05-28 section
   above applies here as well: each accepted request → exactly one
   terminal result; no duplicates; no unaccounted work; queue
   occupancy → zero).
5. Pass criteria for the check — all six rules must hold. Any rule
   violation is a fail, and a fail does not retroactively change
   the underlying queue behavior or any prior section above.

**What this section does NOT change (explicit):**

- **Implementation, release, and rollback ownership stay with
  Yuki's mapped path.** This section does not transfer
  implementation, release, or rollback ownership from Yuki's mapped
  path to anyone else (including alex). The owner map (alex
  primary, yuki backup) is unchanged. The production-ownership
  backup designation is unchanged.
- The eight-waiting cap and the retryable-overflow posture are
  unchanged. They remain as recorded in the 2024-07-05 tenant-fair
  queue section above; this entry only verifies that they hold
  under burst load.
- The v2.19.4 randomized 1–3s `Retry-After` (gate maxima and
  48-hour production check) is unchanged.
- The 2027-01-20 PR 2519 24-hour prod observation closeout is
  unchanged.
- The 2027-05-28 bounded service-discovery membership check is
  unchanged.
- The label-name / label-map alerting path above (still DRAFT,
  still blocked on Nadia's written sign-off and the parity doc) is
  unchanged.
- The OTel collector 0.91 and OTel exporter retry-only sections
  above are unchanged.
- The 2024-01-04 staging rollback-drill hygiene section above is
  unchanged.
- The Mar 17 prod cutover checklist above and the "avoid Friday
  afternoons" rule are unchanged.
- The memory-slope canary stop rule (rb_1789250051828), the OTLP
  partial-success entry (rb_1789273768109), and the HTTP 413
  oversized-batch entry (rb_1789412825310) are unchanged.

## 2027-10-21 — active decoder controls (production-closed observation)

Production observation of the decoder controls has closed. This section
records the active control set as the reference for any later change
to the same code path. The five controls below are now production
behavior; they are not a temporary tuning knob, and the service is
not expected to return to the pre-observation behavior. Implementation,
release, and rollback authority for this code path stay with Yuki's
mapped path.

**Scope and boundaries (explicit):**

- This section records the decoder controls only. It does not roll
  any change forward, does not adjust the 8,000-point whole-batch
  rule below, and does not adjust the eight-waiting-per-tenant
  limit below. Those limits are preserved alongside the new
  controls and remain independently enforced.
- This section does not change the owner map (alex primary, yuki
  backup) or the production-ownership backup designation.
- This section does not transfer implementation, release, or
  rollback authority for this code path away from Yuki's mapped
  path. Yuki's mapped path remains the implementation, release,
  and rollback authority for any change to the decoder controls
  or the surrounding ingest-edge decode path.

**The five active controls (all five must hold at all times):**

1. **One request-wide 1,048,576-byte decoded-attribute limit across
   all gzip members.** The decoded-attribute budget is
   1,048,576 bytes per request, computed across the sum of all
   gzip members in that request. The budget is request-wide, not
   per-member: a single oversized member can spend the whole
   budget, and the sum of small members is also bounded by it.
   This is the only decoded-attribute budget in force; no per-
   member ceiling is layered on top of it. Over-limit requests
   must not be accepted (see control 4).

2. **72-request decode-admission cap with retryable pre-acceptance
   handling above it.** Decode admission is capped at 72 requests.
   Requests above the cap must be handled before acceptance as
   retryable — the caller can act on the failure (e.g. back off on
   the returned `Retry-After`) and resubmit. The cap is the
   admission gate; it is not a queue depth and is not an accepted-
   work count. Pre-acceptance handling means the cap is enforced
   before the request is marked accepted, so cap rejections do not
   count against acceptance reconciliation (control 3 in the
   2027-05-28 and 2027-09-02 sections above still applies to
   accepted work only).

3. **No enqueue of over-limit work.** Requests that exceed either
   the 1,048,576-byte decoded-attribute budget (control 1) or the
   72-request decode-admission cap (control 2) must not be
   enqueued. They must be rejected before acceptance — over the
   cap as a retryable terminal (control 2) or over the budget as
   a client-recoverable failure surfaced to the caller (e.g. an
   HTTP 413 oversized_batch-style response with accepted=0 /
   rejected=submitted count). Over-limit work must not occupy a
   queue slot, must not consume a waiting slot under the eight-
   waiting-per-tenant limit, and must not appear in the accepted-
   work reconciliation.

4. **Exactly one terminal outcome for every accepted request.**
   Every request that ingest-edge marks as accepted must reconcile
   to exactly one caller-visible terminal result: success,
   explicit client-recoverable failure surfaced to the caller, or
   an explicit retryable terminal. No accepted request may produce
   two or more distinct terminal results surfaced to the caller
   (no duplicated accepted work), and no accepted request may be
   missing a terminal result (no unaccounted accepted work).
   This control is the same acceptance-reconciliation gate already
   recorded in the 2027-05-28 Step 5 and the 2027-09-02 rule 3
   sections above; it is restated here so the decoder path is
   covered explicitly, not by reference alone.

5. **Exactly-once slot release after success, rejection, malformed
   input, cancellation, or disconnect.** Every slot consumed by a
   request — whether against the four-active-per-pod limit, the
   two-active-per-tenant limit, the eight-waiting-per-tenant cap,
   or any other slot-shaped resource held on behalf of the
   request — must be released exactly once, and only once, for
   each of the five terminal shapes: success, rejection (cap or
   budget, pre-acceptance or post-acceptance), malformed input,
   cancellation, and disconnect. No double-release (a slot freed
   twice for the same request is a leak symptom and a fail), and
   no missed release (a slot held after the request has reached a
   caller-visible terminal is a leak and a fail). Malformed input,
   cancellation, and disconnect are first-class terminal shapes
   and must release the slot they held; they are not exceptions
   to this control.

**Controls preserved alongside the active decoder controls (do not
relax; do not roll a decoder change forward without re-checking each
of these against the proposed change):**

- **8,000-point whole-batch rule.** The whole-batch point ceiling
  remains 8,000 points. The decoder controls above are layered
  alongside it; neither replaces the other. Over-budget requests
  that also breach the 8,000-point rule must be rejected before
  acceptance under whichever rule fires first, and the rejection
  must surface to the caller as a client-recoverable failure.
- **Eight-waiting-requests-per-tenant limit.** The per-tenant
  waiting cap remains eight waiting requests, as already recorded
  in the 2024-07-05 tenant-fair queue section and the 2027-09-02
  tenant-burst operating check above. The decoder controls do not
  raise, lower, or generalize this cap.
- **Implementation, release, and rollback authority for the
  decoder code path stays with Yuki's mapped path.** This section
  does not transfer that authority to anyone else (including
  alex). Any change to the decoder controls, or to the 8,000-
  point rule, or to the eight-waiting-per-tenant limit, must be
  implemented, released, and (if needed) rolled back through
  Yuki's mapped path.

**Production-closed observation evidence (recorded for reference; not
a re-litigation of the controls):**

- The 1,048,576-byte decoded-attribute budget held across all
  observed request shapes, including requests with multiple gzip
  members and requests with a single large gzip member.
- The 72-request decode-admission cap held under observed load,
  including observed burst windows from the 2027-09-02 check.
- No over-limit request was observed enqueued; cap and budget
  rejections surfaced to the caller before acceptance.
- Every accepted request reconciled to exactly one caller-visible
  terminal result across the observation window.
- Every slot consumed by a request was released exactly once
  across the five terminal shapes above; no double-release and no
  missed release was observed.

## OTel collector 0.91 — production rollout note (2023-07-25 / 2023-07-27)

Closed out after the heightened watch ended. Final note from Yuki on 2023-07-27.

- **Outcome: production-clean.** Error rate stayed flat across the rollout
  and through the >72h follow-up window. CPU stayed flat. Heightened watch
  was closed on 2023-07-25 with no rollback needed.
- **Memory delta to record:** p95 memory settled ~5% above the pre-bump
  collector baseline. This is inside normal headroom and is not an alert
  threshold, but it is the new steady-state — record it so future bumps
  don't get re-litigated from scratch.
- **Future collector bumps still require:**
  1. A staging replay against representative prod-shaped load before any
     production push.
  2. An explicit memory watch during the production rollout window —
     p95 memory vs. the post-0.91 baseline (~5% above pre-0.91), not vs.
     the original pre-bump line.
  "Approved before" is not sufficient justification on its own; each bump
  must clear both gates above.

## OTel exporter retry — retry-only patch note (sha:0a91b7c, 2023-10-09)

Narrow note covering only the retry-only exporter change that has been quiet
in prod since 2023-10-09. Not a collector-wide tuning reference.

- **Scope:** OTLP HTTP exporter retry settings only. The `memory_limiter`
  configuration was deliberately left out of this patch and is tracked
  separately; do not conflate the two.
- **Exporter retry values applied:**
  - `retry_on_failure.max_interval` = 15s
  - `retry_on_failure.max_elapsed_time` = 5m
- **Post-deploy checks (run during the rollout window):**
  1. Dropped-writes counter — must remain flat vs. pre-patch baseline.
  2. Backpressure counters — must remain flat vs. pre-patch baseline.
  3. Retry log volume — observed lower ~24h into the prod deployment
     (2023-10-26); treat lower retry log volume as the expected steady
     state, not as an anomaly.
- **What this note does NOT cover:** batch processor sizing, queue tuning,
  `memory_limiter` thresholds, or any other collector-wide knobs. Those
  remain out of scope for this entry.

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the
operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without
hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real
  backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that
as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

## 2027-05-28 — bounded service-discovery membership check (follow-up to the May 24 zone imbalance)

Follow-up to the May 24 zone imbalance. This section is a single,
bounded operational follow-up: verify service-discovery membership
matches the ready-endpoint set by zone, confirm that load-balancer
traffic distribution has returned to baseline after a refresh, and
close out the imbalance only after caller-visible accounting reconciles
cleanly. It is *not* a new routine, *not* a shift in the operator
rotation, and *not* a change to the owner map.

**Scope and boundaries (explicit):**
- One bounded service-discovery membership check tied to the May 24
  zone imbalance. No change to alerting, no change to the LB
  configuration outside the refresh required to reconcile membership
  with the ready-endpoint set, and no change to any other runbook
  section above.
- The May 24 zone imbalance was an operational event; this section
  records the close-out procedure for that event, not a standing
  check. Do not generalize this procedure into a recurring task.
- Production ownership stays with alex (primary) and yuki (backup).
  The owner map is unchanged. Alex is not becoming the routine
  operator of any new ingest-edge surface as a result of this check;
  alex's role on this section is bounded to the close-out of the
  May 24 imbalance only.

**Step 1 — Compare ready endpoints with load-balancer membership by zone.**
1. Pull the current ready-endpoint set from ingest-edge's readiness
   surface, grouped by zone.
2. Pull the current load-balancer membership (i.e. the endpoints the
   LB is actively routing to), grouped by zone.
3. For each zone, diff the two sets:
   - Endpoints that are ready but not in LB membership → candidates
     to add on refresh.
   - Endpoints that are in LB membership but not ready → candidates
     to remove on refresh.
   - Endpoints present in both → unchanged.
4. Record the diff by zone on the incident card before any refresh.
   If any diff cannot be reconciled to a single, named endpoint
   (e.g. a duplicate or an unidentifiable ID), stop and escalate —
   do not proceed with a refresh against an unreconciled diff.

**Step 2 — Refresh load-balancer membership to match the ready set.**
1. Apply the diff from Step 1 in a single bounded refresh action.
   Do not perform a full LB reset; only add the missing ready
   endpoints and remove the not-ready LB entries.
2. After the refresh, re-pull the LB membership by zone and confirm
   it now equals the ready-endpoint set per zone (Step 1's diff is
   empty).

**Step 3 — Verify traffic distribution has returned to baseline.**
1. Compare per-zone traffic share against the pre-May-24 baseline.
   Use the same metric definition as the May 24 imbalance response
   (do not introduce a new metric).
2. Pass criterion: every zone's traffic share is within the accepted
   envelope of the pre-May-24 baseline. If any zone is outside the
   envelope, do not proceed to Step 4 — re-open the imbalance and
   re-diff ready vs. LB membership before any further refresh.

**Step 4 — Confirm queue occupancy and caller errors remain at baseline.**
1. Queue occupancy: compare against the pre-May-24 baseline. Pass
   criterion is that occupancy is at or below baseline; do not
   accept a transient overshoot as "settled" without an explicit
   observation window (default: 15 minutes of flat-or-declining
   occupancy after the refresh).
2. Caller errors (5xx rate, rejected-for-overload responses, dropped
   points): compare against the pre-May-24 baseline. Pass criterion
   is no increase vs. baseline. Any increase is a stop signal — do
   not declare the imbalance closed while caller errors are elevated.
3. If either check fails, do not proceed to Step 5.

**Step 5 — Reconcile every accepted request to exactly one caller-visible terminal result before closure.**
This is the accounting gate. Before declaring the May 24 zone
imbalance closed, reconcile accepted work end-to-end:

1. For the imbalance window (May 24 → refresh-complete), enumerate
   every request that the platform marked as **accepted**.
2. For each accepted request, identify exactly one
   caller-visible terminal result:
   - Success (200 / accepted points written), OR
   - Explicit client-recoverable failure surfaced to the caller
     (e.g. 4xx with reason, OTLP partial success with a rejected
     count and reason, HTTP 413 oversized_batch with accepted=0 /
     rejected=submitted count), OR
   - An explicit retryable terminal (e.g. a `Retry-After` cap
     response that the caller can act on).
3. Pass criteria for closure — all three must hold:
   - **No duplicated accepted work.** Each accepted request maps to
     exactly one terminal result; no accepted request produced two
     or more distinct terminal results surfaced to the caller
     (e.g. a 200 from one path plus a 200 from a replay path for
     the same accepted request is a duplicate and a fail).
   - **No unaccounted accepted work.** Every accepted request has a
     mapped terminal result; none are missing.
   - **No leaked queue occupancy.** After the reconciliation, queue
     occupancy attributable to the imbalance window is at zero. Any
     residual queue occupancy tied to the imbalance window is a
     fail — it means accepted work has not reached a
     caller-visible terminal and is still being held internally.
4. If any of the three pass criteria fails, do not declare closure.
   Re-open the imbalance, return to Step 1, and surface the specific
   accounting failure on the incident card.

**Step 6 — Close-out only after Steps 1–5 all pass.**
1. Record the per-zone diff, the refresh action, the
   traffic-share comparison, the queue/error comparison, and the
   accounting reconciliation on the incident card.
2. Update last_updated against this entry only when all five steps
   have passed and the accounting reconciliation is signed off.
3. Do not roll any change forward (no new alerting, no new check,
  no LB-config change outside the bounded refresh) as part of
  closure.

**What this section does NOT change (explicit):**
- Production ownership of ingest-edge stays with alex (primary) and
  yuki (backup). The owner map is unchanged.
- Alex is **not** the routine operator of this check. This section
  is a single bounded close-out of the May 24 zone imbalance; it
  does not establish a recurring task, an on-call rotation slot,
  or a standing operator assignment for alex on any new
  ingest-edge surface.
- The label-name / label-map alerting path above (still DRAFT,
  still blocked on Nadia's written sign-off and the parity doc).
- The OTel collector 0.91, OTel exporter retry-only,
  2024-01-04 staging rollback-drill hygiene, v2.19.4 randomized
  Retry-After, tenant-fair queue, and PR 2519 sections above.
- The memory-slope canary stop rule (rb_1789250051828), the OTLP
  partial-success entry (rb_1789273768109), and the HTTP 413
  oversized-batch entry (rb_1789412825310).
- The Mar 17 prod cutover checklist above and the
  "avoid Friday afternoons" rule.

## 2027-09-02 — tenant-burst operating check

A bounded operating check for tenant-burst behavior. The eight-waiting
cap and the retryable-overflow posture are already production behavior
under the 2024-07-05 tenant-fair queue section above; this entry records
the operating check that verifies the cap holds end-to-end under burst
load, that accepted work still reconciles to exactly one terminal
result, and that the burst does not bleed into other tenants or into
caller errors. This entry is a verification record; it does not roll
any change forward, does not adjust the cap, and does not move the
implementation, release, or rollback path.

**Operating rules under tenant burst (all six must hold during the
check):**

1. **Per-tenant waiting cap.** A tenant may have at most eight waiting
   requests at any point during the burst. Requests beyond the eighth
   must not be accepted; they must remain retryable and must fail
   before acceptance (e.g. a queue-cap response with `Retry-After`,
   per the 2024-07-05 tenant-fair queue section above). The cap is
   per tenant, not global.
2. **Retryable overflow.** Excess requests from a capped tenant
   remain retryable — the caller can act on the failure (e.g. back
   off on the returned `Retry-After`) and resubmit. The overflow must
   not be silently dropped, must not be coalesced with a distinct
   request, and must not be accepted-then-failed after acceptance.
3. **Acceptance reconciliation.** Every request that ingest-edge
   marks as accepted must reconcile to exactly one caller-visible
   terminal result: success, explicit client-recoverable failure
   surfaced to the caller, or an explicit retryable terminal (e.g.
   a `Retry-After` cap response). No accepted request may produce
   two or more distinct terminal results surfaced to the caller
   (no duplicated accepted work), and no accepted request may be
   missing a terminal result (no unaccounted accepted work).
4. **Other tenants remain at baseline.** Tenants other than the
   bursting tenant must remain at their pre-burst baseline for
   waiting count, accepted throughput, and queue depth. A burst on
   one tenant must not push a neighbor over the cap, must not starve
   a neighbor of dispatch, and must not increase a neighbor's
   `Retry-After` rate vs. the pre-burst baseline.
5. **Caller errors remain at baseline.** The 5xx rate, the
   rejected-for-overload response rate, and the dropped-point count
   must remain flat vs. the pre-burst baseline for the duration of
   the check. Any increase in any of these during a burst is a stop
   signal, not a successful isolation result.
6. **Queue drains to zero.** After the burst subsides and the
   tenant's queue is emptied, queue occupancy attributable to the
   burst window must end at zero. Any residual queue occupancy tied
   to the burst window is a fail — it means accepted work has not
   reached a caller-visible terminal and is still being held
   internally.

**How to run the check (bounded; not a standing routine):**

1. Confirm the bursting tenant and the burst window on the incident
   card. The check is run against an observed tenant burst, not
   synthesized.
2. Capture the pre-burst baseline for: per-tenant waiting count
   (`waiting_count{tenant}`), accepted throughput, queue depth,
   5xx rate, rejected-for-overload rate, and dropped-point count.
3. During the burst window, observe each of the six operating rules
   above. Record any violation on the incident card with the time,
   the rule that was violated, and the specific metric reading.
4. After the burst subsides, reconcile accepted work end-to-end
   (the accounting gate from Step 5 of the 2027-05-28 section
   above applies here as well: each accepted request → exactly one
   terminal result; no duplicates; no unaccounted work; queue
   occupancy → zero).
5. Pass criteria for the check — all six rules must hold. Any rule
   violation is a fail, and a fail does not retroactively change
   the underlying queue behavior or any prior section above.

entries.body:
Process readiness alone is not the exit condition. In the staging failover drill, all replacement replicas reported ready after 18 seconds, but lease ownership did not converge until 96 seconds. Before declaring the failover complete, verify all of the following: 1. Every partition has exactly one owner. 2. Lease epochs remain monotonic. 3. No stale-owner messages appear for two full lease-renewal intervals. If any of those checks fail, keep the failover open and page the shard-keeper owner. Renewal-warning versus lease transfer: `renewal deadline exceeded` alone does not prove a lease transfer. Check for a changed lease epoch, explicit acquisition or relinquishment, overlapping leadership, and post-event replication convergence. If the holder and epoch remain unchanged, no overlap occurs, and lag returns to baseline, treat the event as a delayed renewal rather than a failover; do not automatically restart.

## Production lease-loss serving-gate invariant

On lease-loss notification, close the old holder's serving gate before it can return another routing response. The periodic poll is only a backup detector, not the serving-safety mechanism. Production verification must include:
- gate closure before any later routing response
- exactly one serving holder throughout the transfer
- lease-loss notification to gate-close latency
- stale routing responses
- replacement acquisition time
- request p99
- errors
- restarts

A slow handoff or convergence warning is an availability signal to investigate separately. By itself, it is not evidence that the old holder served after lease loss or that the serving-safety invariant failed. The owner map and mapped deployment responsibility remain unchanged.

This is a concise record of the signed limited-use agreement on file between Anya and North Pier, for your reference.

Signatory
Anya signed the limited-use agreement herself. She is the sole signatory and the party who granted the license; this record is being relayed on her behalf and does not alter or substitute her signature.

License granted
Anya granted North Pier a limited recording license on the following terms, all unchanged from the executed agreement:

I found the context in session history: the two options are the ones from the July 21 authority-boundary rehearsal — (A) a Lantern-centered combined payload versus (B) a reference model where Lantern links out to Cardinality Guardrails by record ID and source timestamp. The November 17 operating evidence and Iris's completed finding are the grounding material.

Here's the assessment and the draft.

Assessment

Option A (Lantern-centered combined payload) — Lantern carries the 64-pending-batches limit value and the cost semantics in its own payload. This makes Lantern the customer-facing authority for a control Cardinality Guardrails owns and mirrors the original Mosaic request, which we declined because it would put Cardinality Guardrails limit and cost data on an unauthorized customer surface. It also re-opens the write-control side for Harbor's owner-map correction, which the same boundary session declined.

Option B (reference model) — Lantern explains, links to, and navigates to the Cardinality Guardrails record by its own ID and source timestamp; the limit value and cost semantics remain in Cardinality Guardrails. This matches what the November 17 evidence actually showed (Wes reached the Cardinality Guardrails record via the card; the limit did not move into Lantern; Cyrus confirmed cost semantics remained there) and what Iris's completed finding confirmed (no wording presented either link as a Lantern-owned value, write control, or transfer of authority). It also keeps the integration into Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths UNAUTHORIZED, consistent with the 12/17 gating.

Recommendation: Option B.

Draft feedback to Iris (concise — ready for your review, not yet sent)

Iris —

I assessed the two rehearsal options against the November 17 operating evidence and your completed finding.

Option A (Lantern-centered combined payload) would put the 64-pending-batches-per-tenant limit and cost data on the Lantern surface. That makes Lantern the customer-facing authority for a control Cardinality Guardrails owns, and it mirrors the original Mosaic request, which we declined because it would put Cardinality Guardrails limit and cost data on an unauthorized customer surface.

Option B (reference model) keeps Lantern as the explanation and navigation layer; the limit value and cost semantics remain in Cardinality Guardrails; Lantern references the Cardinality Guardrails record by its own ID and source timestamp. This is the path the November 17 evidence showed: Wes reached the Cardinality Guardrails record via the card; the limit did not move into Lantern; Cyrus confirmed cost semantics remained in Cardinality Guardrails; and your completed finding confirmed no wording presented either link as a Lantern-owned value, write control, or transfer of authority.

I'm with Option B. Boundary lines:
- Lantern: explains, navigates, and links out by record ID + source timestamp.
- Cardinality Guardrails: owns the control, the limit value, and cost semantics.
- metrics-router (Wes): owns the operating-limit mapping.

Lantern does not own the linked control or its value. Nothing in Option B transfers authority to Lantern.

— Alex

Notes for you, not for Iris:
- I have not sent this. `list_contacts` is empty in this session and `list_inbox` has no Iris message to reply to, so I don't have a verified channel for her. Tell me where it should go (Slack DM, email address, doc comment on the rehearsal brief) and I'll deliver it.
- Two open constraints I held the line on and would not soften for Iris: (1) no Lantern-owned wording of the limit or cost, and (2) Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer-path integration remains UNAUTHORIZED — the reference model is internal/reference-only on those paths per the 12/17 gate.

## Cardinality Guardrails: label-change preflight (first cut)

Scope: first-cut preflight only. Captures the vocabulary before it
turns into hallway knowledge. This entry is deliberately narrow; it
is not the full Cardinality Guardrails project.

### What this preflight covers

A label-change preflight fires when a config push, schema change, or
relabel rule could add new label keys or change the cardinality shape
of an existing label family. It is a check, not a control: it surfaces
risk; the caller still decides whether to ship.

### First-cut preflight surface

- **New label keys**: any key not already present in the router's known
  label inventory for the affected metric path. Treat as additive
  cardinality risk until proven bounded.
- **Risky label families**: high-cardinality families we have already
  seen wobble — request-scoped IDs, user/path/email-derived fields,
  free-form tag values, raw URLs, and any label whose value set is not
  owned by the service emitting it.
- **Sample distinct counts**: pull a short-window sample from the
  router path the change touches, report distinct-value counts per
  new or modified label key, and flag any sample whose distinct count
  is unbounded in practice (growing with traffic or tenants).
- **Live-path sample requirement for live-path labels**: when the
  change touches the live router path, the sample above must come
  from live canary traffic on that path, or from a representative
  live-path fixture that exercises the same handler/normalization
  chain. A replay or mirror sample alone is not sufficient evidence
  for live-path labels. This applies in particular to normalization
  paths on existing label families — e.g. `route_pattern` and similar
  handler-derived keys — where a normalization change can shift a
  bounded label family into an unbounded one (raw IDs, raw account
  IDs, raw widget IDs, etc.) without adding a new key.
- **Alert-source semantics**: a `validation-only` finding is still
  evidence — it means the change was caught off the live path (no live
  rollback in scope), not that the mismatch is safe to ignore.
  Validation findings feed the same mismatch-investigation queue as
  live findings.
- **Live vs. validation rollback boundary**: a finding on a label
  pushed to the live router path is a live rollback candidate. A
  finding caught in a validation/mirror path is scope-only — recorded,
  investigated, but not an automatic rollback trigger. Replay and
  mirror validation remain investigation evidence and feed the
  mismatch-investigation queue; they are not, on their own, rollback
  criteria for live-path labels.

### First cut, not the whole project

- **Shard-keeper uses the same vocabulary**, but a runbook entry for
  shard-keeper is not in this first cut. It will get its own entry when
  its preflight path is wired up; do not assume the rules below apply
  there yet.
- This preflight does not enforce. It informs the owner of the push.
- This preflight does not replace the existing replay-mismatch panel
  or paired rollback for the metrics cutover; those are separate
  surfaces.

### Explicit non-goals

- Not a telemetry rewrite.
- Not a paired-rollback story.
- Not an ownership change.
- Not a router enforcement mechanism.
- Not a cardinality-control rollout across services. Other services
  get their own preflights; this is the router-facing first cut.

### Incident scope note (added 2023-10-30)

The 2023-10-30 metrics-router rollback surfaced a real hole in this
preflight wording — the original "pull a short-window sample from the
router path the change touches" was too loose for live-path labels
when a handler's normalization path changes. The added live-path
sample bullet above is the targeted fix.

- **This patch is not a claim that the preflight would have prevented
  the incident.** It tightens the evidence required for live-path
  label changes; it does not extend scope into live enforcement, new
  rollback mechanics, or a broader workstream.
- **Replay validation remains valuable as investigation evidence**, just
  not as a standalone rollback criterion for live-path labels. The
  replay-mismatch panel and the validation-only queue are unchanged.
- **`route_pattern` is named here as the worked example**, not as the
  only family in scope. Any handler-derived label whose value set is
  produced by a normalization step (route patterns, endpoint-derived
  keys, handler-emitted IDs that pass through a normalize step) is
  covered by the same rule.

### Known open questions for the first cut

- Where the sample distinct-count threshold for "risky" lives, and who
  owns tuning it.
- Whether new label keys should require an owner field at preflight
  time or only at investigation time.
- How validation-only findings are surfaced alongside live findings
  without being mistaken for either ignored or live-equivalent.
- What counts as a "representative live-path fixture" for handlers
  without an existing canary path.

### First-use review notes — Nov 8, 2023

These notes clarify how to apply the first-cut checklist. They do not make Cardinality Guardrails mature, complete, or a general telemetry rewrite.

- Local metrics-router visibility labels: require owner, source, expected cardinality shape, and evidence from live canary traffic or a representative live-path fixture when the value shape can change on the hot path. Rollup-service signoff is not required for labels that do not cross a service boundary.
- Cross-service label names or meaning changes: require rollup-service parity before promotion. A green metrics-router canary does not substitute for downstream consumers expecting the same label name and semantics.
- `route_pattern`: pass only for normalized route patterns. If a code path could emit raw account IDs, widget IDs, or raw paths on live traffic, reviewers need live-path evidence or a representative live-path fixture; replay validation alone is not enough.
- Replay or mirror validation panels: keep them visible as investigation evidence. Do not describe replay or mirror movement as live rollback criteria.
- Cost examples: keep them directional and advisory. Cyrus/data platform can validate cost intuition, but enforcement gates stay with the service owners.

### Pilot prevention note — Nov 14, 2023

The first concrete prevention case for this first-cut checklist came from a rollup-service validation metrics proposal.

Proposed shape that did not ship:
`rollup_validation_sample_total{validation_result="match|mismatch", replay_source_id="$source_id"}`

Why it failed the checklist:
- `replay_source_id` is a raw replay-stream identifier.
- Cyrus's sample showed the value is effectively unbounded across replay sources, jobs, chunks, and backfills.
- The debugging need was real, but the raw identifier belongs in logs rather than as a metrics label.

Accepted shape:
- Keep raw `replay_source_id` in logs for debugging.
- Use a bounded `source_class` metric label for rollup-service validation dashboards.
- Preserve validation visibility without introducing an unbounded label into the metrics pipeline.

This is evidence that the first-cut Cardinality Guardrails review can prevent a bad label shape without blocking the debugging need. It does not make Cardinality Guardrails mature, complete, or a general telemetry rewrite.

### Raw identifier labels — first-cut review guidance (added 2023-11-23)

Raw identifiers are not automatically forbidden as metric labels, but they need an explicit value-shape check before review treats them as safe.

Use the checklist questions:
- Is the value set bounded and named, or can it grow with requests, jobs, tenants, chunks, backfills, or arbitrary source records?
- Does the dashboard or alerting use case require this as a metric dimension, or is the raw identifier only needed for debugging?
- If the raw identifier is effectively unbounded, keep it in logs or trace context instead of the metrics label set.
- If dashboard grouping is required, prefer a bounded classification label such as `source_class` or another reviewed enum.

This is first-cut Cardinality Guardrails review guidance. It is not a blanket rule that all IDs are forbidden, it is not a general telemetry rewrite, and it does not make Wes the default enforcement owner.

Cardinality Guardrails — onboarding case study (first prevention case)

Purpose: ground the first-cut Cardinality Guardrails checklist in one concrete example, so new reviewers can see the pattern in action rather than learn it from the rules alone. One case. Not a proof of maturity.

Context
- Service: rollup-service (Cyrus / data-platform side).
- Setting: a validation-metrics proposal was being designed to give rollup-service a dashboard view of replay validation outcomes (match vs. mismatch).
- Date: November 14, 2023.
- Reviewers in the loop: Wes (metrics-router), Cyrus (rollup-service / cost angle), Nadia (alert-source semantics).

The proposal that did not ship
The proposed metric shape was:
  rollup_validation_sample_total{validation_result="match|mismatch", replay_source_id="$source_id"}

Why it failed the first-cut checklist
- replay_source_id is a raw replay-stream identifier. The value set grows with replay sources, jobs, chunks, and backfills — effectively unbounded in practice.
- The preflight rule for risky label families flags any label whose value set is not owned by the service emitting it. Replay IDs are owned by the replay pipeline, not rollup-service.
- The debugging need behind the label was real, but the first-cut checklist is explicit: unbounded raw identifiers belong in logs or trace context, not as metric labels.

The shape that shipped
- Keep the raw replay_source_id in logs for debugging.
- Use a bounded source_class metric label for the rollup-service validation dashboard.
- Validation visibility preserved. Unbounded label kept out of the metrics pipeline.

What this case demonstrates
- Cardinality Guardrails is a preflight, not a control. It surfaces risk; the caller still decides whether to ship. In this case the caller accepted the bounded alternative.

What this case does not demonstrate
- It is not evidence that Cardinality Guardrails is mature, complete, or a general telemetry rewrite.
- It is one prevention. The pilot line holds until we have two more comparable cases before reopening scope.
- It is a router/shard-keeper/rollup-service review surface. Other services get their own preflights; this is not a cross-service rollout.

Onboarding takeaway
When you see a proposed label change in this surface, ask four questions in order:
1. Is the value set bounded and named, or does it grow with traffic, tenants, jobs, chunks, or backfills?
2. Does the dashboard or alerting need this as a metric dimension, or is it debugging-only?
3. If unbounded, can it live in logs or trace context instead of the metrics label set?
4. If a metric dimension is required, is there a bounded reviewed enum (e.g. source_class) that preserves the grouping need?

If the proposal fails question 1 or 2, route to logs. If it needs a metric dimension, push for a bounded classification label. Keep the frame: one case, pilot, not a program.

# Cardinality Guardrails: label-change preflight first cut

This entry records the first acceptance-check pass for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work. It is not a mature program, a general telemetry rewrite, a customer-facing surface, or a legacy-aggregator retirement plan.

## Reviewer checklist

### 1. Scope the change
Pass if the PR says whether it touches metrics-router, shard-keeper, rollup-service, or a cross-service label boundary.
Fail if the PR changes label names or label value shapes without naming the affected service boundary.

### 2. New label keys or changed value shapes
Pass if every new label key or changed value shape names an owner, source, expected cardinality shape, and whether it is live-path or validation-only.
Fail if a new label can appear on live metrics-router or shard-keeper traffic without an owner and expected cardinality shape.

### 3. Risky label families
- `customer_id`: high-cardinality by nature, but expected and already budgeted when owner/source are clear. Do not fail solely because this label is high-cardinality.
- `experiment_id`: fail live router pushes unless new experiment labels are explicitly allowed and bounded.
- `route_pattern`: pass only when values are normalized route patterns; fail raw IDs or raw paths.
- `deployment_sha`: okay for canary visibility; fail noisy joins with per-request labels.
- `error_detail`: fail as a metrics label family. Raw error strings or payload fragments should not become metric labels.

### 4. Sample distinct counts before promotion
Pass if the reviewer can see sample distinct counts from realistic traffic for new or changed label value shapes.
Fail if the only evidence is a hand-wavy assertion that the canary is green.

### 5. Rollup-service parity before cross-service label-name changes
Pass if rollup-service expects the same label name and semantics before a label-name change crosses service boundaries.
Fail if metrics-router or shard-keeper ships a label-name change that downstream rollup-service consumers do not recognize.

### 6. Alert-source and rollback semantics
Pass if dashboards and alert text distinguish live metrics-router traffic from replay or mirror validation samples.
Live-path movement can start rollback discussion.
Replay or mirror validation movement is investigation evidence and Q4 controls input, not rollback criteria.
Fail if replay or mirror movement is described as a live rollback trigger.

## Ownership and non-goals
Service-level enforcement tradeoffs stay with Alex's side of the metrics pipeline. Cyrus and data platform can provide cost examples and validate cost intuition, but they do not own router or shard enforcement gates.

Non-goals: no customer-facing dashboard, no release-readiness score, no broad telemetry rewrite, no legacy-aggregator retirement claim, no default ownership change for enforcement, and no claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

tests.answer:
Lantern#1602 — Mira's "stabilize mixed-source chronology" PR. Below is the review. Note: my role here is to inspect and report — I have not submitted the review yet.

==============================================================================
1. WHICH TIMESTAMP CONTROLS VISIBLE ORDER
==============================================================================

The renderer sorts by `processed_at`, descending (most-recently-processed
first). That is the timestamp that controls visible order.

    records.sort((a, b) => b.processed_at.localeCompare(a.processed_at))

The `delayed_retry` fixture makes this concrete: incident_load
(source 08:12, processed 09:03) renders BEFORE deploy_event
(source 08:47, processed 08:50). A customer reading the timeline sees
the incident first even though the deploy happened first in real time.
That inversion is by design of this PR.

This is worth flagging because it diverges from the Lantern PE Q4
posture (2027-10-25): there, 6 source_ts rows processed 2-4d late were
"reconciled exactly once (stable cust-row id), src-time ordering
preserved, unresolved ∅." Ordering by processed_at is a deliberate
change away from that behavior, not a bug — but it must be called out
in the chronology's claims (see §4).

==============================================================================
2. TIMESTAMPS CURRENT POLICY TREATS AS AUDIT-ONLY
==============================================================================

`other_time_fields_carried: [observed_at, serialized_at, processed_at,
retry_at]` minus the sort key leaves three truly audit-only fields:

    - observed_at    carried, not sorted, not gated
    - serialized_at  carried, not sorted, not gated
    - retry_at       carried, not sorted, not gated

`processed_at` is the sort key but not the validation gate.
`source_timestamp` is the validation gate but not the sort key — so it
is also not what orders what the customer sees; it only gates whether
anything is shown at all.

==============================================================================
3. REQUIRED TIMESTAMP MISSING / MALFORMED
==============================================================================

`source_timestamp` is the required (gated) field, validated by
`parseSourceTimestamp`.

Behavior: if any single record in the renderer's input has an absent
or unparseable `source_timestamp`, the entire call returns
`{ chronology: [] }`. This is fail-closed and matches the Lantern /
shard-keeper principle (fail-closed on integrity inputs). The
`malformed_required_source_timestamp` fixture ("2027/13/40 25:61")
exercises this path.

Important consequence: the failure is whole-renderer, not per-row.
One bad `source_timestamp` in a batch blanks the entire customer's
chronology — not just the offending row. If that's intentional it
should be stated; if it's not, the per-row isolation should be
discussed with Mira before merge.

==============================================================================
4. LIMITING THE CLAIMS THE CHRONOLOGY MAY MAKE
==============================================================================

Given §1-§3, the chronology must NOT make any of the following claims:

  (a) That rows are ordered by when the underlying event happened.
      They are ordered by when the system processed them. The
      `delayed_retry` fixture proves this directly.

  (b) That "source-time ordering" is preserved across late-processed
      rows. It is not, by construction of this PR. The Oct 25 PE Q4
      posture (src-time preserved) no longer applies to this
      renderer.

  (c) That one bad row yields a degraded row. The renderer is
      fail-closed whole-batch: one malformed `source_timestamp` =
      empty chronology for the whole customer.

  (d) That "mixed-source" implies a stability guarantee across the
      two account scopes. `account_scope: [Harbor Health, Mosaic
      Commerce]` share the renderer; the PR does not document a
      per-account regression matrix. Before merging I want both
      accounts' representative fixtures run and the result posted.

What the chronology MAY claim, narrowly:

  - "Customer-visible timeline, ordered by Lantern processing time,
     descending."
  - "Renders only when every contributing record has a parseable
     source_timestamp; otherwise renders empty."
  - "Other time fields (observed_at, serialized_at, retry_at) are
     carried for audit and are not part of the visible order."

==============================================================================
REVIEW STATE
==============================================================================

PR is open 12 days, status open, reviewer=alex, review_state=pending.
I have not yet submitted a review on this PR — the analysis above is
my read of the PR contents. If you want me to file the review with
the claims in §4 as the requested scope-narrowing, confirm and I will
submit.
