mcp__dolphinbench_apps__list_calendar_ev.description:
List events overlapping one day in the timezone you specify.

        Args:
            date: Calendar date, YYYY-MM-DD.
            timezone: IANA timezone name, such as America/Los_Angeles or UTC.
                The same timezone is used for every event in this request.

        Returns:
            A list containing each event's id, title, start, end, attendees,
            and any body or location. An event ending exactly at the start of
            this day is excluded. Invalid dates, timezones, or stored event
            times return ok=false and an error, not an empty calendar.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__internal_search_.description:
Search supplied current documents by case-insensitive text in title, body,
        or tags. query must be nonempty. Returns the matching stored records and exact
        document ids, or an empty list. No documents or search results are invented.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__list_slack_chann.description: List the exact channel keys available for posting in this workspace.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__update_calendar_.description:
Change an existing calendar event without replacing its id.

        Args:
            event_id: Existing id from list_calendar_events.
            start: Optional new YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM, optionally with seconds,
                followed by Z or an explicit +HH:MM / -HH:MM offset.
            end: Optional new time in the same format. The resulting end
                must be later than the resulting start, even if only one changes.
            title: Optional nonempty replacement title.
            attendees: Optional replacement list of email addresses. Use []
                to remove all invitees. Use list_contacts to find addresses.
            body: Optional replacement description. Use an empty string to clear it.

        Returns:
            ok=true and the stored event. Omitted or null fields stay unchanged.
            Supply at least one field to change.
            A duplicate time range with a shared attendee is rejected, as on
            creation. Missing ids or invalid values return ok=false and an error;
            the original event stays unchanged.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__update_doc.description:
Change an existing document selected by exact doc_id from list_docs.

        body is literal text. replace stores body as the complete new document body;
        append adds it after one blank line when existing text is present. title and
        folder are optional replacements. mode must be replace or append. An unknown
        id or invalid field returns ok=false without creating or changing a document.
        Returns the complete stored document after the change.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__list_docs.description: List stored documents and the exact ids used by document tools.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__send_slack_messa.description:
Post a message to a workspace Slack channel.

        Args:
            channel: Exact key from list_slack_channels, including the leading #.
                Surrounding whitespace and capitalization are ignored. Unknown
                channels are rejected; this tool never creates channels.
            message: The nonempty message to post.

        Returns:
            A success record with the actual channel key and posted message,
            or an error with no message posted.

Mosaic capacity response — final decision record
Meeting: 2025-09-05 13:00–13:45 ET (scope-decision meeting, evt_faf10d62ac4847789c17ebf8ba035b2c)
Attendees: Hema, Cyrus, Wes, Roman, Nadia, Alex
Status: SCOPE DECIDED. NOT YET IN PRODUCTION.
Record date: 2025-09-05

This document supersedes the 2025-09-03 preparation brief. The scope of the
response was decided at the 2025-09-05 meeting. No production change is
authorized by this record, and nothing is running in production yet.

Forecast (unchanged from prep brief)
- Baseline: 11.8M points/min
- Projected Oct 6 peak: 16M points/min (+35%)
- Mosaic's forecast ramp has not begun.

Replay evidence (Cyrus, @16M)
- metrics-router pending-batch p99: 780ms
- q-full retries: 0.9%
- All other services: baseline (no degradation observed)

Isolated constraint (carried forward)
- Export queue is the FIRST constraint, not cross-service
- Cross-svc impact not observed at forecast load
- Cross-svc impact must remain baseline throughout any stage

DECISION — Scope
- Hema approved a BOUNDED metrics-router response.
- This is NOT a pipeline rewrite.
- The response is scoped to metrics-router only and uses the existing
  retryable backpressure path. No new cross-service behavior is introduced.

DECISION — Bounds (must hold for any stage)
- Global queue ceiling: 2,048 batches.
- Per-tenant ceiling: 64 pending batches.
- Additional work beyond the per-tenant ceiling is sent into the existing
  retryable backpressure path BEFORE acceptance. No silent accept, no drop.
- Bounds are evaluated continuously during any stage.

DECISION — Owners
- Wes — implementation, and load-test evidence for the bounded response.
- Alex — cross-service invariants, AND the future production-window
  opening decision. Alex does NOT own implementation.
- Cyrus + Roman — rollup-service capacity and parity evidence.
- Nadia — queue and refusal alert semantics.
- Hema — may reorder metrics cutover if production forces it
  (carried from prior; not changed by this decision).

DECISION — Stop conditions (any stage must stop on ANY of these)
- Queue-wait p99 exceeds 400 ms for five consecutive minutes.
- Retryable queue-full responses exceed 0.5% for five consecutive minutes.
- Any accepted batch is lost.
- Any consistency check, parity check, dropped-series check, route check,
  or full-health check leaves baseline.

Explicit non-changes (must NOT be inferred from this decision)
- The formal service-owner map is UNCHANGED. Wes does NOT become
  metrics-router primary. Alex remains metrics-router primary.
- Mosaic's forecast ramp HAS NOT BEGUN. This decision does not start it.
- Nothing is running in production yet. No stage is in production today.
- This decision does not authorize any production deployment, production
  rollout, or production-window opening.
- Cross-service invariants (consistency, parity, dropped-series, route,
  full-health) remain baseline requirements; they are also stop conditions.

Stage gating (forward-looking, not a current state)
- A stage may begin only after Wes has load-test evidence for the bounded
  response and Cyrus + Roman have rollup-service capacity and parity
  evidence.
- A production window may open only on Alex's decision, after evidence
  review.
- Any stage stops immediately on any of the stop conditions above.

Meeting outcome
- Bounded response: APPROVED (as scoped above).
- Accountable owners: CONFIRMED.
- Stop conditions: DEFINED.
- Production authorization: NOT GRANTED. No production change is approved
  at this meeting, and none is implied by this record.

Diagnostic and artifact-readiness evidence (accepted 2025-09-22)

The diagnostic finding that bounded the 2025-09-05 scope decision remains
accepted:

  - Baseline: 11.8M points/min.
  - Projected Oct 6 peak: 16M points/min (+35%).
  - Cyrus's @16M replay (the diagnostic that surfaced the bounded-response
    need): metrics-router pending-batch p99 = 780ms; q-full retries = 0.9%;
    all other services at baseline (no degradation observed).
  - Isolated constraint: export queue is the FIRST constraint, not
    cross-service. Cross-svc impact must remain baseline throughout any
    stage.

Artifact-readiness evidence accepted from Wes's operator-diagnostics packet
(2025-09-22), to be re-verified at the Tuesday 2025-09-23 14:00–14:30 ET
opening-evidence check (evt_faa59f77ffe04b47ae1f98eb7ad0531b) before the
owner-led production window opens:

  1. Aggregate metrics carry no tenant identity.
  2. The permissioned snapshot selects every tenant that reached 64
     pending batches OR received a retryable refusal during the interval.
  3. The snapshot displays at most 20 tenant entries and emits an
     overflow count.
  4. 200-tenant stress run: the first 20 affected tenants are listed,
     overflow = 180, and aggregate saturation and refusal counts
     reconcile.
  5. The deploy pipeline produced the signed candidate artifact for the
     approved September 24–26 owner-led window.

Acceptance boundaries (unchanged):

  - Staged order: Wed 2025-09-24 10→50% with verify between stages; Thu
    2025-09-25 100% only after opening evidence and full-health-set at
    baseline; Fri 2025-09-26 monitor only, no push.
  - Stop conditions (any one halts the active stage, 5 continuous minutes
    unless noted): queue-wait p99 > 400 ms; retryable queue-full ratio
    > 0.5%; any accepted-batch loss; baseline departure on consistency,
    parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service,
    or full-health.
  - Role split: Alex opens; Wes runs the bounded implementation slice;
    Cyrus + Roman provide rollup evidence; Nadia owns alert semantics;
    mapped service owners retain execution authority for their pushes
    (formal owner map unchanged).
  - No production movement before 2025-09-24. Eligibility + scheduling
    != production result.

This acceptance updates the 2025-09-05 record with the operator-diagnostics
packet Wes supplied on 2025-09-22. It does NOT start the Mosaic Commerce
forecast ramp, does NOT authorize any production deployment, and does NOT
change any ownership, scope, or boundary recorded above. The decision
record remains NOT IN PRODUCTION.

Opening-evidence preflight (completed 2025-09-23 14:42 ET)

Verified together with Wes, Cyrus, Roman, and Nadia against the operator-diagnostics runbook, immediately before the owner-led production window opens Wednesday 2025-09-24:

  1. Signed deploy-pipeline artifact matches the accepted candidate.
  2. Aggregate metrics carry no tenant identity.
  3. Permissioned diagnostic selects every tenant that reaches 64 pending batches or receives a retryable refusal, with a 20-entry display cap and overflow count.
  4. Source-classified alerts ready (Nadia's v2: q_wait_p99{src}>400 cause, retry_q_full{src}>0.005 symptom; 5min; src∈{live_prod,staged,replay}; halts active stage, live_prod pages).
  5. Rollup-service capacity and parity evidence current (Cyrus + Roman).
  6. Shard-keeper lease health and the full opening health set at baseline.

  - Wes used the deploy pipeline to move the tenant-bounded queue control through 10% and 50%, waiting for the complete health set to return to baseline after each stage.
  - 50% readings: queue-wait p99 = 218 ms; retryable queue-full ratio = 0.05% (both under the operative hard stops).

## 3. Authorization boundary preserved for this review

The Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce two-account read-only boundary remains in effect for the duration of the June 24 review. This frozen package does not extend, narrow, or re-scope it.

- Mode: read-only. No write access, no new account is admitted by this package.
- Effective interval for the review: 2027-04-01 through 2027-06-15 (the frozen window). The 2027-04-01 grant runs through 2027-09-30 and is not modified by this package.
- Same-tenant requirement: a lookup is in scope only when tenant scope matches the requesting account.
- Published-service requirement: ownership rendering is limited to services present in the published owner map.
- Independent freshness and provenance: each contributing source carries its own freshness and provenance; freshness and provenance are not inferred across sources.
- 24-hour source-timestamp limit: contributing sources for a single combined explanation must be no more than 24 elapsed hours apart; otherwise the case is held separate (see section 5) and is not treated as an eligible combined explanation.
- Separate timestamped display without causal wording beyond the 24-hour spread: rendering presents timestamped states without stitching them into a causal narrative.
- Excluded surfaces (rendered as excluded, not as data): cost data; raw incident text; internal room metadata; employee identifiers or employee comparisons; inferred or unpublished ownership; internal-only fallback data; write access; new accounts.

Permitted surface for this review (the four classes of evidence this package reconciles):

1. Provenance-backed deploy movement — deploy events with required provenance and required source timestamp.
2. Published service ownership — ownership rendered only from the published owner map (including alias-resolved identities per the published-alias path).

Status: accepted plan from the Q2 operating-focus discussion with Hema on 2027-04-02 (10:30–11:15 AM ET). Planning material, not a new ownership or product decision. Boundaries below are unchanged.

This document is live evidence only — it does not state that the shadow is complete, that continuing internal operating use is approved, or that any customer exposure is approved.

Status as of 2026-11-13 09:10 ET
- Shadow admitted to bounded internal use on 2026-11-12; observation window opens today.
- Customer paths (Harbor Health, Mosaic Commerce) remain disconnected from Lantern reference integration.
- No mutation capability, no authority-payload copy, no tenant crossing has been authorized in the shadow.

Cumulative render counts
- Run counters for the window start at zero today. Daily counts will be appended here as the window progresses, with a per-day breakdown of: total renders, renders with two preserved references, renders with explicit-unknown from stale or missing authority, denied requests, and adapter calls (expected: zero on denial).
- Total to date across the window will be the sum of the daily counts. No day will be marked closed until the count for that day has been recorded.

Dual-reference identity and timestamp checks
- Every rendered reference must retain its own authority_record_id and its own source_timestamp. The four-part identity is (tenant_id, authority_record_id, authority_type, canonical_service_id); the corrected reference model keys on all four.
- Both insertion orders are in scope: owner-map first then Cardinality Guardrails, and Cardinality Guardrails first then owner-map. All 24 dual-authority cases from the 2026-11-12 evidence review are expected to preserve separate references in both orders inside the shadow as well.
- A render that drops a source_timestamp or collapses two references into one is an evidence defect and will be recorded here with the run identifier and the affected authority_record_id.

Staff operating-use observations
- Scope is restricted to Infra and Product Engineering. Production customer traffic remains on the prior path; no customer-facing service returns Lantern-derived references in this window.
- Observations will be appended as staff use the build in real internal workflows (metrics-router dual-reference cards and similar). Each observation will note the workflow, the references seen, and any unexpected behavior.
- Observations are staff operating use, not approval of continuing operating use. Any request to extend staff use past 2026-11-25 must come back through review.

Iris's interpretation check
- Iris (interpretation owner) reviews whether the references surfaced by the corrected build match the intended semantic distinction between owner-map authority and Cardinality Guardrails authority.
- Check is recorded as a per-run note when a metrics-router dual-reference card is exercised in a real internal workflow (e.g. the 2026-11-17 operating review). Failures and ambiguities are appended with the exact reference ids and the question Iris raised.
- A passing interpretation check on one card does not generalize; Iris's sign-off covers only the cases explicitly reviewed.

Customer-path isolation
- Harbor Health-shaped and Mosaic Commerce-shaped request shapes are exercised inside the shadow, but no shadow run is permitted to create a request or artifact in either customer path. Evidence of isolation is the absence of customer-path side effects across all shadow runs in the window.
- Any observed side effect in a customer path is a containment defect and is appended with the run identifier, the path affected, and the artifact observed.

Final review status
- In progress as of 2026-11-13. Window end is 2026-11-25.
- This document does not state, and is not a basis for anyone to infer, that the shadow is complete, that continuing internal operating use is approved, or that any customer exposure is approved.
- Closing review requires: completed cumulative counts through 2026-11-25, identity and timestamp checks with no unrecorded defects, staff observations captured, Iris's interpretation check recorded for at least one real-workflow card, and customer-path isolation evidence with zero observed side effects. Closing review is a separate decision and is not pre-claimed here.

arguments.body:
Lantern shared-integration continuation — October 2026 operating-handoff decision record

Document type: durable decision record (separate from the completed Jun 16 – Sep 15 evidence-review document and the Sep 8 reference-only rehearsal). This record carries the October operating handoff and is the reference for any future re-authorization, scope question, or suspension trigger.

Decision date: 2026-09-24
Decision meeting: Lantern continuation and platform-boundary decision meeting, 10:30 – 11:15 AM
Authorizing parties: Hema and Theo
Reviewing parties present: Alex (shared-contract owner), Iris (interpretation/adoption), Cyrus (CG authority interface), Wes (metrics-router control mappings and operating evidence), Product Engineering (Lantern implementation)

1. Authorization scope (effective 2026-10-01 through 2027-03-31)

1.1 Authorized accounts
- Harbor Health — authorized to continue.
- Mosaic Commerce — authorized to continue.
- No other account is authorized under this decision.

1.2 Effective window
- Start: 2026-10-01.
- End: 2027-03-31.
- The renewed term does not activate before 2026-10-01. Pre-October-1 operation remains under the prior evidence-review posture.

1.3 Access mode
- Read-only, through the shared authorization wrapper.
- No write capability is authorized.

2. Authorized content surface

The shared integration may render, for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce only:
- Provenance-backed deploy movement.
- Published service ownership.
- Timestamped incident-load summaries, including their source timestamp.
- Explicit unknown states.

Everything below the line is NOT authorized and must never appear on the customer-facing surface:
- Additional accounts beyond Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.
- Cost data.
- CSV export.
- Raw incident text.
- Internal room metadata.
- Employee identifier or comparison.
- Inferred or unpublished ownership.
- Internal-only fallback data.
- Write capability.
- Release-readiness judgment.
- Employee-performance interpretation.

3. Suspension triggers (immediate, both accounts, pending correction)

Any one of the following immediately suspends BOTH Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check:

- Authorization-wrapper bypass.
- Adapter call after denial.
- Cross-tenant material.
- Stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown.
- Deploy event without required provenance.
- Unpublished ownership.
- Incident-load summary without its source timestamp.
- Exposure of an excluded field.
- Loss of read-only enforcement.

Latency and other errors do not independently suspend access unless they cause one of the violations above.

4. Shared-integration contract

- Identity basis: canonical published service identity.
- Integration fields (exactly these five, no additions):
  - tenant_id
  - canonical_service_id
  - authority_type
  - authority_record_id
  - source_timestamp
- No copied authority payload.
- No writeback.

5. Authority map (unaffected by this decision)

- Lantern: explanation layer.
- Cardinality Guardrails: authority for pipeline limits and cost signals. Cyrus owns the CG authority interface and cost semantics.
- Owner map: authority for published responsibility.
- Mosaic limit/cost and Harbor owner-correction remain outside the rendered surface; this decision does not change those boundaries.

6. Internal platform cycle (separate authorization track)

- Hema accepted the reference-only model as the starting point for an internal platform cycle beginning 2026-10-01.
- The internal platform cycle does not begin early.
- This decision does NOT authorize customer exposure of the reference-only integration. Customer exposure still requires a separate later authorization.

7. Operating ownership under this decision

- Shared contract and failure-mode boundaries: Alex (owner).
- Interpretation and adoption criteria: Iris.
- Cardinality Guardrails authority interface and cost semantics: Cyrus.
- metrics-router control mappings and operating evidence: Wes.
- Lantern implementation: Product Engineering.

8. Re-authorization prerequisites

Any continuation beyond 2027-03-31, any expansion of the authorized account set, any addition to the integration field set, any change from read-only, or any customer exposure of this reference-only integration requires a separate later authorization and a new decision record.

9. Cross-references

- Completed evidence-review document (June 16 – September 15 operating evidence; not updated by this record).
- Sep 8 reference-only rehearsal (separate track; not customer-facing).
- Lantern cross-service doc: doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.
- Mosaic closed-state doc: doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937.

End of decision record.

## §9.2  Lantern — reconciled June 16–September 15 evidence (2,476 customer sessions, no listed safety violation)

## §9.3  Growth-focus framing (per Hema's 11-09 rule)

This is owner leverage, not delegating people. (Durable rule from Hema 2026 self-review: do NOT frame this as delegating people.)

# §10  FORM-READY VERSION — revised 2026-11-09 (per Hema's 11-09 feedback)

The three Sphere portal fields, with the quantified anchors from §9 woven in. Word counts re-checked against the portal caps (Outcomes/impact ≤500, How I worked ≤350, Growth focus 2027 ≤200).

## FIELD 1 — Outcomes and impact (≤500 words; ~445)

- Cross-service authority and cardinality invariants defined and adopted (Cardinality Guardrails; tenant-isolation, provenance, and auth-source-timestamp invariants; dup-deploy dedup key pinned to (tenant_id, published_service_id, provenance_source, source_event_id)).

October 22 owner-boundary review confirmed I was not a centralized gate and that routine decisions remained with mapped owners.
- Cardinality Guardrails mechanism gives metrics-router a named authority for its operating control, even when an enforcement location is elsewhere.

## FIELD 2 — How I worked (≤350 words; ~265)

- Reviewer frame, not gate. Routine authority moved to mapped owners (Wes on metrics-router; Cyrus on shard-keeper#190; PE on the Lantern implementation slice). I retained only the named exception path and was not a centralized approval gate.

- Used evidence over claim. Where evidence was reconcilable (e.g., the June 16–September 15 reconciled Lantern window covering 2,476 customer sessions with no listed safety violation), I let the reconciled number carry the argument rather than restating it from memory.

## FIELD 3 — Growth focus for 2027 (≤200 words; ~165)

Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft
Working draft for later revision. Bounded to IC role; no claim of managing people, owning every release, or becoming a centralized approval gate. Organized as Hema requested: cross-service invariants and failure modes, technical outcomes, owner leverage, and boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners.

Frame: I review only where work crosses service boundaries or introduces new failure modes; otherwise it stays with mapped owners. Below are the concrete 2026 items that fit that frame, with the source artifacts that ground each claim.

1. Cross-service invariants and failure modes I reviewed

1.1 Authority boundaries and the Cardinality Guardrails design
- What: Defined the invariants that an authority record must preserve when an internal implementation slice attaches read-only owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references to the same canonical service. The invariants — authority_type + authority_record_id + source_timestamp — must be preserved unchanged; if no reference can be produced, the request is sent to Harbor/Mosaic rather than silently losing provenance.
- Why it crosses a boundary: owner-map references and Cardinality Guardrails touch the model used by Harbor, Mosaic, and downstream consumers. Changing how authority is referenced affects every service that reasons about identity. I treated this as a cross-service invariant, not a routine implementation decision, and surfaced the rule rather than letting it get absorbed into a single team's PR.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 (Oct 22 owner-boundary review, closed).
- Bounded to IC: I defined the invariant; the implementation slice is owned and merged by the mapped owner. I did not become the approval gate for the slice.

1.2 Duplicate-deploy dedup key
- What: Stated the dedup key as (tenant_id, published_service_id, provenance_source, source_event_id); missing any field → "unavailable" rather than best-guess.
- Why it crosses a boundary: dedup spans ingest-edge → metrics-router → shard-keeper. A wrong key in any one of them double-counts downstream; a too-loose key silently drops events. Pinning the key and the missing-field behavior was the cross-service invariant. The implementation in each service stayed with the mapped owner.
- Source: memory, 2025-08-12.

1.3 Tenant isolation for edge-gateway / ingest-edge
- What: Treated tenant isolation as a cross-service invariant, not a per-service detail, and insisted any change that could weaken tenant boundaries be reviewed across services.
- Why it crosses a boundary: a per-tenant bleed in edge-gateway or ingest-edge shows up as misattributed traffic or cardinality in metrics-router. Reviewing it at the boundary is where I add value.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 (scope of Alex review enumerated as: tenant isolation, provenance, auth source timestamps, authority duplication/mutation, customer-path isolation).

1.4 Provenance and auth source timestamps
- What: Reviewed changes touching how provenance_source and auth source timestamps flow through the pipeline, because a drift here corrupts the dedup key and the authority record in 1.1/1.2 simultaneously.
- Source: same closed doc as 1.1/1.3.

2. Technical outcomes

2.1 Mosaic forward-gate criteria, closed 2026-01-22
- What: Documented and validated the forward-gate criteria for Mosaic past the 17.2M forecast: 90 minutes at +15% load, q-p99 ≤ 400ms held for 5 minutes, queue-full ≤ 0.5% held for 5 minutes. Pre-accept backpressure is retryable. Capacity: 2,048 global / 64 per-tenant.
- Outcome: gate criteria were adopted as the cutover bar; the gate is documented (doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937).
- Source: memory, 2026-01-22 entry.

2.2 shard-keeper#190 (Cyrus) cutover, closed 2026-09-17
- What: Confirmed the cutover was closed and scoped to replay-fixture cleanup. Pinned the gate: an id-carrying reject from a prior-epoch must be honored before any comms promise — i.e., verify the address before promising reachability. This is a concrete instance of "review only at boundaries that introduce new failure modes": the prior-epoch reject is exactly the kind of failure mode a comms-only check would have missed.
- Source: memory, 2026-09-17 entry.

2.3 Apr 14 shard-keeper / rollup-service outage
- What: Co-authored the postmortem (doc_postmortem_apr14_outage, 2026-04-21). The postmortem identifies the cross-service failure mode between shard-keeper and rollup-service.
- Bounded to IC: postmortem authorship is review-by-default, not ownership of either service's roadmap. Wes runs responder paths; Nadia runs postmortem process; I am one of the reviewers on cross-service failure cases.
- Source: doc_postmortem_apr14_outage.

3. Owner leverage: where I made a difference without becoming the owner

3.1 Metrics-router ownership transition (Wes primary, Alex backup)
- What: Stood up as backup on metrics-router during Hema's metrics migration so the cutover could proceed without single-point risk. Hema may reorder cutover; backup coverage is what kept the migration reversible.
- Outcome: Wes is the primary owner; I am backup only. The backup role was deliberately scoped to "present and able to act", not "second owner with parallel roadmap authority."
- Bounded to IC: I do not own metrics-router's roadmap, release cadence, or PR queue; I review at boundaries. This is leverage from being the right reviewer at the right moment, not leverage from accumulating ownership.
- Source: user profile; Hema collaboration note.

3.2 Lantern's corrected review routing
- What: The Lantern owner-model was validated as NOT an implementation / release-gate by Hema in the Oct 9 1:1. The routine Lantern work — copy, fixture-naming — stays with the mapped owner. I review only the cross-service slice: tenant isolation, provenance, auth source timestamps, authority duplication/mutation, customer-path isolation. This corrects an earlier drift where Lantern review could have been read as "Alex reviews Lantern changes" in general.
- Outcome: routing is now explicit and bounded. Routine → mapped owner; cross-service → Alex.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.

3.3 October 22 owner-boundary review (closed)
- What: At the Q4 owner-boundary review on 2026-10-22, two routine items were tested against my review scope: PE-routine Lantern copy / fixture-naming, and Wes-routine metrics-router staging route-cache param. Both were off-boundary for me and stayed with the mapped reviewers. The incident-practice split was preserved (Wes = responder paths, Nadia = postmortem process, Alex = cross-service failure cases only).
- Outcome: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation, no Lantern first-slice decision, no internal-shadow decision, no customer/platform-scope decision triggered. The review closed with the boundary intact.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-22 entry.

4. Boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners

4.1 I do not own releases. I review PRs that touch cross-service invariants (authority boundaries, dedup key, tenant isolation, provenance, customer-path isolation, prior-epoch gate semantics). I do not own metrics-router's release calendar, ingest-edge's deploys, or shard-keeper's cutover execution.

4.2 I do not manage people. I author and co-author postmortems and review docs; the people-management actions (hiring, leveling, performance, comp) are not part of my role and are not claimed here.

4.3 I do not act as a centralized approval gate. The Oct 22 review specifically confirmed: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation. Routine work routes to mapped owners; my review appears only at the boundary.

4.4 Internal implementation slices may attach read-only owner-map + Cardinality Guardrails references to the same canonical service, and must preserve authority_type + authority_record_id + source_timestamp; no reference output routes to Harbor/Mosaic. I stated the invariant; the slice is implemented and merged by the mapped owner.

4.5 Incident practice split is intact and was reaffirmed on 2026-10-22: Wes owns responder paths, Nadia owns postmortem process, I review cross-service failure cases only.

5. Items I deliberately did not claim
- Did not claim to own metrics-router, ingest-edge, or shard-keeper.
- Did not claim to run the metrics migration (Hema runs it; I am a reviewer and backup).
- Did not claim to be the postmortem owner (Nadia owns the postmortem process; I am a reviewer and co-author on the cross-service cases).
- Did not claim to have approved or rejected any release on my own authority — my review appears at the boundary, the mapped owner decides.
- Did not claim any centralized approval role; the Oct 22 review explicitly foreclosed that interpretation.

6. Open items for revision before submission
- Refresh doc-id references in §7 against current documents (doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5, doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937, doc_postmortem_apr14_outage) if any have moved.
- Replace any item where I have only the headline with the concrete artifact (PR link, metric, or runbook entry) Hema will want to see.
- Decide which 1.x items to keep in the narrative vs. fold into a single "boundary invariants" paragraph.
- Add the exact 17.2M forecast number and the q-p99 / queue-full numbers into §2.1 if Hema wants the gate numbers in the narrative rather than only in the doc reference.
- Confirm the metrics-router backup scope (present-and-able-to-act vs. deeper) before submission so it does not get read as co-ownership.
- Final portal verification and submission still due Fri 2026-11-13 17:00 ET.

7. Source index
- doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 — closed Lantern review / Oct 22 owner-boundary review (Hema 1:1 validation, owner-model scope, internal-slice invariants).
- doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937 — Mosaic forward gate (2,048 global / 64 per-tenant, +15% load, q-p99 ≤ 400ms × 5m, queue-full ≤ 0.5% × 5m).
- doc_postmortem_apr14_outage — Apr 14 shard-keeper / rollup-service postmortem (2026-04-21).
- Memory entries: 2026-01-22 (Mosaic), 2026-09-17 (shard-keeper#190), 2026-10-22 (owner-boundary review), 2025-08-12 (dedup key).
- User profile: metrics pipeline ownership (Wes primary / Alex backup), Hema collaboration on metrics migration.

8. Dated Q4 examples — owner-boundary review and corrected review routing

These two examples sit in the same week and together show how the boundary actually operated: routine items stayed with mapped owners, and the named boundary case pulled me in without my becoming a centralized gate.

8.1 October 22, 2026 — owner-boundary review (routine stays with mapped owners)
- What I did: At the Q4 owner-boundary review I tested two routine items against my review scope: PE-routine Lantern copy / fixture-naming, and Wes-routine metrics-router staging route-cache param. Both were off-boundary for me and stayed with the mapped reviewers.
- Why this fits the framing: routine implementation work does not pull into my review queue even when the PR shows up next to ones that do. The boundary held without me declining in the abstract — the review itself was the disambiguator.
- Outcome: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation, no Lantern first-slice decision, no internal-shadow decision, no customer/platform-scope decision triggered. Wes = responder paths, Nadia = postmortem process, Alex = cross-service failure cases only. Review closed with the boundary intact.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-22 entry; closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.
- Bounded to IC: I was a reviewer at the boundary meeting, not the meeting's owner; nothing here gives me a release authority, an approval queue, or a reviewer-of-record role on routine Lantern or metrics-router PRs.

8.2 October 27, 2026 — corrected review routing engaged me for a named boundary (defense without takeover)
- Trigger: corrected review routing surfaced an actual named boundary — an order-dependent overwrite between owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references attached to the same canonical service. Each reference is keyed (tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id), each with its own source_timestamp; insertion order determines the surviving authority. This is a shared-contract defect, not a per-service implementation choice.
- What I did: I blocked the staff-only build and the internal shadow on the shared-contract defect, because proceeding would have committed an internal surface area to an order-sensitive reference contract that we could not yet defend. I did not take over Product Engineering's implementation of the fix.
- What I did NOT do: I did not reassign the implementation to myself, did not draft the fix, did not schedule a release, did not authorize internal shadow, and did not expand any customer scope. Product Engineering remained the implementation owner; my role was to refuse to advance an unrepaired defect across the shared contract.
- Resolution (per November 12, 2026 Lantern evidence review): the October 27 order-dependent overwrite is fixed. The corrected dual-authority build passed the bounded contract review (closed) and entered bounded internal shadow for Infra and Product Engineering under the conditions set by that review. The implementation slice remained with Product Engineering throughout. The reference integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce; no internal shadow, no staff-only preview, no dark-launch cohort touches either customer path, and no customer scope changed.
- Why this fits the framing: this is the named-boundary case the Oct 22 review reserved me for. Routine owner-map edits and routine Cardinality Guardrails changes still route to their mapped owners; the order-sensitive overwrite between them was the cross-service invariant the boundary is for. The right response was to block the advance and return the fix to the implementation owner; the right resolution was to verify the contract once the corrected code came back, admit the build to bounded internal shadow, and stop short of any customer-path change. I reviewed the contract and the failure boundary; Product Engineering owned the implementation throughout; the customer paths stayed out of scope.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-27 entry (Lantern first-internal-slice HELD; correction owed by PE); November 12 Lantern evidence review (closed), with corrected build admitted to bounded internal shadow for Infra and PE only.
- Bounded to IC: I added one block on a shared-contract defect and named the invariant that must hold after PE's correction. I did not become Product Engineering's reviewer-of-record, did not take the slice into my roadmap, and did not become a gate on Lantern first-slice decisions beyond the named defect. With the defect fixed and the contract review closed, the boundary returns to its standing rule: routine Lantern work routes to the mapped owner, and my reviewer frame stays reserved for cross-service failure cases.

8.3 Net reading for Hema (one paragraph, no claims beyond §8.1 and §8.2)
The Oct 22 review confirmed routine stays with mapped owners and I am not a centralized gate. The Oct 27 corrected review routing showed what the boundary looks like when it actually fires — a named shared-contract defect, a block on the staff-only build and internal shadow, and an explicit return-to-owner for the fix. The November 12 evidence review then verified the corrected code against the named invariant, closed the contract review, and admitted the build to bounded internal shadow for Infra and Product Engineering only. I reviewed the contract and the failure boundary; Product Engineering owned the implementation throughout; the customer paths stayed out of scope; reference integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce; the build has not graduated to continuing internal operating use.

input.body:
Hey Devika — happy new year. Want to start planning our next short trip with Kibo. Heads up: I didn't have a stored "current travel preference" I could pull when I sat down to draft this, so the shape below is built from the constraints I do know (Kibo's vet in South Slope, the shared-free-wknd rule, your hospitalist shifts, my forearm warmup routine). Tell me if I'm off and I'll redo it.

Proposal: 3 days / 2 nights over a fully shared free weekend, driving rather than flying (calmer for Kibo, no cargo hold). Within ~2-3 hrs of Brooklyn so we're close to his vet if anything comes up. Pet-friendly ground-floor stay or cabin with a fenced outdoor area — no big staircases for his knees.

Structure:
- Day 1: arrive by early afternoon, slow walk to settle him, dinner in
- Day 2: one low-key outing (easy trail or quiet beach), then a real rest block at the stay midday — that's also my forearm recharge window
- Day 3: AM walk + breakfast, pack up, drive home before dark

Split: I'll do AM walk + breakfast for Kibo, you take PM dinner + walk. Built-in buffer if either of us needs a quieter block.

Timing: any weekend we're both fully free, avoiding your hospitalist days and the quarterly docs-update block. A Feb weekend looks like the cleanest fit — let me know what works and I'll start looking at places.

The body is short and procedural, followed by three dated canary notes. The top-level steps cover only OTel collector batch window, p99-vs-baseline comparison, and pipeline rollback on confirmed regression. There is no section on per-pod generation accumulation or cleanup latency.

---

## Canary note — 2023-08-16 (scheduled load-test label noise)

Context: Severity-3 cardinality canary fired while Cyrus was running a scheduled load test against metrics-router. Wes isolated the spike to an unbounded `experiment_id` label coming only from the load-test traffic, checked the deploy path, and confirmed the service itself was not regressing. Cyrus stopped the load test and the canary cleared without escalation or rollback. This note is for the next responder.

- **A cardinality canary during a known scheduled load test is expected to trip, not a service regression.** Before treating the alert as a metrics-router regression, confirm whether a scheduled load test is in progress (check #ops-loadtests / ask Cyrus / check the load-test calendar). If yes, do not rollback.
- **Isolate the label to the load-test traffic first.** Check whether the unbounded labels (`experiment_id`, `user_id`, `request_id`, anything tenant/key-shaped) are present only on load-test traffic or also on production traffic. If load-test-only, the spike is from the load generator, not from metrics-router.
- **Check the deploy path, but do not assume deploy is the cause.** A green canary + a recent config-only change + a load test in flight usually means the load test is the source. Wes's 2023-08-16 investigation pattern is the reference: isolate label → rule out deploy → rule out downstream → confirm load-test scope → ask the load-test owner to stop.
- **Coordinate with the load-test owner before stopping or rolling back.** Cyrus stops the load test on confirmation; do not rollback metrics-router without that conversation. Rollback during a load-test-driven alert is the wrong action and creates a second incident.
- **No cardinality-control project, no ownership change.** This is a documentation note so the next responder does the same fast isolation rather than treating noise as a regression. Cardinality controls on load-test labels are tracked separately and are not owned by the canary response.

---

## Canary note — 2023-09-07 (post-canary CPU-only warmup, not a rollback)

Context: Second day of metrics-router data after the config-checksum cleanup canary. The affected AZ's CPU uplift has settled to ~2–3%, checksum-cache invalidations are back near baseline, cache-cardinality stayed flat, p99 stayed inside the normal 182–188 ms band, error rate stayed at 0.02%, dropped writes stayed clean, and rollup-service lag stayed flat. No user-visible signal moved. Closing as checksum-cache warmup after the config-checksum cleanup, not a rollback case.

- **A small residual CPU uplift in one AZ on the first 1–2 days after a config-checksum cleanup is warmup, not a regression.** Cache entries rehydrate under the new checksum regime; CPU cost comes back to baseline as the cache refills. Do not rollback on CPU alone if p99, error rate, dropped writes, cache-cardinality, and downstream lag are all flat.
- **Re-check the four user-visible signals before any rollback action.** p99 (must stay in the 182–188 ms band), error rate (~0.02% baseline), dropped writes (clean), and rollup-service lag (flat). If all four are flat, the rollout is fine and the residual CPU is warmup.
- **Checksum-cache invalidations returning near baseline is the confirming signal.** Elevated invalidations dominated by `checksum-mismatch-on-read` would be a different problem (would reconsider the rollout). Invalidations back near baseline + cache-cardinality flat means the cache is settling, not churning.
- **Triggers that WOULD change the call:** cache-hit ratio in the affected AZ dropping materially; checksum-cache invalidations dominated by `checksum-mismatch-on-read`; any of the four user-visible signals (p99 / error rate / dropped writes / rollup-service lag) moving off baseline. None of these fired on 2023-09-07.
- **No second-day page expected.** This note exists so the next on-call does not treat CPU-only post-canary warmup as an automatic rollback. If the four user-visible signals stay flat, leave the rollout in place and let the cache finish warming.

---

## Canary note — 2023-09-27 (parser-cache warmup during canary, not a rollback)

Context: Tiny metrics-router parser cleanup canary warmup ran on 2023-09-26; full rollout through the deploy pipeline finished on 2023-09-27 and stayed quiet. p99 stayed in the normal band, error rate held at 0.02%, dropped writes stayed clean, rollup-service lag stayed flat, and parser-cache misses did not repeat on full rollout. Closing as a parser-cache warmup that the canary allowed to hold, not a rollback case. This note is for the next responder who sees parser-cache misses during a future parser-cleanup canary.

- **A short burst of parser-cache misses during a parser-cleanup canary is warmup, not a regression.** The parser cache rehydrates against the new parser path while the canary holds. Treat parser-cache misses during canary the same way as the 2023-09-07 checksum-cache warmup: hold the rollout and verify on the four user-visible signals before any rollback action.
- **Hold and verify on the four user-visible signals.** p99 must return to baseline, and error rate (~0.02%), dropped writes (clean), and rollup-service lag (flat) must stay flat. If all four hold, the warmup is settling and the rollout can proceed.
- **Parser-cache misses stopping on their own is the confirming signal.** Parser-cache misses that recede as the cache fills under the new parser path means the cache is settling, not churning. Continued parser-cache misses at canary traffic level with any of the four user-visible signals moving off baseline is a different problem.
- **Triggers that WOULD change the call:** any of the four user-visible signals (p99 / error rate / dropped writes / rollup-service lag) moving off baseline during the warmup window; parser-cache misses that do not recede as the canary holds; a parser-cache miss rate that grows against steady canary traffic instead of decaying. None of these fired on 2023-09-27.
- **Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged.** The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) and the canary gating criteria still apply. This note only describes how to interpret a parser-cache warmup within those requirements; it does not relax any of them.
- **No parser-cache warmup page expected for a future parser-cleanup canary.** If the four user-visible signals stay flat, hold the rollout through the warmup and let the parser cache finish warming.

pr.title: metrics-router: lengthen OTel collector batch window

tests.answer:
PR data (from get_pr, listing-confirmed id):

  Title:  metrics-router: lengthen OTel collector batch window
  Author: morgan    Branch: morgan/otel-longer-batch-window
  Opened:  2027-12-29 10:20 -05:00    Reviewers: alex    Assignees: morgan
  Status: open
  Diff:    OTel collector config only; no other runtime change.
  Bench:   8 h steady load → collector CPU -7%, resident memory flat.
  PR description explicitly states: no burst-traffic results, no
           historical tuning context, no canary analysis.

Earlier batch-window evidence (from the runbook + prior incidents):

  - `rb_metrics_router_canary` step 1 is "Check the OTel collector batch
    window." Step 2 is "Compare p99 vs baseline." Step 3 is "Roll back
    via pipeline if regression confirmed." The batch window is the FIRST
    diagnostic on a canary or incident for this service — not the
    fourth. That is exactly the knob a longer window weakens.
  - The four user-visible signals tied to it: p99 in 182–188 ms, error
    rate ~0.02%, dropped writes clean, rollup-service lag flat.
  - 2023-09-07 / 2023-09-27 warmup notes: a transient p99 spike that
    recovers while active/retired generation counts stay consistent and
    cleanup pauses stay bounded is warmup, not a regression. Do not
    rollback on p99 alone. But that framing was written for cache
    warmups, not for a config change that lengthens the export queue.
  - 2024-12-26 holiday-evening canary (7/420 errors, all one synthetic
    id, intervals either side clean): canary panel can trip on near-
    idle traffic. A longer batch window makes the panel see less of
    the real export shape during low traffic, which is precisely when
    a batch-window regression would be hardest to distinguish from
    noise — opposite of the safety direction we want.
  - Window rule (2024-07-25, still in force per the 2026-09-13 read):
    window is the unit I open; no window carries forward; mapped
    operators may make single-file pushes only while the full health
    set is at baseline, and each push must return the full health set
    to baseline before the next push lands. Threshold stops (>4
    retired gens or >100 ms cleanup-pause p99) end the window
    automatically.

Why this PR is not yet safe to accept:

  Morgan's evidence covers steady load only. A longer OTel collector
  batch window lengthens the head-of-line buffer; under burst that is
  exactly the regime where p99 inflates, export is delayed, and the
  four user-visible signals are the ones that move. Steady-load -7%
  CPU does not refute a burst p99 excursion — and on this service,
  p99 is the primary canary signal. The PR also omits what value the
  window is being moved to and from, so we cannot tell whether this
  is a small step or a step past a previously known cliff.

Evidence required before acceptance:

  1. Burst-traffic benchmark. Same 8 h duration, but with the current
     production burst profile (and a worst-case shape — burst that
     exceeds batch_size, sustained spike that outlasts the new
     window). Report, at minimum, against the unchanged baseline:
     - collector CPU (should still be ≤ -7% under burst, not higher)
     - p99 of route decisions, against the 182–188 ms baseline band
     - error rate vs ~0.02% baseline
     - dropped writes (must stay clean)
     - rollup-service lag (must stay flat)
     - per-pod retired-generation count and cleanup-pause p99
       (must stay ≤ 4 and ≤ 100 ms — the window-rule ceilings)
     If p99, error rate, dropped writes, or rollup-service lag moves
     off baseline, this change does not pass even before the canary.
  2. Historical tuning context. From/to values of the batch window,
     and the last time this knob was changed (and why). If we have
     previously walked past this value and rolled back, that must be
     cited here, not rediscovered at canary time.
  3. Cardinality Guardrails preflight result for the new config
     (canary gating requirement, unchanged).

Rollout step required before acceptance:

  Stage through the metrics-router canary under an explicit canary
  window I open, mapped to `rb_metrics_router_canary`:
  (a) Open a fresh window for this PR — not a carried-forward
      window. Window rule requires a fresh decision for the first
      window after any prior window's fully observed push closes.
  (b) Single-file push via the deploy pipeline only.
  (c) Watch the batch window itself (step 1), then p99 vs the 182–
      188 ms baseline (step 2). Treat any of the four user-visible
      signals moving off baseline as a hard stop, not warmup — this
      is a config knob change, not a cache rehydration, so the
      warmup framing from 2023-09-07 / 2023-09-27 does not extend
      to it. A retired-gen count above 4 or cleanup-pause p99 above
      100 ms ends the window automatically.
  (d) Pre-authorize the pipeline rollback path (step 3) before the
      push lands, with morgan's confirmation that rollback is a
      one-pipeline-action revert of this exact config change.
  (e) Window closes only after the full health set returns to
      baseline and has held there through one full burst window of
      the production shape from (1).

  Until burst-traffic benchmark, historical tuning context, and a
  canary analysis that names the four signals above land in the PR
  description, the safe response is request_changes citing the three
  gaps morgan already flagged in their own description.

1. Check the OTel collector batch window.

## Canary note — 2023-08-16 (scheduled load-test label noise)

Context: Severity-3 cardinality canary fired while Cyrus was running a scheduled load test against metrics-router. Wes isolated the spike to an unbounded `experiment_id` label coming only from the load-test traffic, checked the deploy path, and confirmed the service itself was not regressing. Cyrus stopped the load test and the canary cleared without escalation or rollback. This note is for the next responder.

- **A cardinality canary during a known scheduled load test is expected to trip, not a service regression.** Before treating the alert as a metrics-router regression, confirm whether a scheduled load test is in progress (check #ops-loadtests / ask Cyrus / check the load-test calendar). If yes, do not rollback.
- **Isolate the label to the load-test traffic first.** Check whether the unbounded labels (`experiment_id`, `user_id`, `request_id`, anything tenant/key-shaped) are present only on load-test traffic or also on production traffic. If load-test-only, the spike is from the load generator, not from metrics-router.
- **Check the deploy path, but do not assume deploy is the cause.** A green canary + a recent config-only change + a load test in flight usually means the load test is the source. Wes's 2023-08-16 investigation pattern is the reference: isolate label → rule out deploy → rule out downstream → confirm load-test scope → ask the load-test owner to stop.
- **Coordinate with the load-test owner before stopping or rolling back.** Cyrus stops the load test on confirmation; do not rollback metrics-router without that conversation. Rollback during a load-test-driven alert is the wrong action and creates a second incident.
- **No cardinality-control project, no ownership change.** This is a documentation note so the next responder does the same fast isolation rather than treating noise as a regression. Cardinality controls on load-test labels are tracked separately and are not owned by the canary response.

---

## Canary note — 2023-09-07 (post-canary CPU-only warmup, not a rollback)

Context: Second day of metrics-router data after the config-checksum cleanup canary. The affected AZ's CPU uplift has settled to ~2–3%, checksum-cache invalidations are back near baseline, cache-cardinality stayed flat, p99 stayed inside the normal 182–188 ms band, error rate stayed at 0.02%, dropped writes stayed clean, and rollup-service lag stayed flat. No user-visible signal moved. Closing as checksum-cache warmup after the config-checksum cleanup, not a rollback case.

- **A small residual CPU uplift in one AZ on the first 1–2 days after a config-checksum cleanup is warmup, not a regression.** Cache entries rehydrate under the new checksum regime; CPU cost comes back to baseline as the cache refills. Do not rollback on CPU alone if p99, error rate, dropped writes, cache-cardinality, and downstream lag are all flat.
- **Re-check the four user-visible signals before any rollback action.** p99 (must stay in the 182–188 ms band), error rate (~0.02% baseline), dropped writes (clean), and rollup-service lag (flat). If all four are flat, the rollout is fine and the residual CPU is warmup.
- **Checksum-cache invalidations returning near baseline is the confirming signal.** Elevated invalidations dominated by `checksum-mismatch-on-read` would be a different problem (would reconsider the rollout). Invalidations back near baseline + cache-cardinality flat means the cache is settling, not churning.
- **Triggers that WOULD change the call:** cache-hit ratio in the affected AZ dropping materially; checksum-cache invalidations dominated by `checksum-mismatch-on-read`; any of the four user-visible signals (p99 / error rate / dropped writes / rollup-service lag) moving off baseline. None of these fired on 2023-09-07.
- **No second-day page expected.** This note exists so the next on-call does not treat CPU-only post-canary warmup as an automatic rollback. If the four user-visible signals stay flat, leave the rollout in place and let the cache finish warming.

---

## Canary note — 2023-09-27 (parser-cache warmup during canary, not a rollback)

Context: Tiny metrics-router parser cleanup canary warmup ran on 2023-09-26; full rollout through the deploy pipeline finished on 2023-09-27 and stayed quiet. p99 stayed in the normal band, error rate held at 0.02%, dropped writes stayed clean, rollup-service lag stayed flat, and parser-cache misses did not repeat on full rollout. Closing as a parser-cache warmup that the canary allowed to hold, not a rollback case. This note is for the next responder who sees parser-cache misses during a future parser-cleanup canary.

- **A short burst of parser-cache misses during a parser-cleanup canary is warmup, not a regression.** The parser cache rehydrates against the new parser path while the canary holds. Treat parser-cache misses during canary the same way as the 2023-09-07 checksum-cache warmup: hold the rollout and verify on the four user-visible signals before any rollback action.
- **Hold and verify on the four user-visible signals.** p99 must return to baseline, and error rate (~0.02%), dropped writes (clean), and rollup-service lag (flat) must stay flat. If all four hold, the warmup is settling and the rollout can proceed.
- **Parser-cache misses stopping on their own is the confirming signal.** Parser-cache misses that recede as the cache fills under the new parser path means the cache is settling, not churning. Continued parser-cache misses at canary traffic level with any of the four user-visible signals moving off baseline is a different problem.
- **Triggers that WOULD change the call:** any of the four user-visible signals (p99 / error rate / dropped writes / rollup-service lag) moving off baseline during the warmup window; parser-cache misses that do not recede as the canary holds; a parser-cache miss rate that grows against steady canary traffic instead of decaying. None of these fired on 2023-09-27.
- **Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged.** The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) and the canary gating criteria still apply. This note only describes how to interpret a parser-cache warmup within those requirements; it does not relax any of them.
- **No parser-cache warmup page expected for a future parser-cleanup canary.** If the four user-visible signals stay flat, hold the rollout through the warmup and let the parser cache finish warming.

## Canary note — 2024-05-30 (generation and cleanup-pause guidance during canary)

Context: The existing canary response covered CPU, memory, queue depth, route-delivery divergence, dropped series, and restarts. It did not cover active-versus-retired generation counts, epoch drain, matcher cleanup, or stop-the-world cleanup pauses. This note adds the missing generation and cleanup evidence without changing the three-step canary response, the four user-visible signals, or any prior warmup-vs-rollback call. The first-cut Cardinality Guardrails preflight, the replay-mirror separation, and the deploy-pipeline-only rule remain in force.

- **Compare p99 by pod alongside active and retired generation counts and cleanup-pause duration.** p99 by pod is the diagnostic; the active-generation count and the retired-generation count describe whether the router has finished draining the previous generation, and the cleanup-pause duration describes whether the stop-the-world matcher cleanup is staying cheap. A transient p99 spike that recovers while active and retired generation counts stay consistent and cleanup pauses stay bounded is warmup-style movement, not a regression. The pre-existing four user-visible signals (p99 in the 182–188 ms band, error rate ~0.02%, dropped writes clean, rollup-service lag flat) still gate the call.
- **Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 ms.** Retired-object accumulation above four means the previous generation has not drained into the active set; cleanup pauses above 100 ms mean the stop-the-world matcher cleanup is no longer cheap enough to ride alongside canary traffic. In either case, hold the rollout pipeline, do not push the next config change, and verify before resuming pushes. This is a pause on pushes, not a rollback — the existing rollback criteria below still decide whether a rollback is warranted.
- **Verify before resuming pushes.** With pushes paused, verify all of the following, in this order: active-generation consistency (every pod reports the same active generation, no mixed-generation pods), route parity (router deliveries match the previous-generation route table for the same label set), dropped series (clean, no new series dropped against the pre-canary baseline), reload failures (none, or back inside the pre-canary rate), and restarts (none, or back inside the pre-canary rate). If any of those five is off, the rollout is not in a state where another configuration push should land; resolve the off-state first, then resume pushes.
- **Capture generation and heap evidence.** Capture the active-generation count, the retired-generation count, the cleanup-pause duration distribution (p50 / p99 / max), the heap occupancy of the matcher against the previous-generation entries, and a short heap snapshot timed against the cleanup-pause window. This evidence is what tells the next responder whether the canary is warmup, drain, or regression, and it is what feeds the mismatch-investigation queue if the rollout later needs to be reopened.
- **Do not roll back solely because a transient p99 spike recovered.** A p99 spike that comes back down on its own while active and retired generation counts stay consistent, cleanup pauses stay bounded, route parity holds, dropped series stay clean, reload failures stay flat, and restarts stay flat is warmup-style movement. Treat it the same way as the 2023-09-07 checksum-cache warmup and the 2023-09-27 parser-cache warmup: hold, verify on the signals above, do not rollback on p99 alone.
- **Rollback still applies to active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.** The pause-on-pushes rule above does not replace the rollback criteria. If active generations are inconsistent across pods, if routes diverge from the previous-generation table, or if dropped series move off baseline, the call is rollback via the deploy pipeline, not hold-and-verify. These are the rollback-class signals and they take precedence over warmup-style framing.
- **Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged.** The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) still applies. This note only adds the generation and cleanup-pause evidence and the pause-on-pushes rule; it does not relax canary gating, does not authorize laptop deploys, does not change the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision.

## Canary note — 2024-07-25 (owner-led window rule: fresh opening decision per window, bounded single-push execution, threshold stops, rollback set unchanged)

Context: The 2024-05-30 note established the pause-on-pushes rule and the five-signal verify-before-resume set, and the 2024-06-18 note encoded the stop / bounded single-push resume / immediate re-pause / rollback boundary that infra review accepted. The 2024-06-18 wording framed each push as if it carried its own per-push approval. That per-push framing is superseded by the owner-led window rule below: windows, not individual pushes, are the unit Alex opens. Each window still permits a sequence of single-file pushes while the threshold conditions hold, but a fresh opening decision from Alex is required for every window — including any window opened after recovery from a threshold stop, and any window opened after a fully observed push closes. The rollback set is unchanged and the three-step canary response, the four user-visible signals, the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and the deploy-pipeline-only rule remain in force. This note supersedes the per-push-approval framing in the 2024-06-18 note; it does not relax canary gating, does not authorize laptop deploys, does not change the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision.

- **Window is the unit Alex opens.** Each configuration-push window requires a fresh opening decision from Alex. A fresh opening decision is required (a) to start the first window after this note, (b) to start any window after a threshold stop, and (c) to start any window after a previous window's fully observed push closes. No window is implicit and no window carries forward from a prior approval. Wes, as practical backup, may open a window only when Alex is unreachable, and Alex remains the primary owner of the opening decision in all other cases. Wes is not becoming the primary owner; Alex remains primary and Wes remains the practical backup.
- **Inside a window, mapped operators may make single-file pushes while the threshold conditions hold.** Mapped operators are the engineers and service owners already assigned to the affected files. While a window is open, those mapped operators may push single-file changes through the deploy pipeline, one at a time, provided every push returns the full health set to baseline before the next push lands. "Full health set to baseline" means: retired-generation count at or below four, cleanup-pause p99 at or below 100 ms, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity against the previous-generation table, dropped series clean against the pre-canary baseline, reload failures at or below the pre-canary rate, and restarts at or below the pre-canary rate. The full health set is the per-push gate inside the window; it is not a substitute for Alex's window-opening decision.
- **Exceeding either threshold stops the window immediately.** The window stops the moment retired generations accumulate above four, or the moment a cleanup pause above 100 ms is observed. "Stop" means no further pushes land via the deploy pipeline for the remainder of that window, no matter how clean the rest of the health set looks. Stop is automatic, not a judgement call; the next push requires a fresh opening decision from Alex and a new window. A threshold stop does not escalate to rollback on its own — rollback is decided by the rollback set at the end of this note — but a threshold stop ends the window unconditionally.
- **After recovery, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed push.** Once the threshold conditions have cleared (retired generations drained back to four or fewer, cleanup pauses back at or below 100 ms, and the full health set returned to baseline), Alex may open a new window. That fresh window, by rule, permits exactly one fully observed push. "Fully observed" means p99, heap, active-generation count, retired-generation count, cleanup-pause duration, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts are all monitored across the entire push window and the post-push drain. No second push may be launched inside that window until the observation window closes cleanly.
- **Another window requires a separate fresh decision after that push returns the full health set to baseline.** The one fully observed push permitted under the fresh window does not authorize a return to steady-state cadence, and it does not roll over into a second push on its own. A second window requires a separate fresh opening decision from Alex, and that decision is only available after the first push's full observation window has closed and the full health set has returned to baseline. The cycle (threshold stop → recovery → fresh decision → exactly one fully observed push → full health set back to baseline → fresh decision → next window) is the only path forward; the cycle does not compress into a single decision and the cycle does not skip steps.
- **Consistency, parity, dropped-series, reload, and restart failures remain rollback conditions.** Rollback via the deploy pipeline is required on any of: active-generation inconsistency across pods, route divergence from the previous-generation table, dropped series off baseline, reload failure, or restart. These five are rollback-class signals. They are not pause-class signals and they are not warmup-style signals; on any one of them the call is rollback, not hold-and-verify, not bounded single-push resume, and not a fresh window. The rollback set in this note is the same set as the 2024-05-30 note and the 2024-06-18 note; this note only restates it alongside the window rule.
- **Pause and rollback are different actions.** A window stop (retired gens > 4 or cleanup pause > 100 ms) ends the window and requires a fresh opening decision from Alex before pushes resume. A rollback condition (active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped series, reload failure, restart) routes through the deploy pipeline to revert. Do not collapse the two: a window stop does not escalate to rollback unless one of the rollback conditions fires, and a single rollback-class signal does not get treated as a window stop.
- **Ownership boundary is unchanged.** Alex remains the primary owner of the window-opening decision. Wes remains the practical backup and may open a window only when Alex is unreachable. Mapped operators remain the ones who execute single-file pushes inside an open window; they do not open windows and they do not make rollback calls. Infra review's accepted boundary on 2024-06-17 (resume prerequisites holding continuously for 10 minutes, identical active-generation sets across all canary pods, cleanup-pause p99 strictly below 100 ms before resuming pushes) still gates entry into a fresh window; the window rule above describes what happens inside a window once those prerequisites are satisfied, and it does not relax them.
- **Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged.** The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) still applies. This note supersedes the per-push-approval framing in the 2024-06-18 note and replaces it with the owner-led window rule; it does not relax canary gating, does not authorize laptop deploys, does not change the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision.

## Canary note — 2024-10-07 (aligned thresholds, recovery-push rule, and the 103 ms stopped-window example) — REFERENCE ACCEPTED 2024-10-08

Context: On 2024-10-07 Alex and Wes re-ran the canary reference session and re-stated the aligned thresholds and the recovery sequence that have been in force under the 2024-05-30 and 2024-07-25 notes. Wes and Alex walked through a real recorded case from the second September push that surfaced the boundary on cleanup-pause duration, and that case is recorded below as the canonical stopped-window example. The 94 ms recovery-push exercise scheduled for 2024-10-08 has been completed; Hema accepted the exercised canary-response reference for future use by Wes and other mapped operators, and that exercise and acceptance are recorded in the 2024-10-08 sub-note below.

**Aligned thresholds (re-stated, unchanged from 2024-05-30 / 2024-07-25):**

- **Retired generations must remain at four or fewer.** Anything above four means the previous generation has not drained into the active set; pushes pause, do not escalate to rollback on this signal alone.
- **Cleanup pauses must remain at or below 100 ms.** Anything above 100 ms means the stop-the-world matcher cleanup is no longer cheap enough to ride alongside canary traffic; pushes pause, do not escalate to rollback on this signal alone.
- **The full health set must return to baseline after every push.** Between pushes inside a window, retired-generation count, cleanup-pause p99, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts must all be back at baseline. A push that returns the full health set to baseline is what permits the next push; a push that does not return the full health set to baseline ends the window.
- **Exceeding either ceiling stops the window.** The window stops the moment retired generations accumulate above four, or the moment a cleanup pause above 100 ms is observed. Stop is automatic; no further pushes land for the remainder of that window, no matter how clean the rest of the health set looks. Stop does not escalate to rollback on its own — rollback is decided by the rollback set below.

**Recovery sequence (re-stated, unchanged from 2024-07-25):**

- After a threshold stop, retired generations drain back to four or fewer, cleanup pauses come back at or below 100 ms, and the full health set returns to baseline. Only then does a fresh opening decision become available.
- A fresh opening decision permits exactly one fully observed recovery push. "Fully observed" means p99, heap, active-generation count, retired-generation count, cleanup-pause duration, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts are all monitored across the entire push window and the post-push drain.
- The recovery push does not reopen a multi-push window. No second push may be launched inside that fresh window until the observation window closes cleanly and the full health set returns to baseline again. A subsequent window requires a separate fresh opening decision after that recovery push's observation window closes.

**Rollback set (unchanged):** Active-generation inconsistency across pods, route divergence from the previous-generation table, dropped series off baseline, reload failure, or restart — on any one, the call is rollback via the deploy pipeline. Pause and rollback remain different actions; do not collapse the two.

**Recorded example — second September push (correctly classified as a stopped window):**

- The push changed the intended single file (single-file push inside an open window).
- Retired generations peaked at four. (At the ceiling, not above it.)
- Cleanup pause was 103 ms. (Above the 100 ms ceiling by 3 ms.)
- The window stopped immediately on the cleanup-pause observation.
- Full health returned seven minutes later: retired generations back at four or fewer, cleanup pauses back at or below 100 ms, the rest of the full health set (active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, restarts) back at baseline.
- No additional push occurred inside that window. The next push required a fresh opening decision and a new window.

Wes classified this case as a **stopped window**, not a completed safe push and not a reopened window. The classification is the point: a push that returns the full health set to baseline is a completed safe push, a push that ends with a threshold stop is a stopped window, and a stopped window does not authorize further pushes inside the same window even after recovery. The recovery sequence above is what governs what comes next.

**103 ms stopped-window classification rules (for the next responder):**

- A push is a **completed safe push** only if every signal in the full health set — retired-generation count ≤ 4, cleanup-pause p99 ≤ 100 ms, active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, restarts — returns to baseline. The 103 ms observation alone disqualifies the September push from this classification regardless of how clean the rest of the health set looked.
- A push is a **stopped window** if either ceiling was exceeded during the push, even by a small margin and even if everything else in the health set returned to baseline. 103 ms vs the 100 ms ceiling is a stopped window, not a near-miss safe push.
- A stopped window is **not** automatically a reopened window after recovery. Recovery makes a fresh opening decision available; it does not carry the prior window forward, and it does not authorize further pushes inside the prior window. The next push requires a fresh decision and a new window.
- The seven-minute full-health recovery time on this case is descriptive, not prescriptive. A future stopped window may take longer or shorter to drain; the rule is full-health-return-to-baseline, not a fixed recovery duration.

**Triggers that WOULD change the call (none fired on the September case):**

- A cleanup-pause observation at or below 100 ms while retired generations stayed at or below four: would have been a completed safe push, not a stopped window.
- An active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped-series movement, reload failure, or restart during the push: would have been rollback, not stop.
- A cleanup pause above 100 ms accompanied by retired-generation accumulation above four: still a stopped window, not a more severe classification.

**2024-10-08 — completed 94 ms recovery-push exercise and Hema's acceptance (closes the prior pending-validation marker):**

- Alex and Wes ran the metrics-router reference exercise on the recorded 94 ms recovery push. Wes identified this push as the one fully observed push authorized by Alex's fresh post-recovery decision, verified that retired generations stayed at four or fewer and that the full health set returned to baseline, and did not describe it as a reopened window. The classification matches the 103 ms rule above: the 94 ms observation is at or below the 100 ms cleanup-pause ceiling, the prior window did not roll forward, and the fresh window contained exactly one fully observed push.
- Hema accepted the exercised canary-response reference for future use by Wes and other mapped operators. The reference is now part of the canary-response record; no change is proposed to the aligned thresholds, the recovery sequence, or the rollback set, and Hema's acceptance does not move ownership of any rollback decision.
- Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged. The three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed) still applies. This 2024-10-08 sub-note closes the prior pending-validation marker; it does not relax canary gating, does not authorize laptop deploys, does not change the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision.
