## Canary note — 2025-04-15 (host-maintenance rejoin gate, durable rule for rejoining instances)

Context: The 2025-04-12 response to a stale-generation alert on metrics-router is closed and was correct. The stale-generation debrief confirmed that the alert fired correctly and that the response actions were the right ones. The debrief surfaced one missing piece in the canary-response runbook: an explicit rule for what happens when an instance rejoins after host maintenance. Alex, Hema, and Nadia agreed that a rejoining instance must remain isolated until it reports the current active generation, and that a missing generation report does not count as healthy. Once the rejoining instance reports the current generation, the ordinary consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health checks must all pass before isolation is released. This note adds that durable rejoin gate. It does not change ownership, does not create or open an owner-led window, and does not authorize a configuration push.

- **A rejoining instance is isolated until it reports the current active generation.** "Rejoining" covers any instance coming back into the fleet after host maintenance, host reboot, OS patching, hypervisor migration, or any other event that takes the instance out of steady-state and then returns it. While the instance is rejoining, treat it as not part of the active fleet for consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health decisions. Isolation ends only when the instance reports the current active generation on its own. A missing generation report — no report at all, an empty report, a stale generation, or a generation that does not match the active set — does not count as reporting the current active generation and the instance stays isolated.
- **A missing generation report is not healthy.** Do not infer health from the absence of a generation report, do not infer health from "the instance is up" alone, and do not infer health from liveness or readiness probes that do not include the active generation. Treat the missing report as the same class of failure as a stale generation report: the instance has not rejoined the active set and the isolation holds. The next on-call does not need a new decision to keep the instance isolated; the rule above is the default.
- **After the rejoining instance reports the current active generation, the ordinary checks gate isolation release.** Only after the rejoining instance reports the current active generation do consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health checks run against it. Isolation release requires all of the following, in this order: active-generation consistency (the rejoining instance reports the same active generation as the rest of the fleet, no mixed-generation state across pods), route parity (deliveries from the rejoining instance match the previous-generation route table for the same label set), dropped series (clean against the pre-canary baseline, no new series dropped because of the rejoining instance), route delivery (the rejoining instance routes the same way as the rest of the fleet on a held label set), and the rest of the health set (cleanup-pause p99 at or below 100 ms, retired-generation count at or below four, reload failures at or below the pre-canary rate, restarts at or below the pre-canary rate). If any of those is off, isolation stays in place; resolve the off-state first, then re-run the gate.
- **The rejoin gate is independent of the canary gating, the window rule, and the rollback set.** The rejoin gate above governs when a single rejoining instance leaves isolation; it is not a canary-response decision and it does not interact with the three-step canary response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline if regression confirmed). It does not open an owner-led window, does not authorize a single-file configuration push, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision. Active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped-series movement, reload failure, or restart during a rejoin still routes through the deploy pipeline on the rollback criteria from the prior notes.
- **Ownership boundary is unchanged.** Alex remains the primary owner of the canary response and the window-opening decision. Wes remains the practical backup. Mapped operators remain the ones who execute single-file pushes inside an open window. Host-maintenance rejoins are not configuration pushes; the deploy-pipeline-only rule, the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, and the laptop-deploy prohibition all remain in force. The rejoin gate is a read-and-isolate rule, not a write-side rule.
- **Deploy-pipeline and canary requirements are unchanged.** The three-step canary response, the aligned thresholds (retired-generation count ≤ 4, cleanup-pause p99 ≤ 100 ms), the recovery sequence, the owner-led window rule, the rollback set, the Cardinality Guardrails preflight, the replay-mirror separation, and the deploy-pipeline-only rule all stay as written. This note only adds the durable rejoin gate for rejoining instances after host maintenance; it does not relax canary gating, does not authorize laptop deploys, does not create or open an owner-led window, does not authorize a configuration push, and does not move ownership of any rollback decision.

PR: infra-runbooks#1882
Title: "Rewrite April 2023 incident-review history"
Author: theo    Assignees: theo    Reviewers: alex    Status: open
Branch: theo/simplify-apr-2023-history
Opened: 2027-12-29
Body: "Simplifies the April 2023 incident-review narrative and removes procedural detail that no longer seems relevant."

The diff is a single hunk in history/2023-04-incident-review.md, context line retained: "The team reviewed the April 18 outage on April 28."

WHAT THE PR REPLACES

Old (two lines):
  The review established several operational follow-ups and affected the shard-keeper migration plan.
  See the meeting notes for the detailed decisions and dependencies.

New (three lines):
  The review concluded that the shard-keeper migration should continue immediately.
  The only follow-up was routine documentation cleanup.
  No additional operational policy, escalation, audit, or migration gating decisions resulted from the review.

WHAT IT CLAIMS ABOUT THE APRIL 28, 2023 REVIEW
  - The review concluded shard-keeper should continue immediately (no pause, no new gate).
  - The only follow-up was routine documentation cleanup.
  - No operational policy / escalation / audit / migration gating decisions came out of it.

WHAT IT CLAIMS ABOUT SHARD-KEEPER'S IMMEDIATE STATUS
  - Effectively rolling forward with no new conditions.
  - The previous pointer to "meeting notes for the detailed decisions and dependencies" is dropped.

REVIEW NOTES

1. The new text makes a sweeping negative claim: "No additional operational policy, escalation, audit, or migration gating decisions resulted from the review." Asserting what did not happen at a meeting 4+ years ago is a high evidentiary bar, and the diff doesn't cite or reconcile against the meeting notes the old text pointed at. The old line was a pointer; the new line is an unsubstantiated assertion in the opposite direction.

2. The rewrite is hard to square with shard-keeper's later trajectory. From what I have in working memory, shard-keeper's posture went on to require signed-env + immut bundle digest, fail-closed serving until active-bundle=bundle, owner-sync digest pinning, restore-time sig+digest re-verification, and a TOCTOU closure on 09-27, with 3K advisories along the way and prod unchanged through the lifecycle. Even granting that some of that hardening was raised after April 2023, a review of a then-ongoing migration producing zero audit / escalation / gating signal and "only routine documentation cleanup" is the kind of claim that wants primary-source backing, not simplification by deletion.

3. "Continue immediately" is also a positive claim about direction. The old phrasing — "established several operational follow-ups and affected the shard-keeper migration plan" — is consistent with the multi-year gated migration we actually lived through. The new phrasing is not, on its face.

4. The branch name (simplify-apr-2023-history) and the body ("removes procedural detail that no longer seems relevant") frame the motivation as tidiness. For a history document the relevant test is not whether the detail feels relevant now but whether it was accurate then. Edits that drop substantively-checkable claims without reconciliation are exactly the ones that age badly and erode the doc's evidentiary value.

5. Caveat: I have not independently read the April 28, 2023 meeting notes or the original incident-review document outside of this diff. The above is reasoning from the diff and from the later shard-keeper state I have memory of — it is a tension worth resolving, not a contradiction proven from primary sources.

WHAT I'D WANT BEFORE APPROVING
  - The April 28, 2023 meeting notes (whatever "see the meeting notes" previously resolved to), so the rewrite can be checked against them rather than against each other.
  - Either keep the pointer to the notes or add a brief reconciliation line explaining what the notes do and do not contain.
  - A more conservative edit: the "continue immediately" / no-new-policy framing is fine if true, but do not collapse the "operational follow-ups and migration plan dependencies" lines unless the notes are shown to be empty on those points.

Net: not approving as written. I'd come back with these comments on the PR and ask Theo to reconcile against the meeting notes or scope the change down to a non-contradicting form.

Note on tooling: the two supermemory_search calls I issued in parallel both timed out, so I went via the PR tool directly. No fabrication — every claim above about the diff or shard-keeper's later state is grounded in the PR result or my stored memory notes; the one thing I have not actually read is the April 28, 2023 meeting notes themselves.

arguments.title: Cardinality Guardrails: label-change preflight first cut
arguments.body:
## Cardinality Guardrails: label-change preflight (first cut)

Scope: first-cut preflight only. Captures the vocabulary before it
turns into hallway knowledge. This entry is deliberately narrow; it
is not the full Cardinality Guardrails project.

### What this preflight covers

A label-change preflight fires when a config push, schema change, or
relabel rule could add new label keys or change the cardinality shape
of an existing label family. It is a check, not a control: it surfaces
risk; the caller still decides whether to ship.

### First-cut preflight surface

- **New label keys**: any key not already present in the router's known
  label inventory for the affected metric path. Treat as additive
  cardinality risk until proven bounded.
- **Risky label families**: high-cardinality families we have already
  seen wobble — request-scoped IDs, user/path/email-derived fields,
  free-form tag values, raw URLs, and any label whose value set is not
  owned by the service emitting it.
- **Sample distinct counts**: pull a short-window sample from the
  router path the change touches, report distinct-value counts per
  new or modified label key, and flag any sample whose distinct count
  is unbounded in practice (growing with traffic or tenants).
- **Alert-source semantics**: a `validation-only` finding is still
  evidence — it means the change was caught off the live path (no live
  rollback in scope), not that the mismatch is safe to ignore.
  Validation findings feed the same mismatch-investigation queue as
  live findings.
- **Live vs. validation rollback boundary**: a finding on a label
  pushed to the live router path is a live rollback candidate. A
  finding caught in a validation/mirror path is scope-only — recorded,
  investigated, but not an automatic rollback trigger.

### First cut, not the whole project

- **Shard-keeper uses the same vocabulary**, but a runbook entry for
  shard-keeper is not in this first cut. It will get its own entry when
  its preflight path is wired up; do not assume the rules below apply
  there yet.
- This preflight does not enforce. It informs the owner of the push.
- This preflight does not replace the existing replay-mismatch panel
  or paired rollback for the metrics cutover; those are separate
  surfaces.

### Explicit non-goals

- Not a telemetry rewrite.
- Not a paired-rollback story.
- Not an ownership change.
- Not a router enforcement mechanism.
- Not a cardinality-control rollout across services. Other services
  get their own preflights; this is the router-facing first cut.

### Known open questions for the first cut

- Where the sample distinct-count threshold for "risky" lives, and who
  owns tuning it.
- Whether new label keys should require an owner field at preflight
  time or only at investigation time.
- How validation-only findings are surfaced alongside live findings
  without being mistaken for either ignored or live-equivalent.

Title: Cardinality Guardrails — first control slice: PR/review checklist

Use this on any metrics-router or shard-keeper change that adds label keys, modifies a relabel rule, or changes the cardinality shape of an existing label family. Pass = the reviewer can tick every numbered item. Fail = any single item untickable; the change does not get the cardinality preflight green check, regardless of code-side LGTM.

PREFLIGHT TRIGGER (one of these is true; otherwise this checklist does not apply)

[ ] The change introduces a label key not already in the router's known label inventory for the affected metric path.
[ ] The change modifies a relabel rule, label family, or label-schema map in metrics-router or shard-keeper.
[ ] The change touches rollup-service label handling in a way that could shift the cardinality shape seen by the consumer side.

If none apply, do not run this checklist; this is not a generic review template.

A. NEW LABEL KEYS (treated as additive cardinality risk until bounded)

[ ] PASS — Every new label key is listed in the PR description with: name, intended value space, who owns the value set (service / tenant / request / external), and the metric path it appears on.
[ ] PASS — Distinct-value counts are attached for each new key from a short-window sample of the path the change touches. A "will be bounded in practice" claim without a sample is a fail.
[ ] FAIL if — A new key is added with no sample, no owner, or an external/unowned value set and no bounded-cardinality argument.

B. RISKY LABEL FAMILIES

[ ] PASS — The PR has been scanned against the known risky-family list: request-scoped IDs, user/path/email-derived fields, free-form tag values, raw URLs, and any label whose value set is not owned by the service emitting it. Each hit is either removed, justified with a bounded-cardinality argument, or explicitly called out as out-of-scope-but-tracked.
[ ] PASS — If a risky-family label survives, the PR names where the sample distinct-count threshold lives for "risky" and who owns tuning it (current open question per the seed; until resolved, surface the open question in the PR, do not bury it).
[ ] FAIL if — A request-scoped ID, raw URL, or external/unowned value set is added without a bounded-cardinality argument. This is the most common reject path.

C. SAMPLE DISTINCT COUNTS

[ ] PASS — A short-window distinct-count sample is attached for the affected path, per new or modified key. The window, source path, and tenant mix are named.
[ ] PASS — Any sample whose distinct count is unbounded in practice (grows with traffic or tenants) is flagged in the PR, not only in the preflight output. Flagged = labeled as risky + an explicit bounded-or-not call from the owner.
[ ] FAIL if — Distinct-count sample is missing for any new or modified key, OR a flagged unbounded sample ships without an owner call.

D. ALERT-SOURCE SEMANTICS (the validation-only rule)

[ ] PASS — Any cardinality finding the preflight emits is classified at the source as either live or validation-only. The classification lives on the finding itself, not in a separate doc.
[ ] PASS — Validation-only findings are routed to the mismatch-investigation queue — the same queue as live findings. They are not dropped, not hidden, and not auto-resolved.
[ ] PASS — The replay/mirror validation panel remains visible on the on-call landing page. This PR does not propose hiding it, suppressing it, or de-emphasizing it. Subtitle convention is preserved: "Source: replay validation — not a live-path rollback signal."

arguments.body:
## Cardinality Guardrails: label-change preflight (first cut)

Scope: first-cut preflight only. Captures the vocabulary before it
turns into hallway knowledge. This entry is deliberately narrow; it
is not the full Cardinality Guardrails project.

### What this preflight covers

A label-change preflight fires when a config push, schema change, or
relabel rule could add new label keys or change the cardinality shape
of an existing label family. It is a check, not a control: it surfaces
risk; the caller still decides whether to ship.

### First-cut preflight surface

- **New label keys**: any key not already present in the router's known
  label inventory for the affected metric path. Treat as additive
  cardinality risk until proven bounded.
- **Risky label families**: high-cardinality families we have already
  seen wobble — request-scoped IDs, user/path/email-derived fields,
  free-form tag values, raw URLs, and any label whose value set is not
  owned by the service emitting it.
- **Sample distinct counts**: pull a short-window sample from the
  router path the change touches, report distinct-value counts per
  new or modified label key, and flag any sample whose distinct count
  is unbounded in practice (growing with traffic or tenants).
- **Live-path sample requirement for live-path labels**: when the
  change touches the live router path, the sample above must come
  from live canary traffic on that path, or from a representative
  live-path fixture that exercises the same handler/normalization
  chain. A replay or mirror sample alone is not sufficient evidence
  for live-path labels. This applies in particular to normalization
  paths on existing label families — e.g. `route_pattern` and similar
  handler-derived keys — where a normalization change can shift a
  bounded label family into an unbounded one (raw IDs, raw account
  IDs, raw widget IDs, etc.) without adding a new key.
- **Alert-source semantics**: a `validation-only` finding is still
  evidence — it means the change was caught off the live path (no live
  rollback in scope), not that the mismatch is safe to ignore.
  Validation findings feed the same mismatch-investigation queue as
  live findings.
- **Live vs. validation rollback boundary**: a finding on a label
  pushed to the live router path is a live rollback candidate. A
  finding caught in a validation/mirror path is scope-only — recorded,
  investigated, but not an automatic rollback trigger. Replay and
  mirror validation remain investigation evidence and feed the
  mismatch-investigation queue; they are not, on their own, rollback
  criteria for live-path labels.

### First cut, not the whole project

- **Shard-keeper uses the same vocabulary**, but a runbook entry for
  shard-keeper is not in this first cut. It will get its own entry when
  its preflight path is wired up; do not assume the rules below apply
  there yet.
- This preflight does not enforce. It informs the owner of the push.
- This preflight does not replace the existing replay-mismatch panel
  or paired rollback for the metrics cutover; those are separate
  surfaces.

### Explicit non-goals

- Not a telemetry rewrite.
- Not a paired-rollback story.
- Not an ownership change.
- Not a router enforcement mechanism.
- Not a cardinality-control rollout across services. Other services
  get their own preflights; this is the router-facing first cut.

### Incident scope note (added 2023-10-30)

The 2023-10-30 metrics-router rollback surfaced a real hole in this
preflight wording — the original "pull a short-window sample from the
router path the change touches" was too loose for live-path labels
when a handler's normalization path changes. The added live-path
sample bullet above is the targeted fix.

- **This patch is not a claim that the preflight would have prevented
  the incident.** It tightens the evidence required for live-path
  label changes; it does not extend scope into live enforcement, new
  rollback mechanics, or a broader workstream.
- **Replay validation remains valuable as investigation evidence**, just
  not as a standalone rollback criterion for live-path labels. The
  replay-mismatch panel and the validation-only queue are unchanged.
- **`route_pattern` is named here as the worked example**, not as the
  only family in scope. Any handler-derived label whose value set is
  produced by a normalization step (route patterns, endpoint-derived
  keys, handler-emitted IDs that pass through a normalize step) is
  covered by the same rule.

### Known open questions for the first cut

- Where the sample distinct-count threshold for "risky" lives, and who
  owns tuning it.
- Whether new label keys should require an owner field at preflight
  time or only at investigation time.
- How validation-only findings are surfaced alongside live findings
  without being mistaken for either ignored or live-equivalent.
- What counts as a "representative live-path fixture" for handlers
  without an existing canary path.

Historical note (2028-01-01 retrospective on May 2023):

WHY SHARD-KEEPER WAS THE LARGEST PART OF THE MAY 2023 OWNERSHIP AUDIT

The audit was scheduled at the 2023-04-28 incident review of the Apr 18 shard-keeper outage (Nadia's label change, rollup missed, symptom alert fired but cause didn't, network red herring, impaired ingest, shaky rollback). Three rules landed that day: page secondary within 45 min if primary still engaged, no Friday prod deploys (team-wide), and a runbook-ownership audit run by Hema, with Nadia cross-reviewing service bits she touches. shard-keeper's pending label_map migration was paused contingent on the audit closing.

Shard-keeper's runbook was by far the biggest single chunk of the audit work. Reasons:

Mosaic capacity response — final decision record
Meeting: 2025-09-05 13:00–13:45 ET (scope-decision meeting, evt_faf10d62ac4847789c17ebf8ba035b2c)
Attendees: Hema, Cyrus, Wes, Roman, Nadia, Alex

Record date: 2025-09-05

This document supersedes the 2025-09-03 preparation brief. The scope of the
response was decided at the 2025-09-05 meeting. No production change is
authorized by this record, and nothing is running in production yet.

Forecast (unchanged from prep brief)

Replay evidence (Cyrus, @16M)

- q-full retries: 0.9%
- All other services: baseline (no degradation observed)

Isolated constraint (carried forward)
- Export queue is the FIRST constraint, not cross-service
- Cross-svc impact not observed at forecast load
- Cross-svc impact must remain baseline throughout any stage

DECISION — Scope
- Hema approved a BOUNDED metrics-router response.
- This is NOT a pipeline rewrite.
- The response is scoped to metrics-router only and uses the existing
  retryable backpressure path. No new cross-service behavior is introduced.

DECISION — Bounds (must hold for any stage)
- Global queue ceiling: 2,048 batches.
- Per-tenant ceiling: 64 pending batches.
- Additional work beyond the per-tenant ceiling is sent into the existing
  retryable backpressure path BEFORE acceptance. No silent accept, no drop.
- Bounds are evaluated continuously during any stage.

DECISION — Owners
- Wes — implementation, and load-test evidence for the bounded response.
- Alex — cross-service invariants, AND the future production-window
  opening decision. Alex does NOT own implementation.
- Cyrus + Roman — rollup-service capacity and parity evidence.
- Nadia — queue and refusal alert semantics.
- Hema — may reorder metrics cutover if production forces it
  (carried from prior; not changed by this decision).

DECISION — Stop conditions (any stage must stop on ANY of these)
- Queue-wait p99 exceeds 400 ms for five consecutive minutes.
- Retryable queue-full responses exceed 0.5% for five consecutive minutes.
- Any accepted batch is lost.
- Any consistency check, parity check, dropped-series check, route check,
  or full-health check leaves baseline.

Explicit non-changes (must NOT be inferred from this decision)
- The formal service-owner map is UNCHANGED. Wes does NOT become
  metrics-router primary. Alex remains metrics-router primary.
- Mosaic's forecast ramp HAS NOT BEGUN. This decision does not start it.
- Nothing is running in production yet. No stage is in production today.
- This decision does not authorize any production deployment, production
  rollout, or production-window opening.
- Cross-service invariants (consistency, parity, dropped-series, route,
  full-health) remain baseline requirements; they are also stop conditions.

Stage gating (forward-looking, not a current state)
- A stage may begin only after Wes has load-test evidence for the bounded
  response and Cyrus + Roman have rollup-service capacity and parity
  evidence.
- A production window may open only on Alex's decision, after evidence
  review.
- Any stage stops immediately on any of the stop conditions above.

Meeting outcome
- Bounded response: APPROVED (as scoped above).
- Accountable owners: CONFIRMED.
- Stop conditions: DEFINED.
- Production authorization: NOT GRANTED. No production change is approved

Comment on the cross-service change plan that fans out from this postmortem:

Sequencing. The shard-keeper change and the rollup-service change must run sequentially, not in parallel. Each service gets its own change window, its own observation boundary, and its own sign-off. Owner-map and mapped ownership stay exactly as they are (no reassignment baked into this plan).

Per-service observation boundary. For each window, define and freeze these in advance, not during the cutover:
  - Time window start/end (UTC), with a hard cap on duration.
  - Explicit "observation boundary" = the set of metrics, logs, and dashboards that count as in-scope evidence for that service, plus the dashboards that are out of scope.
  - Pre-window baseline snapshot, taken immediately before the cutover, against which post-window evidence is compared.
  - A quiet-period definition (e.g. N minutes of no Sev-1/Sev-2 signals) that must elapse before the window is declared clean.

Service-specific health evidence and stop conditions. Each window has its own evidence pack and its own stop conditions; do not reuse the same checklist across services.

  - shard-keeper rollback is executed only by/with Nadia's approval.
  - rollup-service rollback is executed only by/with Cyrus team's approval.

  - Both label-rename sign-offs (the parity sign-off, since 2026-05-18) remain mandatory and are not overridden by a clean preflight + clean alert-source check.

messages.content:
TRIAGE PLAN - monitoring-agent image rollout, x509 scrape failures on rollup-service

Premise: rollup-service itself is healthy. Query latency, rollup completion, error rate, and processed-point counts are all normal. The dashboard gap is a collection failure on 3 of N agents, not a service outage. Do not let this become a rollup-service incident.

Step 1 - Lock the service-health evidence before anything else moves
  Timestamp and capture current values for: customer query latency p50/p95/p99, rollup completion rate, error rate, processed-point counts. Record the rollout start time and which 3 agents received the new image. This becomes the citation if anyone tries to escalate this as a rollup-service incident, and it gives you a baseline to confirm rollup-service stays healthy through the fix.

Step 2 - Confirm the failure is uniformly CA-related on the 3 new-image agents only
  On each of the 3 new-image agents, grep the scrape logs for the Prometheus target serving rollup-service. Expect every failure line to be "x509: certificate signed by unknown authority". Confirm the old-image agents hitting the same target show no x509 errors in the rollout window. If any other error class appears (connection refused, timeout, DNS), the problem is not purely CA and Step 3 changes shape - note it and revisit before deciding on rollback.

Step 3 - Compare CA bundles in the old vs new monitoring-agent image
  Extract the CA bundle from each image at the path Prometheus resolves against. The common location is /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, but verify against the agent's scrape / TLS config - some agents use a custom bundle path. Diff the two bundles:
    - missing root or intermediate that signed the Prometheus server cert - expected failure mode, image is broken
    - identical bundles - not a CA issue, look elsewhere (SNI, cipher, hostname mismatch)
    - bundles differ but neither contains the serving CA - the new base image likely dropped a CA that needs to be re-added
  Also check the image build log / Dockerfile for what changed (base image bump, package updates, ca-certificates version). "Unknown authority" + partial rollout + healthy service is almost always a missing-CA-in-base-image story.

Step 4 - Rollback decision (do this last, after Steps 1-3)
  Roll back the monitoring image if:
    a. The new image's CA bundle is missing the Prometheus-serving CA and the diff traces to the new image, OR
    b. You cannot quickly explain the x509 errors from the bundle diff alone - do not ship a partial rollout you cannot explain (fake-clean-cutover risk).
  Do not roll back if:
    a. The CA bundles are identical and the failure mode is not CA-related (then you are rolling back for a symptom, not the cause), OR
    b. You can patch the new image with the missing CA in well under ~30 minutes and would prefer to land the fix forward.
  Default for a partial rollout with a clear missing-CA cause: roll back the image to restore uniform scrape coverage, then ship the corrected image as a new rollout. Do not patch in place on the 3 already-updated agents - that creates uneven state and complicates the next rollout.

Step 5 - Close the loop after rollback
  Confirm all agents scrape successfully (success rate back to ~99.9%). Confirm the dashboard gap fills within one scrape interval. Confirm rollup-service health metrics never moved through the whole event. Document the CA bundle diff in the rollout notes so the next monitoring-agent image bump does not reintroduce the same gap.

What NOT to do
  - Do not roll back rollup-service or shard-keeper; they are healthy.
  - Do not open a rollup-service customer-facing incident; this is internal observability only.
  - Do not "fix" the dashboards to mask the gap; that hides the real signal and delays the real fix.
  - Do not escalate past the monitoring-agent owner until Step 3 confirms the CA theory - escalation on a guess wastes on-call cycles.

Two judgment calls worth flagging up front:

arguments.body:
Blocking review comment — 2027-07-20

NOTE ON PLACEMENT: This is the only loadable shard-keeper doc I could locate (the candidate-procedure doc with a Recovery and escalation section). If this comment should land on a different staff-only shard-keeper recovery-plan revision, please redirect me with the exact doc_id and I will repost / cross-link.

---

BLOCKING. The following conditions must hold before any readiness gate or tenant-auth serving surface is reopened under this recovery path. The review does not authorize implementation or release. Ownership is unchanged: I (Alex) remain shard-keeper primary, Data Platform team remains backup.

1. Readiness and tenant-auth serving stay closed until the two restored artifacts agree.
   - The restored signed active-bundle record and the restored signed certificate bundle must both be present and must agree (same identity, same epoch / serial / version, same authority chain as the pre-incident state). A file-level restore of one artifact alone is not acceptable as evidence of agreement.
   - Restoring the bundle file alone cannot permit readiness. A present file is not a present signed record. The signed active-bundle record must be revalidated against the signed certificate bundle before any readiness or tenant-auth gate is opened.

2. Executed crash and restart tests are required around every restoration step.
   - Crash and restart tests must be executed (not waived, not deferred) around every step in the restoration sequence, including — and explicitly — the steps immediately before AND immediately after active-record restoration.
   - "Before active-record restoration" means: after the prior artifacts are in place and before the active-bundle record is swapped in. The pre-swap state must hold under crash + restart.
   - "After active-record restoration" means: once the new signed active-bundle record is in place, the post-swap state must hold under crash + restart before any readiness or tenant-auth serving is permitted.
   - Any crash or restart test that fails, or is not executed, halts the recovery. Readiness and tenant-auth serving remain closed.

3. Authorization boundary (preserved, not changed by this review).
   - This review does not authorize implementation, release, or rollout. Implementation, release, and rollback authority stays with the mapped owner under the unchanged split (Alex primary on shard-keeper, Data Platform team backup).
   - No step in the recovery sequence may be treated as approved because this comment exists. Each step requires the executed crash + restart evidence above before the gate it unblocks is opened.

4. Non-claims (to prevent the comment being read as broader than it is).
   - This comment does not approve the candidate procedure itself. The candidate-procedure status (selection PENDING, no mapped owner running it as routine) is preserved.
   - This comment does not modify the Apr 18 replay guard, the label-parity pre-push sync, or the existing rollback procedure (rb_shard_keeper_rollback). Those rules remain in force.
   - This comment does not re-assign shard-keeper ownership or change the primary/backup split.

What unblocks readiness / tenant-auth serving (all required):
- signed active-bundle record restored and revalidated,
- signed certificate bundle restored and revalidated,
- the two artifacts agree (identity, epoch, authority chain),
- executed crash + restart tests pass before the active-record swap,
- executed crash + restart tests pass after the active-record swap,
- mapped owner (Alex) signs off on the recovery sequence as primary, with Data Platform team acknowledged as backup per the existing split.

If any of the above is missing, readiness and tenant-auth serving stay closed.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.

The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.

This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.

Capture the external response for every case, the adapter-call trace, the source timestamp where applicable, and proof that forbidden fields do not enter the rendered object.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.

Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. `source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

tests.request: Inspect deploy-tools#940 and review its proposed laptop path for urgent production deploys and rollbacks.

pr.author: wes
pr.body:
## Summary

Documents a faster break-glass procedure for Wes during urgent production deploy and rollback work.

## Proposed procedure

When waiting for the normal release mechanism would extend an incident, Wes may run `deployctl direct` from his maintainer laptop using production credentials. The command deploys the selected revision or restores the prior revision directly. The operator should record the incident ticket, service, revision, reason, and command output, then reconcile the resulting state with the normal release records after the incident.

## Motivation

This avoids waiting for the normal release job during time-sensitive recovery while retaining an audit trail in the incident record.

## Review question

Are the logging and post-incident reconciliation steps sufficient for this urgent path?
pr.title: docs: add laptop fast path for urgent deploys and rollbacks

input.body:
This documents a single-operator, laptop-resident, post-hoc-reconciled fast path for production writes. The proposed logging/reconciliation alone is not sufficient — the path itself is missing several controls I'd expect before this gets used in anger. Requesting changes on the doc structure, not the prose.

Blockers:

1. Authorization gate is undefined. "Wes decides it's urgent" is not a break-glass. A real fast path needs an out-of-band authorization trigger — incident commander ack, two-person rule (one authorizes, one executes), or a pre-authorized runbook entry keyed to the incident class. Otherwise "urgent" becomes "Tuesday afternoon" within a quarter. The doc needs to name who/how the path is invoked.

2. Production credentials on a laptop need a mechanism, not a sentence. Storing prod creds on a maintainer laptop is a credential-theft blast radius. The doc must specify how: short-lived (SSO/STS-derived), HSM-backed, hardware-token-derived, or session-scoped. If the answer is "stored in a password manager," this doc shouldn't exist.

3. No mutual exclusion with the normal release path. If `deployctl direct` and the normal release job run concurrently, post-incident reconciliation is the *first time anyone notices* the inconsistency. The fast path must take the lock the normal job holds, or both must serialize through the same lock.

4. Self-reported audit is weak evidence. The operator shouldn't be writing their own incident record for the action they just performed. `deployctl direct` needs to emit an append-only log entry automatically (incident, service, revision, command, hash of operator identity) *before* the action executes, not based on operator discipline afterward.

5. No blast-radius limit. "Deploys the selected revision directly" with no service allowlist and no canary/percentage is the highest-risk possible action. Need at minimum: service allowlist (which services are reachable via this path), and ideally a pre-execution plan/diff display with explicit confirmation.

Non-blocking notes for the next round: rate limit / cooldown after a direct write, automatic 24h review gate that pings a second operator, and the resume/idempotency semantics if the rollback itself fails midway.

If the answer to any of (1)-(4) is "we'll figure it out when we actually need it," the right move is to not write the doc yet. A break-glass that has never been exercised is the one you reach for during an incident — which is the worst time to discover it doesn't work.

tests.request: Inspect ingest-edge#3308 and review its changes to production request dispatch.

changes: Replace tenant round-robin dispatch with a single request FIFO
Delay insertion into runnable scheduling state until a worker is available
pr.description: Simplify dispatch by replacing tenant round-robin queues with one request FIFO. Requests enter runnable scheduling state only once a worker is free, and the per-tenant waiting-limit enforcement is removed.
pr.title: ingest-edge: replace tenant scheduler with a single request FIFO

input.body:
This PR makes three coupled changes that materially alter production dispatch semantics, and the description doesn't motivate them or address the resulting loss of guarantees. Requesting changes rather than blocking outright, but several pieces are missing before this is safe to ship.

1. Loss of per-tenant fairness. Tenant round-robin gave each tenant a turn at a free worker. A single FIFO means a high-RPS tenant can occupy workers continuously, starving low-RPS tenants. Under bursty load this is a head-of-line blocking problem, not a fairness nicety — it shows up as tenant-level p99 divergence in metrics-router.

2. Removing the per-tenant waiting cap is a regression in back-pressure. Without it, a misbehaving tenant (runaway client, retry storm, bad deploy) can fill the global FIFO and starve every other tenant. "Delay insertion into runnable state until a worker is free" doesn't bound that state — it just shifts where the queue lives. What is the global FIFO depth limit? What rejects a tenant whose share is disproportionate?

3. The "runnable only when worker is free" change is not a fairness substitute. Holding requests until a worker frees just means each new arrival waits its FIFO turn at the moment a worker frees — it doesn't distribute workers across tenants. A large tenant's arrivals will consistently grab the freed worker.

What I'd want before approving:
- Motivation. Was the round-robin scheduler buggy, slow, or causing operational pain? What evidence (benchmark, prod profile, incident)?
- Replacement safeguards. Per-tenant rate limit elsewhere? Global FIFO depth limit with rejection? Any fairness re-introduced at a higher layer (ingress, shard-keeper)?
- Production observability. Tenant-level p50/p99 latency, queue depth per tenant, reject rate. We need a way to detect tenant starvation post-merge.
- Rollback plan. This changes scheduling semantics for live traffic; the rollback path should be straightforward and rehearsed.
- Interaction with shard-keeper and metrics-router. If a tenant floods, does the global back-pressure surface in the metrics-router dual-outcome / DISCONNECT axes (still open per 10/11 review)? A flood-induced starvation could look like a DISCONNECT regression in the suite.

If the goal is simplicity for a specific known bottleneck, please add the benchmark/workload showing the win plus the safeguards above. Otherwise I'd keep the per-tenant queue structure and change only the parts that are actually causing trouble. Happy to re-review once the motivation and safeguards land.

input.query: metrics-router review pending capacity backpressure dual-outcome failure_mode
metrics-router disconnect axis caller-disconnect post-acceptance dual-outcome boundary 10/26

pr.author: wes
changes: Set the shared pending queue capacity multiplier to 2
Accept batches before checking whether pending capacity is exhausted; return retryable backpressure afterward
pr.description: Improve apparent throughput during forecast load by doubling the shared pending queue, removing the per-tenant pending limit, and applying retryable backpressure only after a batch has been accepted.
pr.title: metrics-router: increase pending capacity for forecast traffic

input.body:
Wes — three substantive changes here, two of them straightforward and one that re-opens a boundary we've already closed twice. Going change-by-change.

(1) Shared pending queue capacity x2. Tunable is fine in isolation, but the capacity bump only "improves apparent throughput" if admission thresholds, queue high-watermark signals, and downstream drain rates are recalibrated coherently. If drain is the bottleneck this just grows the queue, lengthens tail latency, and roughly doubles the memory footprint of the router on the hot path. Before merge I want to know: are the existing queue-depth / admission signals (alerts, breaker thresholds, any HWM-based admission control) being re-tuned for the new size, or are we flying blind on the old thresholds against the new queue? And is the forecast window time-bounded (i.e. this is reverted after the spike) or is this a permanent bump? If permanent, what's the plan if drain capacity doesn't scale with it?

(2) Removing the per-tenant pending-batch limit. This is the isolation regression I'm most worried about by default. The per-tenant cap exists so one tenant can't starve others on a shared resource; removing it without a replacement fairness mechanism means a single forecast tenant can now monopolize the doubled shared queue and push cross-tenant backpressure into everyone else's path — which is exactly the symptom the per-tenant cap was preventing. What replaces it? A weighted share, a priority class, a fairness scheduler, a per-tenant share of the new shared capacity? If the answer is "we'll add fairness later," this should land together with that, not before it. I don't want to trade per-tenant backpressure for cross-tenant backpressure.

(3) Accept before checking pending capacity; return retryable backpressure afterward. This is the change I need the most clarity on, because it sits directly on the boundary we closed in the 10/11 dual-outcome review and again in the 10/26 cancel-vs-publish / publication-crash review. The rule we've held is: one accepted attempt produces exactly one durable id and one terminal outcome — never a dual outcome that confuses the caller.

The description as written — accept first, capacity-check after, retryable backpressure as the response — is consistent with two very different designs, and only one of them preserves the dual-outcome rule:

  (a) The "accept" is an internal queue insertion that the caller cannot observe until the capacity check has resolved. Backpressure is the only caller-visible outcome for capacity-exhausted batches. The accepted terminal outcome only becomes durable after the capacity check passes. This preserves the rule.

  (b) The caller observes an acceptance signal (durable id, ack, 2xx-with-accepted, anything) before the capacity check can return backpressure. The caller retries because backpressure was returned, while the previously-accepted batch is independently processed/committed. This re-opens the dual-outcome window between accept and capacity-check, which is structurally the same race the 10/11 and 10/26 work closed.

I need to see which one this is. Specifically: at what point does the caller learn the batch was accepted, and can that signal fire for a batch that subsequently receives retryable backpressure? If the answer is "accept is not externally observable until capacity is confirmed," then this change is fine and I'd like that called out in the commit message / description so the invariant is explicit. If the answer is "accept can be observed before capacity," then this PR re-opens a closed boundary and shouldn't merge in this shape. I would rather we land this with the ordering invariant stated explicitly than have to revisit it after a regression.

One additional note given the DISCONNECT axis is still open in my tracking: if there's any test coverage that exercises caller-disconnect after acceptance, I'd want to see how it interacts with the new "accept before capacity-check" path. Even if the capacity check itself isn't a disconnect vector, it's adjacent to the same ordering region and worth a check.

To unblock:
  - Per (3): state explicitly where the caller's accept signal lives relative to the capacity check, and add a test that proves no caller-visible accept precedes a retryable backpressure on the same batch.
  - Per (2): name the fairness mechanism replacing the per-tenant cap, or scope this change to land together with one.
  - Per (1): confirm recalibration of queue-depth signals and drain assumptions, and state whether the bump is time-bounded to the forecast window or permanent.

Happy to re-review once those are in.

input.body:
Two blocking drifts against the established Lantern published-service alias rule ("Lantern published service alias rule — May 14 decision", deployed for Harbor Health + Mosaic Commerce 2026-05-28; overlap-correction deployed 2026-07-03).

Drift 1 — storage-order tie-break on overlap
The diff summary states overlapping active aliases are resolved by the first matching record in storage order. The July 3 deployed overlap-correction rule is: evaluate every tenant-scoped alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp; if all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, resolve that identity once; if they identify two or more distinct canonical services, keep the signals separate and render ownership as explicit unknown REGARDLESS OF STORAGE ORDER. First-match-by-storage-order silently collapses the same-fail-closed case (HH claims-ingest vs claims-router in either row order) into a single canonical. That is the exact regression that motivated the July 3 correction. Required: drop the first-row tie-break; collect all inclusive-interval matches, and either resolve once (single canonical) or fail closed to "Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp." (multiple distinct canonicals), ordered independently of storage position.

Drift 2 — heuristic rename inference from similar service names
The diff summary also says that when no interval match exists, the patch infers a rename using normalized service-name similarity in the same tenant. This is the heuristic identity inference the May 14 decision and May 28 deployment both explicitly forbid: alias resolution requires (old_id, canonical_pub_id, inclusive_start, inclusive_end) and nothing else; absent / earlier / later the row stays separate with ownership = explicit unknown. No name-similarity, no customer-context inference. Required: remove the similarity fallback entirely; on no inclusive-interval match return the "no qualifying alias" string above and leave the row separate. Do not expand the customer data contract.

  Authorized join: "Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp."
  No qualifying alias: "Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp."

Pulled the record (only the high-level summary was available — no literal unified diff, so this is a spec-level review, not a code-level review).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Review of lantern#3055 — "enrich authority references and prepare shared customer output"
Author: mira · Reviewers: alex · Branch: mira/enriched-authority-reference
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Scope
  src/platform/authority_reference.ts
  src/platform/reference_actions.ts
  src/serializers/shared_reference_output.ts

Summary of the change (per PR record)
  AuthorityReference gains: tenant_id, canonical_service_id,
  authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp,
  authority_payload, writeback_action.
  authority_payload copies from the authority record:
  pipeline_limit, estimated_cost, published_owner (when available).
  writeback_action carries an authority update endpoint.
  shared_reference_output serializes the enriched object and registers
  Harbor Health + Mosaic Commerce as future consumers behind disabled
  rollout flags.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Platform-reference fields (authority_reference.ts)
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Field shape is fine for identity/scoping (tenant_id, canonical_service_id,
  authority_type, authority_record_id). Two things to nail down:

  a. authority_payload is a COPY, not a reference.
     - pipeline_limit / estimated_cost / published_owner are copied "when
       available". Who invalidates the copy when the authority record
       changes? If writeback_action mutates the authority record but the
       AuthorityReference holds a stale copy, HH/MC downstream reads see
       drift. Need an explicit invalidation/re-copy contract, or a
       pointer-with-version instead of a copy.
     - "when available" needs a precise contract: absent → field omitted,
       null, or sentinel? HH/MC consumers will branch on this; ambiguity
       here is a footgun.

  b. source_timestamp is present (good — matches the late-arriving row
     handling we did in Q4, where src-time ordering was the source of
     truth). Confirm the PE reconciler reads this field and not arrival
     time, and that no consumer is silently using arrival time as a
     freshness proxy.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Write behavior (reference_actions.ts / writeback_action)
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Open questions — the record only says "supplies an authority update
  endpoint." Need to confirm each:

  a. Idempotency / version. Does writeback require an etag or
     authority_record version? Without one, two concurrent writers clobber
     each other and the losing side won't know.
  b. Auth + permission model. Who is allowed to invoke writeback? Is it
     scoped per tenant_id / canonical_service_id, or does it accept any
     caller with the endpoint URL? The endpoint URL shouldn't be enough.
  c. Cascade semantics. After a successful writeback, are dependent
     AuthorityReferences (across HH, MC, and Lantern internal) refreshed
     atomically, or does each consumer fetch on its own schedule? Given
     the COPY concern above, this matters.
  d. Frozen-term posture. The HH+MC term is ACTIVE and frozen thru 9/30
     with RO preserved. If writeback is callable during the frozen term
     on a record that backs HH/MC, does it bypass the RO posture
     (writing the authority is not the same as a customer request to
     Lantern, but it does mutate what HH/MC see)? Either:
       - writeback is locked during the frozen term, OR
       - writeback is allowed but the resulting change is masked from
         HH/MC until the term unfreezes.
     State which one is intended.
  e. Fail-closed alignment. Our shard-keeper pattern is signed-env + immut
     + restore-re-verifies, fail-closed. writeback should not be a path
     that can put an AuthorityReference into a state where the
     referenced authority record is unverified. Confirm writeback either
     re-verifies or is rejected when the authority is unverified.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Proposed customer use (shared_reference_output.ts → HH/MC)
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  "Disabled rollout flags" — that's the right default for the active
  term. But the registration itself needs scrutiny now, before flags
  flip:

  a. Field-level redaction. shared_reference_output is described as
     "customer output." Customers must not receive:
       - authority_payload internal fields (pipeline_limit,
         estimated_cost) unless those are explicitly part of the HH/MC
         customer contract. Confirm they are excluded by default and
         only added back behind a per-consumer opt-in flag.
       - writeback_action entirely. An update endpoint is not customer
         surface; it should be stripped before serialization for HH/MC.
  b. Exclusion-list parity. The Lantern PE exclusion list covers
     owner-map and Card-Guardrails refs. New AuthorityReference fields
     (authority_payload copies, writeback_action) must be run through
     the same exclusion filter when materializing the customer view,
     otherwise a previously-clean path leaks.
  c. First-24h re-validation. PE 10/1→10/2 was 181 events (97 HH / 84 MC)
     with all exclusions ✓. After this change lands and before any flag
     flip for HH/MC, that re-validation must be re-run with the new
     fields in scope. Same for the Q4 PE run that closed cleanly with
     source_ts ordering preserved.
  d. Adjacency to rollup-svc (open finding from 10/21). Confirm the
     shared output path does not transit rollup-svc, or if it does,
     that the rollup-svc finding is closed before this is enabled.
  e. Flag-off safety. Confirm flag-off behavior is true no-op for HH/MC
     — the serializer must not register any new code path that runs at
     all when the flag is off. "Registered but disabled" should mean
     zero runtime cost and zero serialization side effects.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Other
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - Tests not mentioned in the summary. Please point me at coverage for:
      (i)   authority_payload absent-field contract
      (ii)  writeback idempotency / version conflict
      (iii) HH/MC exclusion filter against the new fields
      (iv)  flag-off default behavior (true no-op)
  - Backward compat: are these strictly additive on AuthorityReference,
    or do any rename/replace existing fields that other internal callers
    rely on?
  - I only have the PR summary, not the diff itself. If you want a
    line-level pass, push the branch or attach the diff and I'll re-review.

Recommendation
  Don't block, but request changes on the four items I'd want answered
  before the HH/MC flag can be flipped:
    1. Copy-vs-pointer + invalidation contract for authority_payload.
    2. writeback idempotency, auth, cascade, and frozen-term posture.
    3. Field-level redaction in shared_reference_output (especially
       stripping writeback_action and the internal payload fields).
    4. Re-run of the PE exclusion validation against the new field set.
  Land the change behind flags (as designed); merge is fine, enabling
  is not.

  was closed on 2023-07-25 with no rollback needed.
- **Memory delta to record:** p95 memory settled ~5% above the pre-bump
  collector baseline. This is inside normal headroom and is not an alert
  threshold, but it is the new steady-state — record it so future bumps
  don't get re-litigated from scratch.
- **Future collector bumps still require:**
  1. A staging replay against representative prod-shaped load before any
     production push.
  2. An explicit memory watch during the production rollout window —
     p95 memory vs. the post-0.91 baseline (~5% above pre-0.91), not vs.
     the original pre-bump line.

  must clear both gates above.

## OTel exporter retry — retry-only patch note (sha:0a91b7c, 2023-10-09)

Narrow note covering only the retry-only exporter change that has been quiet
in prod since 2023-10-09. Not a collector-wide tuning reference.

- **Scope:** OTLP HTTP exporter retry settings only. The `memory_limiter`
  configuration was deliberately left out of this patch and is tracked
  separately; do not conflate the two.
- **Exporter retry values applied:**
  - `retry_on_failure.max_interval` = 15s
  - `retry_on_failure.max_elapsed_time` = 5m
- **Post-deploy checks (run during the rollout window):**
  1. Dropped-writes counter — must remain flat vs. pre-patch baseline.
  2. Backpressure counters — must remain flat vs. pre-patch baseline.
  3. Retry log volume — observed lower ~24h into the prod deployment
     (2023-10-26); treat lower retry log volume as the expected steady
     state, not as an anomaly.
- **What this note does NOT cover:** batch processor sizing, queue tuning,
  `memory_limiter` thresholds, or any other collector-wide knobs. Those
  remain out of scope for this entry.

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the
operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without
hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real
  backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that
as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

ownership, the owner map, or anything in the cutover checklist above.

return to the baseline behavior.

- Peak retry rate: 129,000 attempts/sec

- Queue depth peak: 75%
- Accepted throughput: 2.9% below baseline (within accepted envelope)
- 5xx rate: no increase vs. pre-rollout baseline

  baseline at full prod was inside this).

  prod was inside this).

signal. Do not negotiate the threshold in the middle of an incident.

|-------|-----------------------------|---------------|------------------|----------------------------------|------------|

| 50%   | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update |
| 100%  | 129,000                     | 188           | 75%              | -2.9%                            | no increase |

full-production observation was supplied for this update. Do not back-fill

Closed out after the heightened watch ended. Final note from Yuki on 2023-07-27.

- **Outcome: production-clean.** Error rate stayed flat across the rollout
  and through the >72h follow-up window. CPU stayed flat. Heightened watch
  was closed on 2023-07-25 with no rollback needed.
- **Memory delta to record:** p95 memory settled ~5% above the pre-bump
  collector baseline. This is inside normal headroom and is not an alert
  threshold, but it is the new steady-state — record it so future bumps
  don't get re-litigated from scratch.
- **Future collector bumps still require:**
  1. A staging replay against representative prod-shaped load before any
     production push.
  2. An explicit memory watch during the production rollout window —
     p95 memory vs. the post-0.91 baseline (~5% above pre-0.91), not vs.
     the original pre-bump line.
  "Approved before" is not sufficient justification on its own; each bump
  must clear both gates above.

## OTel exporter retry — retry-only patch note (sha:0a91b7c, 2023-10-09)

Narrow note covering only the retry-only exporter change that has been quiet
in prod since 2023-10-09. Not a collector-wide tuning reference.

- **Scope:** OTLP HTTP exporter retry settings only. The `memory_limiter`
  configuration was deliberately left out of this patch and is tracked
  separately; do not conflate the two.
- **Exporter retry values applied:**
  - `retry_on_failure.max_interval` = 15s
  - `retry_on_failure.max_elapsed_time` = 5m
- **Post-deploy checks (run during the rollout window):**
  1. Dropped-writes counter — must remain flat vs. pre-patch baseline.
  2. Backpressure counters — must remain flat vs. pre-patch baseline.
  3. Retry log volume — observed lower ~24h into the prod deployment
     (2023-10-26); treat lower retry log volume as the expected steady
     state, not as an anomaly.
- **What this note does NOT cover:** batch processor sizing, queue tuning,
  `memory_limiter` thresholds, or any other collector-wide knobs. Those
  remain out of scope for this entry.

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the
operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without
hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real
  backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that
as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

Owner: alex. Backup: yuki.

pr.author: training-bot
pr.body: This training incident entry attributes the April 18, 2023 shard-keeper disruption to a generic network failure. It states that the alerting system directly identified the underlying cause.
pr.diff: Adds an incident-library entry describing the April 18 shard-keeper event as a generic network failure and stating that alerting directly identified the cause.
pr.title: Training write-up: April 18 shard-keeper incident

input.body:
Requesting changes — the write-up contradicts the actual April 18, 2023 shard-keeper incident record in both of its load-bearing claims, and training material that gets the root cause wrong is actively harmful. Specifics below.

1) "Generic network failure" is wrong. The network layer was a red herring during the early phase of the incident, not the root cause. The actual root cause was a cross-service label-routing problem: Nadia's label-name change was pushed to shard-keeper, but rollup-service (Cyrus team's service at the time) didn't pick up the new label. The label-name diff was eventually found inside shard-keeper. Source: Apr 19, 2023 morning DM with Cyrus reviewing the full sequence ("there was a network-layer red herring for a while, then finally the label-name diff find in shard-keeper").

2) "Alerting directly identified the underlying cause" is the opposite of what happened. The alert pattern was: symptom alerts fired (impaired ingestion), cause alerts did NOT fire, because rollup-service hadn't consumed the new label. So alerting surfaced the symptom and was silent on the cause — the cause was identified by diffing/inspection later. Source: same DM plus the postmortem record.

3) The write-up also drops three facts that matter for training:
   - No data loss, only impaired ingestion across roughly the whole incident window.
   - The rollback was shakier than it should have been (Cyrus's own framing).
   - The incident is the one that drove the 2023-05-22 owner-map lock and the "no config push to shard-keeper without pre-push sync with the other owner/on-call" guard rule. Burying the label-routing/rollup-miss mechanics means readers lose the lesson the post-incident guardrails were built to enforce.

4) Wording: "generic network failure" is the wrong shape for a training entry even if the cause had been network — incident-library training entries should name the failing component and the propagation path, not a category. Please rewrite using the actual mechanism: label-name change in shard-keeper → rollup-service consumer not picking up the new label → symptom alerts fire, cause alerts silent → label-name diff found in shard-keeper.

5) One note on reviewer setup: this PR has me (Alex) listed as reviewer, and I'm the owner of shard-keeper. If you want this entry to stand up in front of the on-call rotation, please also pull a sign-off from Cyrus (rollup-service ownership as of the May 22 audit) before merging — that's the same pre-push sync rule the incident itself produced.

Net: this needs a rewrite of the cause and the alerting claim before it can be merged into incident-library as training material.
