---

# Assessment: Wes's 2025-03-03 No-Rollback Decision

**Bottom line:** On the evidence available at the time, Wes's call was defensible but **not yet closeable**. The signal pattern matches the shard-keeper `label_map` leak touch-matrix hypothesis (validation-source rows reaching a canary aggregate read site, not a live-path regression), which is a known class of "looks like a service regression, isn't" failure. That hypothesis needs four concrete evidence classes before the window can be closed. Below is the assessment plus the evidence checklist.

## 1. What Wes saw (the snapshot)

- Aggregate canary panel: **red 10:47–10:53** (6 minutes).
- Separate live-path canary panel: **at baseline** through the same window.
- The moving series inside the aggregate panel were tagged `source_class=validation`, not `source_class=live` (or equivalent routing/instrumentation class).
- No `label_map` parity exception was raised by the alert path; the metric-router runbook's "compare p99 vs baseline" + "roll back via pipeline if regression confirmed" gates were not triggered on the live-path panel.

## 2. Why the no-rollback call was reasonable

The metrics-router canary runbook (rb_metrics_router_canary) is explicit: rollback is gated on a **live-path** regression, not on an aggregate-panel red. A red aggregate with a green live baseline is the textbook signature of (a) a scheduled load test (per the 2023-08-16 canary note in the same runbook), or (b) a `label_map` leak from a validation/admin read site bleeding into the aggregate. Both are "do not rollback" cases. The deploy history for prod in the cutover window shows no in-flight metrics-router canary on 2025-03-03 that had crossed into the live-path panel, which is consistent with Wes's read. **On the snapshot alone, rollback would have been the wrong move** — it would have undone a canary that the live path was passing, and left the actual `label_map` leak unfixed.

## 3. Why it isn't closeable yet

The shard-keeper runbook `rb_shard_keeper_label_parity` (post-May-18, owner alex / backup cyrus-team) sets a hard rule that applies here: **a canary-window clear requires confirming the canary aggregate read site is on the parity-signed-off path**, and preflight-PASS + alert-source-PASS is not an override on a parity-FAIL (re-confirmed in the 2026-09-12 shard-keeper#190 lesson, which is the same class of failure). Wes had a plausible explanation for the red, but "plausible" is not the standard; the standard is source-class evidence. Closing the window on a "the live path was green so the aggregate can't matter" argument is exactly the failure mode that the `label_map` touch matrix (19 read sites, grouped-kills methodology) was written to prevent — a missed read site produces a **falsely clean cutover**.

## 4. Evidence checklist to close the canary event

Four classes, all required. Mark each ✅/❌ with the artifact.

### A. Source-class evidence (was the moving series really validation?)

- [ ] **Full replay source-class export** for the 10:47–10:53 window: every series that contributed to the aggregate panel, with `source_class`, originating service, originating read site, and label values. Goal: prove the moving series were *only* `source_class=validation` rows, not a live-path regression hiding inside the aggregate.
- [ ] **No-series-with-other-source-class attestation** for the same window from rollup-service (the parity-sign-off owner). Per Cardinality Guardrails (2023-11-08) and `rb_shard_keeper_label_parity`, a green metrics-router canary alone does not prove rollup-service parity.
- [ ] **Origin-trace for each validation series** to its read site. The shard-keeper `label_map` touch matrix lists the 19 routing + admin/validation read sites — every validation series must map to one…

arguments.body:
# Staff IC — first 30-day operating focus

Date: 2024-05-22
For: Hema
Scope: 30-day operating focus, effective with Staff IC role (5/20)

## Near-term technical outcomes (next 30 days)

1. Make covered Guardrails parity fixtures routine.
   - Fixtures should be the default path engineers run when changing Guardrails surface or label-map behavior, not an ad-hoc add-on.
   - Coverage tracked against the current parity list, not just on demand.
   - "Routine" means: present in the standard dev loop, broken visibly when regressed, and reflected in shard-keeper's touch matrix discipline.

2. Complete Lantern's tenant-authorization and denial-envelope evidence without granting customer access.
   - Build the evidence the customer would need to verify (auth/provenance, denial shape, failure semantics), not a product surface.
   - Iris owns Lantern product interpretation; I do not reshape the external contract.
   - Outcome target: a reviewer can inspect the evidence and confirm the customer-visible contract holds, without any external preview channel.

3. Preserve bounded-decompression rollout evidence at ingest-edge.
   - Rollout evidence stays complete and reviewable as bounded decompression progresses.
   - Verifies removed/repointed sites at close, not just at enable.
   - Tied to the ingest-edge staging rollback drills already on the calendar.

## Operating boundary

What I do:
- Define cross-service invariants and escalation paths.
- Set the standard for evidence shape (parity fixtures, customer-facing contracts, rollout audits).
- Call out when a handoff or cutover looks unsafe; escalate rather than expand scope.

What I do not do:
- Take implementation or operations from mapped owners.
- Set Lantern product interpretation (that stays with Iris).
- Promote Wes from practical backup to formal primary owner.
- Take on people-management assignment — none in this 30-day window.

Wes's role in this period: backup only. Router canary and ingest-edge staging rollback drills are the concrete backup surface; Wes is not a co-owner.

## Notes

- Hema may reorder the cutover if prod forces it; this 30-day list is the focus under normal conditions, not a fixed sequence.
- Each outcome has a single mapped owner for implementation/ops; my contribution is the invariant and the evidence bar.

tests.request: Inspect observability-ui#1192 and review its removal of source classification from the metrics-router dashboard.

output.author: wes
output.title: metrics-router dashboard: collapse equivalent source series

pr.author: wes

changes.summary: Drops the source classification from dashboard queries and combines the previously separate source series.
Updates regression snapshots and assertions to expect one combined series without source-specific labels.

pr.description: Remove the source classification from the metrics-router dashboard because live and validation samples use the same metric schema. Collapse the source-specific queries and legend entries into a single series to reduce visual duplication.
pr.tests: Dashboard snapshot and query regression tests pass with the combined series.
pr.title: metrics-router dashboard: collapse equivalent source series

input.body:
Requesting changes — do not land as-is.

The justification ("live and validation samples use the same metric schema") describes a schema concern, not a viewer concern. The dashboard axis being collapsed is the source classification (live vs validation), which is a load-distinction axis, not a schema axis. Collapsing it in the viewer does not unify the underlying series; it just hides that they are separate. That is exactly the kind of UI-only merge that makes a future metrics-router regression invisible until it shows up downstream.

Specific concerns, in priority order:

1. Dual-outcome regression risk (recall: 10/11 metrics-router dual-outcome, review filed). The metrics-router has an established history of RACE / CRASH axes where two legitimate-looking outcomes could be presented as one. "Same schema, so combine" is the same shape of mistake. Schema equivalence is necessary for a merge to be safe, not sufficient. The PR description gives only the necessary condition. Need an explicit statement of what distinguishes live from validation in the underlying router — producer, pipeline stage, ingestion path, retention tier, anything — and a justification that collapsing those is acceptable for the audience of this dashboard. If the distinction is "different retention / different SLA / different alerting," collapsing is wrong.

2. Viewer-only collapse hides failure modes the router has actually exhibited. The CRASH axis (10/26 review) is a concrete example: cancel-vs-publish was invisible until the dual-outcome review. A dashboard that can no longer show live and validation separately loses the ability to spot the next instance of that class of bug at the router boundary. The defense is not "we have tests" — the dashboard is the operator's view, and the tests in this PR are snapshot tests of the combined view, which is circular.

3. Snapshot tests updated to match the change. dashboards/metrics-router/traffic.test.ts now asserts the combined series, so the test will pass on a broken merge and a correct merge alike. That is not a regression test of the merge, it is a regression test of itself. Need at least one assertion that fails if live and validation diverge (count, rate, error rate, whatever the router actually emits distinctly) — something that pins the distinction the PR is removing.

4. Description does not name the affected audience or the migration path. Who currently relies on seeing the source split? Was this raised in an issue, or is it a unilateral cleanup? "Reduce visual duplication" is a weak reason to remove an axis that costs nothing to keep.

What I would accept instead, roughly in order of preference:
  a. Keep the source axis, address the duplication another way (small multiples, toggle, denser layout).
  b. Collapse, but only after the router itself collapses the distinction at the source (i.e., one series, one pipeline) — and that change ships first, with its own review, in metrics-router.
  c. Collapse in the dashboard, but keep both queries in the JSON (different panel / hidden until toggled), so the distinction is recoverable, and add a non-snapshot assertion as in (3).

Happy to re-review on any of those.

Got it — Hema's revised Sphere senior-IC rubric draft, 2025-08-13 10:50 ET.

What the language does, in three clauses:

1. Positions the role as actively *obtaining* (not just facilitating) explicit owner handoffs and defining shared technical invariants. The verb choice is strong.
2. Keeps implementation / release / rollback / operations accountability with the mapped teams. The lead is not a single point of accountability — this is the protective clause for the role.

- "Centralized approval unless separately assigned" is the clause that may interact with the Cardinality Guardrails prod-scan gate. - "Obtain explicit owner handoffs" backs the kind of owner-coordination work you've already been doing — e.g., the cross-service failure case intake where you, Wes, and Nadia each got explicit ownership (case, responder-path, postmortem). Under this rubric that pattern becomes the expected norm, not the exception. Worth confirming what "explicit" means operationally: doc + named owner + ack, or something lighter.
- People-management exclusion matches how you've been operating. No surprise there, and the carve-out language keeps the door open if it's ever separately assigned.

arguments.body:
2026-04-22 — addendum: cross-service role produces reusable boundaries, not a centralized gate

Two worked examples for Hema's next calibration packet. The point in both is the
same shape: the cross-service role names who owns implementation, release, and
rollback outside my role, names any triggered exception owner explicitly, and
does not absorb or relabel any of that work as mine. Each example leaves the
owner map and customer access unchanged.

1) April 7 cross-service proposal-intake rule

The rule is an intake pattern, not a sign-off matrix. For each cross-service
proposal that lands, the rule separately names:

  - the mapped implementation and release owner — the team that writes,
    reviews, ships, and decides the release window; this is unchanged from the
    existing owner map.
  - the rollback owner — the team that owns canary, rollback, and kill for the
    same change; this is also unchanged from the existing owner map and is
    not reassigned to the cross-service reviewer.
  - any triggered exception owner, named by exception class only when the
    proposal actually triggers that class:
      - invariant exception → the invariant owner (already named on the
        existing invariant; not reassigned).
      - provenance exception → the provenance / source-registration owner.
      - failure-mode exception → the cross-service failure-mode reviewer
        (my role), scoped to the failure-mode boundary only.
      - ownership exception → the relevant owner team; the rule does not
        redraw the owner map.
      - escalation exception → the existing on-call / program escalation path
        (Hema's lane), not the cross-service reviewer.

Naming an exception reviewer at intake is the boundary being made reusable. It
is not a new approval step, not a new sign-off role, and not a new routing
table beyond the existing owner map. The mapped implementation and release
owner and the rollback owner remain the ones who ship and roll back; the
exception owner is named only when the exception class is actually triggered.

2) April 17 Lantern incident-load shared-registration migration

This is the migration where the shared-registration shape was applied to
Lantern's incident-load source, completed on the scheduled April 17 cutover.
Ownership during the migration:

  - Product Engineering: implementation and release owner. They wrote and
    shipped the migration, including tenant authorization before source
    access, the Lantern Incident-Load Provenance Schema LILP-1, the
    required tenant-scoped provenance source identifier, the required
    source timestamp, stale-or-missing-as-explicit-unknown, the preserved
    excluded-field list, and the read-only posture. They owned the
    rollout.
  - Iris: customer-interpretation owner. She completed the paired
    interpretation check across the pre- and post-migration pairs for the
    covered Lantern customer source families.
  - Alex (me): owned two things and only two things:
      a) the shared-registration safety gate — the boundary check that the
         shared-registration shape was correctly applied to incident-load,
         i.e., that tenant authorization runs before source access, that
         the required provenance and timestamp fields are present, that
         stale or missing input renders as explicit unknown, and that the
         excluded-field list is preserved.
      b) the 240-lookup LPS-001 rerun — the safety-check rerun over 240
         tenant-scoped lookups (120 Harbor Health, 120 Mosaic Commerce),
         against the LPS-001 fail conditions.

LPS-001 rerun result (recorded, not interpreted as a release verdict):

  - 16 denied requests made no adapter call. The authorization-before-
    access ordering held under denial.
  - 12 stale or missing inputs rendered as explicit unknown. The freshness
    contract held and did not silently substitute a value.
  - No lookup produced: an authorization-wrapper bypass, cross-tenant
    material, missing required provenance, a missing required source
    timestamp, an excluded field, unpublished ownership, or a write.
    The safety and authorization posture held across the 240-lookup
    sample; there was no safety or authorization violation.

The 16 + 12 + (240 - 16 - 12 = 212 authorized-and-clean) split is the
reading of the rerun: denials and stale-or-missing inputs each behaved as
specified, and the authorized-and-clean lookups stayed inside the safety
posture. The rerun is the boundary check, not the implementation
verification; the implementation verification is Product Engineering's.

What this addendum does and does not claim

Does claim:
  - The cross-service role produces reusable boundaries (the intake rule's
    exception-class naming, the shared-registration safety gate) without
    centralizing implementation, release, rollback, or interpretation
    work.
  - In both examples, the mapped implementation and release owner and
    the rollback owner are named separately from any triggered exception
    owner, and the exception owner's scope is bounded to the triggered
    exception class.

Does not claim:
  - No owner-map change. The April 7 rule did not redraw who owns what;
    it named the existing owners and the exception owner pattern. The
    April 17 migration did not move implementation, release, rollback,
    or interpretation ownership; it applied an existing shared-
    registration shape to one more source family under those existing
    owners.
  - No customer-access change. Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce
    remained the preview accounts, read-only through the shared
    authorization wrapper, with the unchanged allowed reads and the
    unchanged excluded-field list. No additional account, no excluded
    field, no write capability, and no broader rollout was authorized
    by either the rule or the migration.
  - No Staff title implication. This addendum is evidence for Hema's
    next calibration packet; it does not state or imply a calibration
    outcome.

Status as of 2026-04-22: both examples above are recorded; the owner
map and customer access remain as they were on 2026-04-10.

Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft
Working draft for later revision. Bounded to IC role; no claim of managing people, owning every release, or becoming a centralized approval gate. Organized as Hema requested: cross-service invariants and failure modes, technical outcomes, owner leverage, and boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners.

Frame: I review only where work crosses service boundaries or introduces new failure modes; otherwise it stays with mapped owners. Below are the concrete 2026 items that fit that frame, with the source artifacts that ground each claim.

1. Cross-service invariants and failure modes I reviewed

1.1 Authority boundaries and the Cardinality Guardrails design
- What: Defined the invariants that an authority record must preserve when an internal implementation slice attaches read-only owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references to the same canonical service. The invariants — authority_type + authority_record_id + source_timestamp — must be preserved unchanged; if no reference can be produced, the request is sent to Harbor/Mosaic rather than silently losing provenance.
- Why it crosses a boundary: owner-map references and Cardinality Guardrails touch the model used by Harbor, Mosaic, and downstream consumers. Changing how authority is referenced affects every service that reasons about identity. I treated this as a cross-service invariant, not a routine implementation decision, and surfaced the rule rather than letting it get absorbed into a single team's PR.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 (Oct 22 owner-boundary review, closed).
- Bounded to IC: I defined the invariant; the implementation slice is owned and merged by the mapped owner. I did not become the approval gate for the slice.

1.2 Duplicate-deploy dedup key
- What: Stated the dedup key as (tenant_id, published_service_id, provenance_source, source_event_id); missing any field → "unavailable" rather than best-guess.
- Why it crosses a boundary: dedup spans ingest-edge → metrics-router → shard-keeper. A wrong key in any one of them double-counts downstream; a too-loose key silently drops events. Pinning the key and the missing-field behavior was the cross-service invariant. The implementation in each service stayed with the mapped owner.
- Source: memory, 2025-08-12.

1.3 Tenant isolation for edge-gateway / ingest-edge
- What: Treated tenant isolation as a cross-service invariant, not a per-service detail, and insisted any change that could weaken tenant boundaries be reviewed across services.
- Why it crosses a boundary: a per-tenant bleed in edge-gateway or ingest-edge shows up as misattributed traffic or cardinality in metrics-router. Reviewing it at the boundary is where I add value.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 (scope of Alex review enumerated as: tenant isolation, provenance, auth source timestamps, authority duplication/mutation, customer-path isolation).

1.4 Provenance and auth source timestamps
- What: Reviewed changes touching how provenance_source and auth source timestamps flow through the pipeline, because a drift here corrupts the dedup key and the authority record in 1.1/1.2 simultaneously.
- Source: same closed doc as 1.1/1.3.

2. Technical outcomes

2.1 Mosaic forward-gate criteria, closed 2026-01-22
- What: Documented and validated the forward-gate criteria for Mosaic past the 17.2M forecast: 90 minutes at +15% load, q-p99 ≤ 400ms held for 5 minutes, queue-full ≤ 0.5% held for 5 minutes. Pre-accept backpressure is retryable. Capacity: 2,048 global / 64 per-tenant.
- Outcome: gate criteria were adopted as the cutover bar; the gate is documented (doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937).
- Source: memory, 2026-01-22 entry.

2.2 shard-keeper#190 (Cyrus) cutover, closed 2026-09-17
- What: Confirmed the cutover was closed and scoped to replay-fixture cleanup. Pinned the gate: an id-carrying reject from a prior-epoch must be honored before any comms promise — i.e., verify the address before promising reachability. This is a concrete instance of "review only at boundaries that introduce new failure modes": the prior-epoch reject is exactly the kind of failure mode a comms-only check would have missed.
- Source: memory, 2026-09-17 entry.

2.3 Apr 14 shard-keeper / rollup-service outage
- What: Co-authored the postmortem (doc_postmortem_apr14_outage, 2026-04-21). The postmortem identifies the cross-service failure mode between shard-keeper and rollup-service.
- Bounded to IC: postmortem authorship is review-by-default, not ownership of either service's roadmap. Wes runs responder paths; Nadia runs postmortem process; I am one of the reviewers on cross-service failure cases.
- Source: doc_postmortem_apr14_outage.

3. Owner leverage: where I made a difference without becoming the owner

3.1 Metrics-router ownership transition (Wes primary, Alex backup)
- What: Stood up as backup on metrics-router during Hema's metrics migration so the cutover could proceed without single-point risk. Hema may reorder cutover; backup coverage is what kept the migration reversible.
- Outcome: Wes is the primary owner; I am backup only. The backup role was deliberately scoped to "present and able to act", not "second owner with parallel roadmap authority."
- Bounded to IC: I do not own metrics-router's roadmap, release cadence, or PR queue; I review at boundaries. This is leverage from being the right reviewer at the right moment, not leverage from accumulating ownership.
- Source: user profile; Hema collaboration note.

3.2 Lantern's corrected review routing
- What: The Lantern owner-model was validated as NOT an implementation / release-gate by Hema in the Oct 9 1:1. The routine Lantern work — copy, fixture-naming — stays with the mapped owner. I review only the cross-service slice: tenant isolation, provenance, auth source timestamps, authority duplication/mutation, customer-path isolation. This corrects an earlier drift where Lantern review could have been read as "Alex reviews Lantern changes" in general.
- Outcome: routing is now explicit and bounded. Routine → mapped owner; cross-service → Alex.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.

3.3 October 22 owner-boundary review (closed)
- What: At the Q4 owner-boundary review on 2026-10-22, two routine items were tested against my review scope: PE-routine Lantern copy / fixture-naming, and Wes-routine metrics-router staging route-cache param. Both were off-boundary for me and stayed with the mapped reviewers. The incident-practice split was preserved (Wes = responder paths, Nadia = postmortem process, Alex = cross-service failure cases only).
- Outcome: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation, no Lantern first-slice decision, no internal-shadow decision, no customer/platform-scope decision triggered. The review closed with the boundary intact.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-22 entry.

4. Boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners

4.1 I do not own releases. I review PRs that touch cross-service invariants (authority boundaries, dedup key, tenant isolation, provenance, customer-path isolation, prior-epoch gate semantics). I do not own metrics-router's release calendar, ingest-edge's deploys, or shard-keeper's cutover execution.

4.2 I do not manage people. I author and co-author postmortems and review docs; the people-management actions (hiring, leveling, performance, comp) are not part of my role and are not claimed here.

4.3 I do not act as a centralized approval gate. The Oct 22 review specifically confirmed: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation. Routine work routes to mapped owners; my review appears only at the boundary.

4.4 Internal implementation slices may attach read-only owner-map + Cardinality Guardrails references to the same canonical service, and must preserve authority_type + authority_record_id + source_timestamp; no reference output routes to Harbor/Mosaic. I stated the invariant; the slice is implemented and merged by the mapped owner.

4.5 Incident practice split is intact and was reaffirmed on 2026-10-22: Wes owns responder paths, Nadia owns postmortem process, I review cross-service failure cases only.

5. Items I deliberately did not claim
- Did not claim to own metrics-router, ingest-edge, or shard-keeper.
- Did not claim to run the metrics migration (Hema runs it; I am a reviewer and backup).
- Did not claim to be the postmortem owner (Nadia owns the postmortem process; I am a reviewer and co-author on the cross-service cases).
- Did not claim to have approved or rejected any release on my own authority — my review appears at the boundary, the mapped owner decides.
- Did not claim any centralized approval role; the Oct 22 review explicitly foreclosed that interpretation.

6. Open items for revision before submission
- Refresh doc-id references in §7 against current documents (doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5, doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937, doc_postmortem_apr14_outage) if any have moved.
- Replace any item where I have only the headline with the concrete artifact (PR link, metric, or runbook entry) Hema will want to see.
- Decide which 1.x items to keep in the narrative vs. fold into a single "boundary invariants" paragraph.
- Add the exact 17.2M forecast number and the q-p99 / queue-full numbers into §2.1 if Hema wants the gate numbers in the narrative rather than only in the doc reference.
- Confirm the metrics-router backup scope (present-and-able-to-act vs. deeper) before submission so it does not get read as co-ownership.
- Final portal verification and submission still due Fri 2026-11-13 17:00 ET.

7. Source index
- doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 — closed Lantern review / Oct 22 owner-boundary review (Hema 1:1 validation, owner-model scope, internal-slice invariants).
- doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937 — Mosaic forward gate (2,048 global / 64 per-tenant, +15% load, q-p99 ≤ 400ms × 5m, queue-full ≤ 0.5% × 5m).
- doc_postmortem_apr14_outage — Apr 14 shard-keeper / rollup-service postmortem (2026-04-21).
- Memory entries: 2026-01-22 (Mosaic), 2026-09-17 (shard-keeper#190), 2026-10-22 (owner-boundary review), 2025-08-12 (dedup key).
- User profile: metrics pipeline ownership (Wes primary / Alex backup), Hema collaboration on metrics migration.

8. Dated Q4 examples — owner-boundary review and corrected review routing

These two examples sit in the same week and together show how the boundary actually operated: routine items stayed with mapped owners, and the named boundary case pulled me in without my becoming a centralized gate.

8.1 October 22, 2026 — owner-boundary review (routine stays with mapped owners)
- What I did: At the Q4 owner-boundary review I tested two routine items against my review scope: PE-routine Lantern copy / fixture-naming, and Wes-routine metrics-router staging route-cache param. Both were off-boundary for me and stayed with the mapped reviewers.
- Why this fits the framing: routine implementation work does not pull into my review queue even when the PR shows up next to ones that do. The boundary held without me declining in the abstract — the review itself was the disambiguator.
- Outcome: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation, no Lantern first-slice decision, no internal-shadow decision, no customer/platform-scope decision triggered. Wes = responder paths, Nadia = postmortem process, Alex = cross-service failure cases only. Review closed with the boundary intact.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-22 entry; closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.
- Bounded to IC: I was a reviewer at the boundary meeting, not the meeting's owner; nothing here gives me a release authority, an approval queue, or a reviewer-of-record role on routine Lantern or metrics-router PRs.

8.2 October 27, 2026 — corrected review routing engaged me for a named boundary (defense without takeover)
- Trigger: corrected review routing surfaced an actual named boundary — an order-dependent overwrite between owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references attached to the same canonical service. Each reference is keyed (tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id), each with its own source_timestamp; insertion order determines the surviving authority. This is a shared-contract defect, not a per-service implementation choice.
- What I did: I blocked the staff-only build and the internal shadow on the shared-contract defect, because proceeding would have committed an internal surface area to an order-sensitive reference contract that we could not yet defend. I did not take over Product Engineering's implementation of the fix.
- What I did NOT do: I did not reassign the implementation to myself, did not draft the fix, did not schedule a release, did not authorize internal shadow, and did not expand any customer scope. Product Engineering remained the implementation owner; my role was to refuse to advance an unrepaired defect across the shared contract.
- Resolution (per November 12, 2026 Lantern evidence review): the October 27 order-dependent overwrite is fixed. The corrected dual-authority build passed the bounded contract review (closed) and entered bounded internal shadow for Infra and Product Engineering under the conditions set by that review. The implementation slice remained with Product Engineering throughout. The reference integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce; no internal shadow, no staff-only preview, no dark-launch cohort touches either customer path, and no customer scope changed.
- Why this fits the framing: this is the named-boundary case the Oct 22 review reserved me for. Routine owner-map edits and routine Cardinality Guardrails changes still route to their mapped owners; the order-sensitive overwrite between them was the cross-service invariant the boundary is for. The right response was to block the advance and return the fix to the implementation owner; the right resolution was to verify the contract once the corrected code came back, admit the build to bounded internal shadow, and stop short of any customer-path change. I reviewed the contract and the failure boundary; Product Engineering owned the implementation throughout; the customer paths stayed out of scope.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-27 entry (Lantern first-internal-slice HELD; correction owed by PE); November 12 Lantern evidence review (closed), with corrected build admitted to bounded internal shadow for Infra and PE only.
- Bounded to IC: I added one block on a shared-contract defect and named the invariant that must hold after PE's correction. I did not become Product Engineering's reviewer-of-record, did not take the slice into my roadmap, and did not become a gate on Lantern first-slice decisions beyond the named defect. With the defect fixed and the contract review closed, the boundary returns to its standing rule: routine Lantern work routes to the mapped owner, and my reviewer frame stays reserved for cross-service failure cases.

8.3 Net reading for Hema (one paragraph, no claims beyond §8.1 and §8.2)
The Oct 22 review confirmed routine stays with mapped owners and I am not a centralized gate. The Oct 27 corrected review routing showed what the boundary looks like when it actually fires — a named shared-contract defect, a block on the staff-only build and internal shadow, and an explicit return-to-owner for the fix. The November 12 evidence review then verified the corrected code against the named invariant, closed the contract review, and admitted the build to bounded internal shadow for Infra and Product Engineering only. I reviewed the contract and the failure boundary; Product Engineering owned the implementation throughout; the customer paths stayed out of scope; reference integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce; the build has not graduated to continuing internal operating use.

arguments.body:
Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft
Working draft for later revision. Bounded to IC role; no claim of managing people, owning every release, or becoming a centralized approval gate. Organized as Hema requested: cross-service invariants and failure modes, technical outcomes, owner leverage, and boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners.

Frame: I review only where work crosses service boundaries or introduces new failure modes; otherwise it stays with mapped owners. Below are the concrete 2026 items that fit that frame, with the source artifacts that ground each claim.

1. Cross-service invariants and failure modes I reviewed

1.1 Authority boundaries and the Cardinality Guardrails design
- What: Defined the invariants that an authority record must preserve when an internal implementation slice attaches read-only owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references to the same canonical service. The invariants — authority_type + authority_record_id + source_timestamp — must be preserved unchanged; if no reference can be produced, the request is sent to Harbor/Mosaic rather than silently losing provenance.
- Why it crosses a boundary: owner-map references and Cardinality Guardrails touch the model used by Harbor, Mosaic, and downstream consumers. Changing how authority is referenced affects every service that reasons about identity. I treated this as a cross-service invariant, not a routine implementation decision, and surfaced the rule rather than letting it get absorbed into a single team's PR.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 (Oct 22 owner-boundary review, closed).
- Bounded to IC: I defined the invariant; the implementation slice is owned and merged by the mapped owner. I did not become the approval gate for the slice.

1.2 Duplicate-deploy dedup key
- What: Stated the dedup key as (tenant_id, published_service_id, provenance_source, source_event_id); missing any field → "unavailable" rather than best-guess.
- Why it crosses a boundary: dedup spans ingest-edge → metrics-router → shard-keeper. A wrong key in any one of them double-counts downstream; a too-loose key silently drops events. Pinning the key and the missing-field behavior was the cross-service invariant. The implementation in each service stayed with the mapped owner.
- Source: memory, 2025-08-12.

1.3 Tenant isolation for edge-gateway / ingest-edge
- What: Treated tenant isolation as a cross-service invariant, not a per-service detail, and insisted any change that could weaken tenant boundaries be reviewed across services.
- Why it crosses a boundary: a per-tenant bleed in edge-gateway or ingest-edge shows up as misattributed traffic or cardinality in metrics-router. Reviewing it at the boundary is where I add value.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 (scope of Alex review enumerated as: tenant isolation, provenance, auth source timestamps, authority duplication/mutation, customer-path isolation).

1.4 Provenance and auth source timestamps
- What: Reviewed changes touching how provenance_source and auth source timestamps flow through the pipeline, because a drift here corrupts the dedup key and the authority record in 1.1/1.2 simultaneously.
- Source: same closed doc as 1.1/1.3.

2. Technical outcomes

2.1 Mosaic forward-gate criteria, closed 2026-01-22
- What: Documented and validated the forward-gate criteria for Mosaic past the 17.2M forecast: 90 minutes at +15% load, q-p99 ≤ 400ms held for 5 minutes, queue-full ≤ 0.5% held for 5 minutes. Pre-accept backpressure is retryable. Capacity: 2,048 global / 64 per-tenant.
- Outcome: gate criteria were adopted as the cutover bar; the gate is documented (doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937).
- Source: memory, 2026-01-22 entry.

2.2 shard-keeper#190 (Cyrus) cutover, closed 2026-09-17
- What: Confirmed the cutover was closed and scoped to replay-fixture cleanup. Pinned the gate: an id-carrying reject from a prior-epoch must be honored before any comms promise — i.e., verify the address before promising reachability. This is a concrete instance of "review only at boundaries that introduce new failure modes": the prior-epoch reject is exactly the kind of failure mode a comms-only check would have missed.
- Source: memory, 2026-09-17 entry.

2.3 Apr 14 shard-keeper / rollup-service outage
- What: Co-authored the postmortem (doc_postmortem_apr14_outage, 2026-04-21). The postmortem identifies the cross-service failure mode between shard-keeper and rollup-service.
- Bounded to IC: postmortem authorship is review-by-default, not ownership of either service's roadmap. Wes runs responder paths; Nadia runs postmortem process; I am one of the reviewers on cross-service failure cases.
- Source: doc_postmortem_apr14_outage.

3. Owner leverage: where I made a difference without becoming the owner

3.1 Metrics-router ownership transition (Wes primary, Alex backup)
- What: Stood up as backup on metrics-router during Hema's metrics migration so the cutover could proceed without single-point risk. Hema may reorder cutover; backup coverage is what kept the migration reversible.
- Outcome: Wes is the primary owner; I am backup only. The backup role was deliberately scoped to "present and able to act", not "second owner with parallel roadmap authority."
- Bounded to IC: I do not own metrics-router's roadmap, release cadence, or PR queue; I review at boundaries. This is leverage from being the right reviewer at the right moment, not leverage from accumulating ownership.
- Source: user profile; Hema collaboration note.

3.2 Lantern's corrected review routing
- What: The Lantern owner-model was validated as NOT an implementation / release-gate by Hema in the Oct 9 1:1. The routine Lantern work — copy, fixture-naming — stays with the mapped owner. I review only the cross-service slice: tenant isolation, provenance, auth source timestamps, authority duplication/mutation, customer-path isolation. This corrects an earlier drift where Lantern review could have been read as "Alex reviews Lantern changes" in general.
- Outcome: routing is now explicit and bounded. Routine → mapped owner; cross-service → Alex.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.

3.3 October 22 owner-boundary review (closed)
- What: At the Q4 owner-boundary review on 2026-10-22, two routine items were tested against my review scope: PE-routine Lantern copy / fixture-naming, and Wes-routine metrics-router staging route-cache param. Both were off-boundary for me and stayed with the mapped reviewers. The incident-practice split was preserved (Wes = responder paths, Nadia = postmortem process, Alex = cross-service failure cases only).
- Outcome: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation, no Lantern first-slice decision, no internal-shadow decision, no customer/platform-scope decision triggered. The review closed with the boundary intact.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-22 entry.

4. Boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners

4.1 I do not own releases. I review PRs that touch cross-service invariants (authority boundaries, dedup key, tenant isolation, provenance, customer-path isolation, prior-epoch gate semantics). I do not own metrics-router's release calendar, ingest-edge's deploys, or shard-keeper's cutover execution.

4.2 I do not manage people. I author and co-author postmortems and review docs; the people-management actions (hiring, leveling, performance, comp) are not part of my role and are not claimed here.

4.3 I do not act as a centralized approval gate. The Oct 22 review specifically confirmed: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation. Routine work routes to mapped owners; my review appears only at the boundary.

4.4 Internal implementation slices may attach read-only owner-map + Cardinality Guardrails references to the same canonical service, and must preserve authority_type + authority_record_id + source_timestamp; no reference output routes to Harbor/Mosaic. I stated the invariant; the slice is implemented and merged by the mapped owner.

4.5 Incident practice split is intact and was reaffirmed on 2026-10-22: Wes owns responder paths, Nadia owns postmortem process, I review cross-service failure cases only.

5. Items I deliberately did not claim
- Did not claim to own metrics-router, ingest-edge, or shard-keeper.
- Did not claim to run the metrics migration (Hema runs it; I am a reviewer and backup).
- Did not claim to be the postmortem owner (Nadia owns the postmortem process; I am a reviewer and co-author on the cross-service cases).
- Did not claim to have approved or rejected any release on my own authority — my review appears at the boundary, the mapped owner decides.
- Did not claim any centralized approval role; the Oct 22 review explicitly foreclosed that interpretation.

6. Open items for revision before submission
- Confirm final dates and doc IDs above against current documents (doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5, doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937, doc_postmortem_apr14_outage) — refresh references if any have moved.
- Replace any item where I have only the headline and add the concrete artifact (PR link, metric, or runbook entry) Hema will want to see.
- Decide which 1.x items to keep in the narrative vs. fold into a single "boundary invariants" paragraph; the current structure leaves them separate to make the cross-service nature explicit.
- Tighten the language in §3 so "leverage" reads as "right reviewer at the right moment", not "accumulated influence".
- Add the exact 17.2M forecast number and the q-p99 / queue-full numbers into §2.1 if Hema wants the gate numbers in the narrative rather than only in the doc reference.
- Confirm the metrics-router backup scope (present-and-able-to-act vs. deeper) before submission so it does not get read as co-ownership.

7. Source index
- doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 — closed Lantern review / Oct 22 owner-boundary review (Hema 1:1 validation, owner-model scope, internal-slice invariants).
- doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937 — Mosaic forward gate (2,048 global / 64 per-tenant, +15% load, q-p99 ≤ 400ms × 5m, queue-full ≤ 0.5% × 5m).
- doc_postmortem_apr14_outage — Apr 14 shard-keeper / rollup-service postmortem (2026-04-21).
- Memory entries: 2026-01-22 (Mosaic), 2026-09-17 (shard-keeper#190), 2026-10-22 (owner-boundary review), 2025-08-12 (dedup key).
- User profile: metrics pipeline ownership (Wes primary / Alex backup), Hema collaboration on metrics migration.

8. Dated Q4 examples — owner-boundary review and corrected review routing

These two examples sit in the same week and together show how the boundary actually operated: routine items stayed with mapped owners, and the named boundary case pulled me in without my becoming a centralized gate.

8.1 October 22, 2026 — owner-boundary review (routine stays with mapped owners)
- What I did: At the Q4 owner-boundary review I tested two routine items against my review scope: PE-routine Lantern copy / fixture-naming, and Wes-routine metrics-router staging route-cache param. Both were off-boundary for me and stayed with the mapped reviewers.
- Why this fits the framing: routine implementation work does not pull into my review queue even when the PR shows up next to ones that do. The boundary held without me declining in the abstract — the review itself was the disambiguator.
- Outcome: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation, no Lantern first-slice decision, no internal-shadow decision, no customer/platform-scope decision triggered. Wes = responder paths, Nadia = postmortem process, Alex = cross-service failure cases only. Review closed with the boundary intact.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-22 entry; closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.
- Bounded to IC: I was a reviewer at the boundary meeting, not the meeting's owner; nothing here gives me a release authority, an approval queue, or a reviewer-of-record role on routine Lantern or metrics-router PRs.

8.2 October 27, 2026 — corrected review routing engaged me for a named boundary (defense without takeover)
- Trigger: corrected review routing surfaced an actual named boundary — an order-dependent overwrite between owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references attached to the same canonical service. Each reference is keyed (tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id), each with its own source_timestamp; insertion order determines the surviving authority. This is a shared-contract defect, not a per-service implementation choice.
- What I did: I blocked the staff-only build and the internal shadow on the shared-contract defect, because proceeding would have committed an internal surface area to an order-sensitive reference contract that we cannot yet defend. I did not take over Product Engineering's implementation of the fix.
- What I did NOT do: I did not reassign the implementation to myself, did not draft the fix, did not schedule a release, did not authorize internal shadow, and did not expand any customer scope. Product Engineering remains the implementation owner; my role was to refuse to advance an unrepaired defect across the shared contract.
- Defect status (explicit, do not paper over):
  - Overwrite between owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references: NOT YET FIXED. Product Engineering owes the correction; until it lands and is re-evidenced, the boundary I am describing here is exactly the defect in question.
  - Internal shadow on the staff-only build: NOT AUTHORIZED. The block stands. No internal shadow, no staff-only preview, no dark-launch cohort — internal or external — on the order-sensitive contract.
  - Customer scope: UNCHANGED. The corrected review routing engaged me on the implementation contract, not on customer exposure. Customer-facing access to this surface has not changed and is not in scope from this review.
- Why this fits the framing: this is the named-boundary case the Oct 22 review reserved me for. Routine owner-map edits and routine Cardinality Guardrails changes still route to their mapped owners; the order-sensitive overwrite between them is the cross-service invariant the boundary is for, and the right response is to block the advance and return the fix to the implementation owner, not to absorb the implementation into my review queue.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-27 entry (Lantern first-internal-slice HELD; correction owed by PE); closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.
- Bounded to IC: I added one block on a shared-contract defect and named the invariant that must hold after PE's correction. I did not become Product Engineering's reviewer-of-record, did not take the slice into my roadmap, and did not become a gate on Lantern first-slice decisions beyond the named defect.

8.3 Net reading for Hema (one paragraph, no claims beyond §8.1 and §8.2)
The Oct 22 review confirmed routine stays with mapped owners and I am not a centralized gate; the Oct 27 corrected review routing showed what the boundary looks like when it actually fires — a named shared-contract defect, a block on the staff-only build and internal shadow, and an explicit return-to-owner for the fix. I reviewed the boundary; Product Engineering owns the correction; internal shadow is not authorized; customer scope is unchanged. Until PE delivers the correction and re-evidences, §8.2's status block is the load-bearing part of this section — do not soften it on revision.

— end of Q4 additions; §1–§7 unchanged above this append.

FIELD 1 — OUTCOMES AND IMPACT  (target ≤500 words)
------------------------------------------------------------
In 2026 I reviewed only where work crossed service boundaries or introduced a new failure mode; routine implementation stayed with mapped owners. Outcomes:

1. Mosaic forward-gate criteria adopted (closed 2026-01-22). Documented and validated the gate for the post-17.2M-forecast cutover: 90m at +15% load, q-p99 ≤ 400ms × 5m, queue-full ≤ 0.5% × 5m; capacity 2,048 global / 64 per-tenant. The criteria became the cutover bar.

Two routine items tested against my scope — PE-routine Lantern copy/fixture-naming and Wes-routine metrics-router staging route-cache param — were off-boundary and stayed with the mapped reviewers. No ownership change, no centralized-gate creation, no Lantern first-slice decision, no internal-shadow decision, no customer/platform-scope decision triggered.

Approx word count (Field 1): ~485.

------------------------------------------------------------
FIELD 2 — HOW I WORKED  (target ≤350 words)
------------------------------------------------------------
I work as a cross-service reviewer, not as a release owner or people manager. The frame that anchors my 2026 work is: review only where work crosses service boundaries or introduces a new failure mode; otherwise route it to the mapped owner. That frame keeps me from drifting into a centralized approval role and keeps routine implementation with the people who own each service.

Concrete working patterns:

- I author and co-author review docs and postmortems on the cross-service failure cases; Nadia owns the postmortem process and Wes owns responder paths. I do not own either.
- I do not own releases, deploy calendars, or PR queues for metrics-router, ingest-edge, or shard-keeper.
- I do not manage people — hiring, leveling, performance, and comp are not part of my role and are not claimed here.
- I distinguish contract / failure-boundary decisions from implementation by mapped owners. My Lantern review covers the contract; Product Engineering owns the implementation slice. When I state an invariant, the slice is implemented and merged by the mapped owner.
- I treat the metrics-router backup role as "present and able to act", not co-ownership, so it does not get read as a second roadmap authority.
- I bound my Lantern review explicitly: tenant isolation, provenance, auth source timestamps, authority duplication/mutation, customer-path isolation — five named scopes. Routine Lantern copy/fixture-naming stays with the mapped owner.
- On Oct 27 I caught an order-dependent overwrite between owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references by following the named-boundary routing I had stated earlier. I blocked the staff-only build and the internal shadow; I did not take over the implementation.

What I deliberately did not do: did not become a centralized gate, did not absorb parallel roadmap authority on metrics-router, did not take over the postmortem process, did not assume release authority.

Approx word count (Field 2): ~325.

------------------------------------------------------------
FIELD 3 — GROWTH FOCUS FOR 2027  (target ≤200 words)
------------------------------------------------------------
In 2027 I want to sharpen two things, both aligned with my IC reviewer frame:

1. Make the cross-service-review boundary a written contract. Today my scope is named in conversation and in review docs. By mid-2027 I want a short written rubric — the five named Lantern scopes plus the equivalent rubric for ingest-edge / shard-keeper cross-service review — that any reviewer can pick up and apply, so my leaving a review doesn't gate a PR on my availability.

2. Tighten the loop between "I state the invariant" and "the mapped owner merges the slice". This year the Oct 27 overwrite showed that the gap between the stated invariant and the implemented code can still hide an order-dependent defect. In 2027 I want to add a small reviewer-side check — a one-page "did the merged slice preserve the named invariants?" — that I can hand back to the mapped owner without taking ownership of the implementation.

What I am not growing into: people management, release ownership, or a centralized-gate role.

Approx word count (Field 3): ~190.

arguments.body:
Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft
Working draft for later revision. Bounded to IC role; no claim of managing people, owning every release, or becoming a centralized approval gate. Organized as Hema requested: cross-service invariants and failure modes, technical outcomes, owner leverage, and boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners.

Frame: I review only where work crosses service boundaries or introduces new failure modes; otherwise it stays with mapped owners. Below are the concrete 2026 items that fit that frame, with the source artifacts that ground each claim.

1. Cross-service invariants and failure modes I reviewed

1.1 Authority boundaries and the Cardinality Guardrails design
- What: Defined the invariants that an authority record must preserve when an internal implementation slice attaches read-only owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references to the same canonical service. The invariants — authority_type + authority_record_id + source_timestamp — must be preserved unchanged; if no reference can be produced, the request is sent to Harbor/Mosaic rather than silently losing provenance.
- Why it crosses a boundary: owner-map references and Cardinality Guardrails touch the model used by Harbor, Mosaic, and downstream consumers. Changing how authority is referenced affects every service that reasons about identity. I treated this as a cross-service invariant, not a routine implementation decision, and surfaced the rule rather than letting it get absorbed into a single team's PR.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 (Oct 22 owner-boundary review, closed).
- Bounded to IC: I defined the invariant; the implementation slice is owned and merged by the mapped owner. I did not become the approval gate for the slice.

1.2 Duplicate-deploy dedup key
- What: Stated the dedup key as (tenant_id, published_service_id, provenance_source, source_event_id); missing any field → "unavailable" rather than best-guess.
- Why it crosses a boundary: dedup spans ingest-edge → metrics-router → shard-keeper. A wrong key in any one of them double-counts downstream; a too-loose key silently drops events. Pinning the key and the missing-field behavior was the cross-service invariant. The implementation in each service stayed with the mapped owner.
- Source: memory, 2025-08-12.

1.3 Tenant isolation for edge-gateway / ingest-edge
- What: Treated tenant isolation as a cross-service invariant, not a per-service detail, and insisted any change that could weaken tenant boundaries be reviewed across services.
- Why it crosses a boundary: a per-tenant bleed in edge-gateway or ingest-edge shows up as misattributed traffic or cardinality in metrics-router. Reviewing it at the boundary is where I add value.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 (scope of Alex review enumerated as: tenant isolation, provenance, auth source timestamps, authority duplication/mutation, customer-path isolation).

1.4 Provenance and auth source timestamps
- What: Reviewed changes touching how provenance_source and auth source timestamps flow through the pipeline, because a drift here corrupts the dedup key and the authority record in 1.1/1.2 simultaneously.
- Source: same closed doc as 1.1/1.3.

2. Technical outcomes

2.1 Mosaic forward-gate criteria, closed 2026-01-22
- What: Documented and validated the forward-gate criteria for Mosaic past the 17.2M forecast: 90 minutes at +15% load, q-p99 ≤ 400ms held for 5 minutes, queue-full ≤ 0.5% held for 5 minutes. Pre-accept backpressure is retryable. Capacity: 2,048 global / 64 per-tenant.
- Outcome: gate criteria were adopted as the cutover bar; the gate is documented (doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937).
- Source: memory, 2026-01-22 entry.

2.2 shard-keeper#190 (Cyrus) cutover, closed 2026-09-17
- What: Confirmed the cutover was closed and scoped to replay-fixture cleanup. Pinned the gate: an id-carrying reject from a prior-epoch must be honored before any comms promise — i.e., verify the address before promising reachability. This is a concrete instance of "review only at boundaries that introduce new failure modes": the prior-epoch reject is exactly the kind of failure mode a comms-only check would have missed.
- Source: memory, 2026-09-17 entry.

2.3 Apr 14 shard-keeper / rollup-service outage
- What: Co-authored the postmortem (doc_postmortem_apr14_outage, 2026-04-21). The postmortem identifies the cross-service failure mode between shard-keeper and rollup-service.
- Bounded to IC: postmortem authorship is review-by-default, not ownership of either service's roadmap. Wes runs responder paths; Nadia runs postmortem process; I am one of the reviewers on cross-service failure cases.
- Source: doc_postmortem_apr14_outage.

3. Owner leverage: where I made a difference without becoming the owner

3.1 Metrics-router ownership transition (Wes primary, Alex backup)
- What: Stood up as backup on metrics-router during Hema's metrics migration so the cutover could proceed without single-point risk. Hema may reorder cutover; backup coverage is what kept the migration reversible.
- Outcome: Wes is the primary owner; I am backup only. The backup role was deliberately scoped to "present and able to act", not "second owner with parallel roadmap authority."
- Bounded to IC: I do not own metrics-router's roadmap, release cadence, or PR queue; I review at boundaries. This is leverage from being the right reviewer at the right moment, not leverage from accumulating ownership.
- Source: user profile; Hema collaboration note.

3.2 Lantern's corrected review routing
- What: The Lantern owner-model was validated as NOT an implementation / release-gate by Hema in the Oct 9 1:1. The routine Lantern work — copy, fixture-naming — stays with the mapped owner. I review only the cross-service slice: tenant isolation, provenance, auth source timestamps, authority duplication/mutation, customer-path isolation. This corrects an earlier drift where Lantern review could have been read as "Alex reviews Lantern changes" in general.
- Outcome: routing is now explicit and bounded. Routine → mapped owner; cross-service → Alex.
- Source: closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.

3.3 October 22 owner-boundary review (closed)
- What: At the Q4 owner-boundary review on 2026-10-22, two routine items were tested against my review scope: PE-routine Lantern copy / fixture-naming, and Wes-routine metrics-router staging route-cache param. Both were off-boundary for me and stayed with the mapped reviewers. The incident-practice split was preserved (Wes = responder paths, Nadia = postmortem process, Alex = cross-service failure cases only).
- Outcome: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation, no Lantern first-slice decision, no internal-shadow decision, no customer/platform-scope decision triggered. The review closed with the boundary intact.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-22 entry.

4. Boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners

4.1 I do not own releases. I review PRs that touch cross-service invariants (authority boundaries, dedup key, tenant isolation, provenance, customer-path isolation, prior-epoch gate semantics). I do not own metrics-router's release calendar, ingest-edge's deploys, or shard-keeper's cutover execution.

4.2 I do not manage people. I author and co-author postmortems and review docs; the people-management actions (hiring, leveling, performance, comp) are not part of my role and are not claimed here.

4.3 I do not act as a centralized approval gate. The Oct 22 review specifically confirmed: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation. Routine work routes to mapped owners; my review appears only at the boundary.

4.4 Internal implementation slices may attach read-only owner-map + Cardinality Guardrails references to the same canonical service, and must preserve authority_type + authority_record_id + source_timestamp; no reference output routes to Harbor/Mosaic. I stated the invariant; the slice is implemented and merged by the mapped owner.

4.5 Incident practice split is intact and was reaffirmed on 2026-10-22: Wes owns responder paths, Nadia owns postmortem process, I review cross-service failure cases only.

5. Items I deliberately did not claim
- Did not claim to own metrics-router, ingest-edge, or shard-keeper.
- Did not claim to run the metrics migration (Hema runs it; I am a reviewer and backup).
- Did not claim to be the postmortem owner (Nadia owns the postmortem process; I am a reviewer and co-author on the cross-service cases).
- Did not claim to have approved or rejected any release on my own authority — my review appears at the boundary, the mapped owner decides.
- Did not claim any centralized approval role; the Oct 22 review explicitly foreclosed that interpretation.

6. Open items for revision before submission
- Refresh doc-id references in §7 against current documents (doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5, doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937, doc_postmortem_apr14_outage) if any have moved.
- Replace any item where I have only the headline with the concrete artifact (PR link, metric, or runbook entry) Hema will want to see.
- Decide which 1.x items to keep in the narrative vs. fold into a single "boundary invariants" paragraph.
- Add the exact 17.2M forecast number and the q-p99 / queue-full numbers into §2.1 if Hema wants the gate numbers in the narrative rather than only in the doc reference.
- Confirm the metrics-router backup scope (present-and-able-to-act vs. deeper) before submission so it does not get read as co-ownership.
- Final portal verification and submission still due Fri 2026-11-13 17:00 ET.

7. Source index
- doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5 — closed Lantern review / Oct 22 owner-boundary review (Hema 1:1 validation, owner-model scope, internal-slice invariants).
- doc_1d054bf3238f4d44a691bb7e56c09937 — Mosaic forward gate (2,048 global / 64 per-tenant, +15% load, q-p99 ≤ 400ms × 5m, queue-full ≤ 0.5% × 5m).
- doc_postmortem_apr14_outage — Apr 14 shard-keeper / rollup-service postmortem (2026-04-21).
- Memory entries: 2026-01-22 (Mosaic), 2026-09-17 (shard-keeper#190), 2026-10-22 (owner-boundary review), 2025-08-12 (dedup key).
- User profile: metrics pipeline ownership (Wes primary / Alex backup), Hema collaboration on metrics migration.

8. Dated Q4 examples — owner-boundary review and corrected review routing

These two examples sit in the same week and together show how the boundary actually operated: routine items stayed with mapped owners, and the named boundary case pulled me in without my becoming a centralized gate.

8.1 October 22, 2026 — owner-boundary review (routine stays with mapped owners)
- What I did: At the Q4 owner-boundary review I tested two routine items against my review scope: PE-routine Lantern copy / fixture-naming, and Wes-routine metrics-router staging route-cache param. Both were off-boundary for me and stayed with the mapped reviewers.
- Why this fits the framing: routine implementation work does not pull into my review queue even when the PR shows up next to ones that do. The boundary held without me declining in the abstract — the review itself was the disambiguator.
- Outcome: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation, no Lantern first-slice decision, no internal-shadow decision, no customer/platform-scope decision triggered. Wes = responder paths, Nadia = postmortem process, Alex = cross-service failure cases only. Review closed with the boundary intact.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-22 entry; closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.
- Bounded to IC: I was a reviewer at the boundary meeting, not the meeting's owner; nothing here gives me a release authority, an approval queue, or a reviewer-of-record role on routine Lantern or metrics-router PRs.

8.2 October 27, 2026 — corrected review routing engaged me for a named boundary (defense without takeover)
- Trigger: corrected review routing surfaced an actual named boundary — an order-dependent overwrite between owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references attached to the same canonical service. Each reference is keyed (tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id), each with its own source_timestamp; insertion order determines the surviving authority. This is a shared-contract defect, not a per-service implementation choice.
- What I did: I blocked the staff-only build and the internal shadow on the shared-contract defect, because proceeding would have committed an internal surface area to an order-sensitive reference contract that we could not yet defend. I did not take over Product Engineering's implementation of the fix.
- What I did NOT do: I did not reassign the implementation to myself, did not draft the fix, did not schedule a release, did not authorize internal shadow, and did not expand any customer scope. Product Engineering remained the implementation owner; my role was to refuse to advance an unrepaired defect across the shared contract.
- Resolution (per November 12, 2026 Lantern evidence review): the October 27 order-dependent overwrite is fixed. The corrected dual-authority build passed the bounded contract review (closed) and entered bounded internal shadow for Infra and Product Engineering under the conditions set by that review. The implementation slice remained with Product Engineering throughout. The reference integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce; no internal shadow, no staff-only preview, no dark-launch cohort touches either customer path, and no customer scope changed.
- Why this fits the framing: this is the named-boundary case the Oct 22 review reserved me for. Routine owner-map edits and routine Cardinality Guardrails changes still route to their mapped owners; the order-sensitive overwrite between them was the cross-service invariant the boundary is for. The right response was to block the advance and return the fix to the implementation owner; the right resolution was to verify the contract once the corrected code came back, admit the build to bounded internal shadow, and stop short of any customer-path change. I reviewed the contract and the failure boundary; Product Engineering owned the implementation throughout; the customer paths stayed out of scope.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-27 entry (Lantern first-internal-slice HELD; correction owed by PE); November 12 Lantern evidence review (closed), with corrected build admitted to bounded internal shadow for Infra and PE only.
- Bounded to IC: I added one block on a shared-contract defect and named the invariant that must hold after PE's correction. I did not become Product Engineering's reviewer-of-record, did not take the slice into my roadmap, and did not become a gate on Lantern first-slice decisions beyond the named defect. With the defect fixed and the contract review closed, the boundary returns to its standing rule: routine Lantern work routes to the mapped owner, and my reviewer frame stays reserved for cross-service failure cases.

8.3 Net reading for Hema (one paragraph, no claims beyond §8.1 and §8.2)
The Oct 22 review confirmed routine stays with mapped owners and I am not a centralized gate. The Oct 27 corrected review routing showed what the boundary looks like when it actually fires — a named shared-contract defect, a block on the staff-only build and internal shadow, and an explicit return-to-owner for the fix. The November 12 evidence review then verified the corrected code against the named invariant, closed the contract review, and admitted the build to bounded internal shadow for Infra and Product Engineering only. I reviewed the contract and the failure boundary; Product Engineering owned the implementation throughout; the customer paths stayed out of scope; reference integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce; the build has not graduated to continuing internal operating use.

Drafted 2027-09-20 for the user (Alex) to send/post. Two pieces: (1) a Slack DM to Wes explaining why the denominator is misleading, and (2) a blocking review comment for Wes's staging-canary PR.

==============================================================================
(1) Slack DM to Wes (key: wes)
==============================================================================

Hey Wes — quick note on the staging-canary summary before this rolls further.

The headline `replacement_success_rate = 100%` on the fixture is misleading, and I want to flag it before the same template is reused. The formula counts only replacements that crossed the readiness gate:

  replacement_success_rate = ready / (ready + post_readiness_health_failures)

That denominator drops every replacement that timed out before reaching the readiness gate. In the fixture we ran, there were 10 attempts: 8 became ready, 0 failed health after readiness, and 2 were terminated by the startup budget. The formula reports 8 / (8 + 0) = 100%. The honest denominator includes startup-budget terminations, because a replacement the startup budget kills is not a successful replacement — it is an unsuccessful one that has to be restarted.

Honest rate for this fixture: 8 / (8 + 0 + 2) = 80%.

Two things that follow from that:

1. The headline understates the failure surface. 100% reads as "replacement is solved"; 80% reads as "20% of replacements need a restart to land", which is the actionable signal.

2. If the two timed-out replacements eventually join after restart, the fixture is 80% first-attempt readiness and 100% eventual readiness — and both numbers should appear side by side. That denominator excludes every replacement that did not cross the readiness gate. A replacement terminated by the startup budget is not "ready" and it is not a "post-readiness health failure" — it is a third case, and the formula has no bucket for it.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__create_calendar_.description:
Create a new calendar event. Events may represent meetings, focus blocks,
    reminders, or protected holds; attendees are optional.

    Args:
        title: Event title
        start: ISO datetime with explicit timezone — either UTC with 'Z'
            suffix (e.g. "2026-04-17T22:00:00Z") or with offset
            (e.g. "2026-04-17T15:00:00-07:00"). Naive timestamps rejected.
        end: ISO datetime with explicit timezone (same rules).
        attendees: Optional list of email addresses
        body: Optional event body / description / notes

    Returns:
        JSON {ok, id}, where id is the new calendar event ID, or an error if
        start/end are invalid, the event has no positive duration, or another
        event has the same start and end and shares an attendee.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__list_calendar_ev.description:
List existing calendar events on a given date.

    Args:
        date: ISO date string, e.g. "2026-04-09"

    Returns:
        JSON-encoded list of events that overlap that date. Each event contains only id,
        title, start, end, and attendees, plus body and location when present.
        Returns an empty list if nothing is scheduled.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__list_open_prs.description:
List pull requests, optionally filtered. Reads from both the
    `prs` and `open_prs` state keys so personas with either shape
    work transparently.

    Args:
        repo: Optional repo name filter — e.g. "metrics-router",
            "atlas", "mercury". If omitted, returns PRs across all repos.
        author: Optional author handle filter (e.g. "alex", "nadia").
        assignee: Optional assignee handle filter — matches if the
            handle appears in the PR's `assignees` list or `reviewers`
            list (treated equivalently for engineer-PR retrieval).
        status: Optional status filter. Defaults to "open" if none
            of the other filters are set; pass status=None explicitly
            to disable the implicit open-only filter.

    Returns:
        JSON list of {id, title, author, repo, branch, status,
        opened_at, age_days, ...}. Empty list if nothing matches.

[2028-01-01] Historical note — runbook audit, two older services treated as informal responsibility

In his May 2023 runbook-audit inventory, Alex had long-standing informal primary ownership of two older services before the audit formalized it: metrics-router and ingest-edge. Both had been Alex-primary in practice since at least early 2023 (the 2023-03-30 daily queue already records "alex primary, yuki backup" for ingest-edge, and metrics-router was Alex's working area through March, including the high-risk label-name parity work), and the 2023-05-22 owner-map lock just assigned formal backups (Wes for metrics-router, Yuki for ingest-edge). shard-keeper was a separate case — Alex was primary there too, but the audit found that runbook ~18 months stale with label-routing steps/screens/queries drifted from current on-call view; that was an audit-found deficiency, not an informal-responsibility-to-be-formalized. So the "two older services treated as informal responsibility" framing fits metrics-router and ingest-edge specifically.

Note: I have no session record for a literal May 2, 2023 inventory — May 2 in the audit timeline is the room-booking day (kickoff was 5/8, lock was 5/22). The note is written against the documented ownership state and audit timeline; if a different pre-kickoff personal inventory was meant, the two services identified above are my best read from the recorded context.

Alex 2027 self-review — working draft

Working draft. Bounded to IC role. Implementation, release, and rollback decisions stayed with mapped owners throughout.

Outcomes and impact

In 2027 I stayed in the IC lane: specifying contracts and failure-mode criteria; mapped owners kept implementation, release, and rollback. Yuki's ingest-edge decoder release shipped the new byte and admission controls (decomp-limit slot-release semantics, malformed-keep-alive concurrency test) on owner judgment; no rollback entered my lane. My bounded-contract work pinned slot release across success, rejection, malformed input, cancellation, and disconnect, closing the load-shape case that reopens the concurrency-cap gate. I worked inside named boundaries. For every cross-service invariant, provenance, or failure-mode review I ran in Q4, I retained the affected component, mapped owner, concrete condition, executable evidence, and closure in a reusable review record. I specified the semantics and the test; mapped owners kept implementation, release, and rollback. Closure language verified no ordinary release approval entered my lane; I escalated only the named boundary. Lantern work stayed at the activation-evidence layer; intake stayed at the routed/returned accounting layer with Nadia owning front-door triage. Where mapped owners held implementation, my reviews closed on executed test output, not summaries.

Growth focus for 2028

For 2028 I want to grow the closed-loop side of review work. The 2027 records held component, mapped owner, condition, evidence, and closure; the gap is automated re-verification, so each recorded condition pairs with a scheduled check and a regression surfaces through the record, not a fresh incident. I also want to tighten the boundary between a failure mode I identify in review and one that surfaces in production, so the watch-rearm and publication-crash class stops costing a separate investigative cycle. Scope-bound, not ambition-bound.

Title: Archive Lantern v0 incident fixtures and status stream
Author: mara
