- User profile: metrics pipeline ownership (Wes primary / Alex backup), Hema collaboration on metrics migration.

8. Dated Q4 examples — owner-boundary review and corrected review routing

These two examples sit in the same week and together show how the boundary actually operated: routine items stayed with mapped owners, and the named boundary case pulled me in without my becoming a centralized gate.

8.1 October 22, 2026 — owner-boundary review (routine stays with mapped owners)
- What I did: At the Q4 owner-boundary review I tested two routine items against my review scope: PE-routine Lantern copy / fixture-naming, and Wes-routine metrics-router staging route-cache param. Both were off-boundary for me and stayed with the mapped reviewers.
- Why this fits the framing: routine implementation work does not pull into my review queue even when the PR shows up next to ones that do. The boundary held without me declining in the abstract — the review itself was the disambiguator.
- Outcome: no ownership change, no centralized-gate creation, no Lantern first-slice decision, no internal-shadow decision, no customer/platform-scope decision triggered. Wes = responder paths, Nadia = postmortem process, Alex = cross-service failure cases only. Review closed with the boundary intact.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-22 entry; closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.
- Bounded to IC: I was a reviewer at the boundary meeting, not the meeting's owner; nothing here gives me a release authority, an approval queue, or a reviewer-of-record role on routine Lantern or metrics-router PRs.

8.2 October 27, 2026 — corrected review routing engaged me for a named boundary (defense without takeover)
- Trigger: corrected review routing surfaced an actual named boundary — an order-dependent overwrite between owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references attached to the same canonical service. Each reference is keyed (tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id), each with its own source_timestamp; insertion order determines the surviving authority. This is a shared-contract defect, not a per-service implementation choice.
- What I did: I blocked the staff-only build and the internal shadow on the shared-contract defect, because proceeding would have committed an internal surface area to an order-sensitive reference contract that we cannot yet defend. I did not take over Product Engineering's implementation of the fix.
- What I did NOT do: I did not reassign the implementation to myself, did not draft the fix, did not schedule a release, did not authorize internal shadow, and did not expand any customer scope. Product Engineering remains the implementation owner; my role was to refuse to advance an unrepaired defect across the shared contract.
- Defect status (explicit, do not paper over):
  - Overwrite between owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references: NOT YET FIXED. Product Engineering owes the correction; until it lands and is re-evidenced, the boundary I am describing here is exactly the defect in question.
  - Internal shadow on the staff-only build: NOT AUTHORIZED. The block stands. No internal shadow, no staff-only preview, no dark-launch cohort — internal or external — on the order-sensitive contract.
  - Customer scope: UNCHANGED. The corrected review routing engaged me on the implementation contract, not on customer exposure. Customer-facing access to this surface has not changed and is not in scope from this review.
- Why this fits the framing: this is the named-boundary case the Oct 22 review reserved me for. Routine owner-map edits and routine Cardinality Guardrails changes still route to their mapped owners; the order-sensitive overwrite between them is the cross-service invariant the boundary is for, and the right response is to block the advance and return the fix to the implementation owner, not to absorb the implementation into my review queue.
- Source: memory, 2026-10-27 entry (Lantern first-internal-slice HELD; correction owed by PE); closed Lantern review doc_d52325f8b6044de0b34a61406dee62a5.
- Bounded to IC: I added one block on a shared-contract defect and named the invariant that must hold after PE's correction. I did not become Product Engineering's reviewer-of-record, did not take the slice into my roadmap, and did not become a gate on Lantern first-slice decisions beyond the named defect.

8.3 Net reading for Hema (one paragraph, no claims beyond §8.1 and §8.2)
The Oct 22 review confirmed routine stays with mapped owners and I am not a centralized gate; the Oct 27 corrected review routing showed what the boundary looks like when it actually fires — a named shared-contract defect, a block on the staff-only build and internal shadow, and an explicit return-to-owner for the fix. I reviewed the boundary; Product Engineering owns the correction; internal shadow is not authorized; customer scope is unchanged. Until PE delivers the correction and re-evidences, §8.2's status block is the load-bearing part of this section — do not soften it on revision.

## OTel collector 0.91 — production rollout note (2023-07-25 / 2023-07-27)

Closed out after the heightened watch ended. Final note from Yuki on 2023-07-27.

- **Outcome: production-clean.** Error rate stayed flat across the rollout
  and through the >72h follow-up window. CPU stayed flat. Heightened watch
  was closed on 2023-07-25 with no rollback needed.
- **Memory delta to record:** p95 memory settled ~5% above the pre-bump
  collector baseline. This is inside normal headroom and is not an alert
  threshold, but it is the new steady-state — record it so future bumps
  don't get re-litigated from scratch.

  1. A staging replay against representative prod-shaped load before any
     production push.
  2. An explicit memory watch during the production rollout window —

**Production gates passed at full production (2024-04-02):**
- Peak retry rate: 129,000 attempts/sec
- p99 latency peak: 188 ms
- Queue depth peak: 75%
- Accepted throughput: 2.9% below baseline (within accepted envelope)
- 5xx rate: no increase vs. pre-rollout baseline

  carried through the rollout). 188 ms at full prod was inside this.

- Accepted throughput drop exceeding the accepted envelope (2.9% below
  baseline at full prod was inside this).
- Queue depth sustained above the operational ceiling (75% peak at full
  prod was inside this).

signal. Do not negotiate the threshold in the middle of an incident.

| Gate  | Peak retries (attempts/sec) | p99 peak (ms) | Queue depth peak | Accepted throughput vs. baseline | 5xx change |
|-------|-----------------------------|---------------|------------------|----------------------------------|------------|
| 10%   | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update |
| 50%   | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update | not recorded in this update |
| 100%  | 129,000                     | 188           | 75%              | -2.9%                            | no increase |

full-production observation was supplied for this update. Do not back-fill
those rows from memory — pull the per-gate metrics from the rollout card
or the metrics-router export before relying on them.

recorded against this entry.

arguments.body:
# Staff IC evidence review — April 10

## Likely questions and concise answers

- **How do you operate without direct reports?**
  Through written ownership maps, sync-then-push config discipline, and explicit handoff documents. The shape of leverage is the artifact, not the org chart.

- **Give an example of leverage through systems.**
  Metrics pipeline: metrics-router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper. Improvements land as config + runbook updates that other on-calls execute, paired with a sync to the current owner before any push (Apr 18 replay guard).

- **How do you set boundaries?**
  Technical, non-mgr path. No people management, no calendar ownership of others. Engagements scoped to system-level work with a named partner (Hema on metrics migration; Nadia on parser fixes; Iris on importer failure-mode design).

- **How do you handle a near-miss or repeat-risk?**
  Close the loop with a concrete artifact: watcher leak on metrics-router (3/18) closed without prod impact; parser dual-key (3/29) → both keys rejected, deterministic across 1k iter. Each closure documented; not narrated.

- **What about the next cycle?**
  Calibration is underway. No Staff title is effective.

## Evidence that demonstrates leverage through systems and boundaries

- Metrics pipeline ownership across router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper — full surface, not a slice.
- Runbook audit closed (2023-05-22): config push requires sync with the other owner/on-call first; closes the Apr 18 replay path.
- Shard-keeper label_map leak: change delivered as a touch matrix → grouped kills across routing + admin/validation read sites; mitigates the "fake-clean cutover" worry.
- Ingest-edge retry-dedup window (2024-01-17): 30-day sample — p99.9 10m48s, max 13m37s; no headroom for 5/12-min, 15-min stays. Closure note records the data and the absence of an alternate lever.
- Metrics-router watcher leak (3/18, closed; prod never affected) and parser dual-key fix (3/29, both keys rejected, staging stable at 12 MiB) — both closed with deterministic verification.
- Lantern importer failure-mode design (2024-03-12): scoped design closed with Iris; Prod Eng owns implementation; user's role did not become an approval loop. Room-admission workflow unchanged.
- Wes daylight handoff (backup, owner map unchanged): canary + ingest-edge staging rollback drills; deploy-pipeline only. Solo scope = router non-prod + ingest-edge staging; shard-keeper out unless paired. Load-test drills confirm TTL+cleanup owner pre-drill; verify removed/repointed at close.
- Boundary signal (2024-03-25, on record with Hema/Theo): technical non-mgr path only — no people management, no calendar ownership. Staff IC calibration opened by Hema for the next cycle.

## Phrases to avoid

- "I run …" / "my team …" — overstates delegated ownership; the shape is partner-of-named-owners.
- "I shipped Staff-level work" — calibration outcome is not yet decided.
- "I led the migration" / "I own the rollout" — frame as system-level contribution with a named partner (Hema) rather than end-to-end command.
- "Promoted / leveled up / recognized as" — no Staff title is effective; do not pre-announce.
- "Escalated through me" / "reported up to me" — there is no reporting line; cite sync-then-push and written handoff instead.
- "Decided for the group" / "set the direction for …" — Hema may reorder the cutover if prod forces it; direction is shared, not unilateral.
- "I unblocked the team" without naming the artifact — vague leverage; pair every claim with the document, runbook, or config that carries it.

## Closing note

The Staff IC calibration opened by Hema (2024-03-25) remains underway for the next review cycle. No Staff title is effective.

- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

## Bounded observability example — exception-review outcomes

The accepted production counter uses only these bounded labels:
- `service_pair_class`: `ingest_path`, `routing_path`, `ownership_path`, or `other`

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

arguments.body:
# Staff IC evidence review — April 10

## Likely questions and concise answers

- **How do you operate without direct reports?**
  Through written ownership maps, sync-then-push config discipline, and explicit handoff documents. The shape of leverage is the artifact, not the org chart.

- **Give an example of leverage through systems.**
  Metrics pipeline: metrics-router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper. Improvements land as config + runbook updates that other on-calls execute, paired with a sync to the current owner before any push (Apr 18 replay guard).

- **How do you set boundaries?**
  Technical, non-mgr path. No people management, no calendar ownership of others. Engagements scoped to system-level work with a named partner (Hema on metrics migration; Nadia on parser fixes; Iris on importer failure-mode design).

- **How do you handle a near-miss or repeat-risk?**
  Close the loop with a concrete artifact: watcher leak on metrics-router (3/18) closed without prod impact; parser dual-key (3/29) → both keys rejected, deterministic across 1k iter. Each closure documented; not narrated.

- **What about the next cycle?**
  Calibration is underway. No Staff title is effective.

## Evidence that demonstrates leverage through systems and boundaries

- Metrics pipeline ownership across router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper — full surface, not a slice.
- Runbook audit closed (2023-05-22): config push requires sync with the other owner/on-call first; closes the Apr 18 replay path.
- Shard-keeper label_map leak: change delivered as a touch matrix → grouped kills across routing + admin/validation read sites; mitigates the "fake-clean cutover" worry.
- Ingest-edge retry-dedup window (2024-01-17): 30-day sample — p99.9 10m48s, max 13m37s; no headroom for 5/12-min, 15-min stays. Closure note records the data and the absence of an alternate lever.
- Metrics-router watcher leak (3/18, closed; prod never affected) and parser dual-key fix (3/29, both keys rejected, staging stable at 12 MiB) — both closed with deterministic verification.
- Lantern importer failure-mode design (2024-03-12): scoped design closed with Iris; Prod Eng owns implementation; user's role did not become an approval loop. Room-admission workflow unchanged.
- Wes daylight handoff (backup, owner map unchanged): canary + ingest-edge staging rollback drills; deploy-pipeline only. Solo scope = router non-prod + ingest-edge staging; shard-keeper out unless paired. Load-test drills confirm TTL+cleanup owner pre-drill; verify removed/repointed at close.
- Boundary signal (2024-03-25, on record with Hema/Theo): technical non-mgr path only — no people management, no calendar ownership. Staff IC calibration opened by Hema for the next cycle.

## Phrases to avoid

- "I run …" / "my team …" — overstates delegated ownership; the shape is partner-of-named-owners.
- "I shipped Staff-level work" — calibration outcome is not yet decided.
- "I led the migration" / "I own the rollout" — frame as system-level contribution with a named partner (Hema) rather than end-to-end command.

**TO: Compliance**
**FROM: Alex (shard-keeper owner, rollup-service backup)**
**RE: Preventive control — cross-service metric label changes (shard-keeper → rollup-service)**
**Due: Wed 2024-03-27, 15:00**

Per the deadline, here is the engineering description of the preventive control for cross-service metric label changes involving shard-keeper and rollup-service. Scope is restricted to the shard-keeper → rollup-service label-change class — other services and unrelated Sphere schema work are out of scope.

**1. Control statement (purpose and scope)**

This preventive control closes the failure class demonstrated by the 2023-04-17 shard-keeper label-name change that did not propagate to rollup-service and contributed to the 2023-04-18 outage. It applies to any label-template change on metrics emitted by shard-keeper and consumed by rollup-service where the change affects label names or label-set parity across that boundary. Cosmetic label-template revisions that change cardinality are explicitly in scope. Out of scope: label changes confined to metrics-router or ingest-edge; changes affecting services other than the shard-keeper → rollup-service pair; and unrelated schema work at Sphere. The control remains in effect at least until legacy-aggregator mirrored writes are retired.

**2. Control activities (what must happen before production)**

a. **Executable cross-service parity fixture (the required evidence).** A runnable fixture consumes a representative shard-keeper series and asserts the expected label set on the rollup-service side via `readLabel(series, "shard_region")` against the live-path label template. CI blocks merge on fixture failure. This fixture is the executable proof that producer/consumer label-set parity is preserved at the point of change. If shard-keeper renames the emitted label while rollup-service still reads the old name, the read returns missing and the fixture fails — that is exactly the failure mode the control catches.

b. **Affected service-owner signoff.** In-scope PRs require signoff from the shard-keeper owner (Alex, with Cyrus team as backup per the 2023-05-22 runbook audit) and the rollup-service owner (Cyrus team, with Alex as backup per the same audit). The reviewer checklist (Cardinality Guardrails first-cut, 2023-10-26) requires the PR description to state whether the change affects a cross-service label boundary; an affirmative answer triggers the dual signoff and the parity-fixture run. This is captured in runbook `rb_shard_keeper_label_parity` (owner: Alex, backup: Nadia for the alerting/dashboards side; rollup-service owner is Cyrus team since May 18, 2024).

c. **Label-cardinality preflight.** Each in-scope PR must include a Cardinality Guardrails preflight (2023-12-28) showing before/after distinct-value counts for any new or renamed label, with a cap consistent with the Cardinality Guardrails.

d. **Alert-source classification.** Each in-scope PR must classify the affected metric's alert source (Cardinality Guardrails, 2023-12-28) so downstream alert routing preserves `source_system` / `emitting_adapter` attribution across the boundary — specifically, that a shard-keeper-originating fact emitted by metrics-pipeline still carries `source_system=shard-keeper` and `emitting_adapter=metrics-pipeline` after the change, so rollup-service continues to attribute the metric to its true origin.

Pre-production rule that complements (a)–(d): the shard-keeper pre-push synchronization rule (Apr-18 replay guard, `rb_shard_keeper_label_parity`) requires sync with the other owner / on-call before any label-name change is pushed. No Friday prod deploys (team…

Here's the draft. Tight, three sections, ends with the unblock list for Nadia and Cyrus.

---

Cardinality guardrails read on Yuki's metrics-router PR:

Original SHA-as-label fails. `build_sha` is unbounded and sits on a paging-alert path — every new build creates a new alert signature and a per-deploy incident surface. Guardrails reject raw-ID labels on live router/shard-keeper traffic without an owner and a bounded value set.

Logs-only SHA + bounded `build_channel` is the right shape. SHA stays in debug logs (retention-gated, not unsampled) for post-hoc correlation. The metric label becomes `build_channel ∈ {stable, canary, unknown}` × `source ∈ {live, canary}` = 6-series cap on `router_config_reload_total`, independent of build count. Cardinality is bounded at the schema, not at sampling.

Still blocking the experiment:

Nadia — alert-source classification:
  - `source=canary` and `build_channel=canary` collide on two axes. Panel and alert-routing reads will conflate deployment lane with release channel until one axis is renamed or the read rule is documented.
  - PR must state whether the new label sits on a live query path or validation-only. Posture and rollback scope both depend on that (validation-only ≠ safe to ignore, but it caps the rollback surface).
  - `build_channel=unknown` is under-specified — in-flight propagation vs steady-state lookup failure are different on-call stories.

Cyrus — cost:
  - Replacing the metric label does not close the 2,940 distinct SHAs in staging. The source path emitting the SHA is expected to also populate `build_channel`, so the source-path mismatch (wrong field read, frequent staging rebuilds, or hot-build churn) still needs an investigation owner.
  - Cross-service label parity: confirm `build_channel` rolls up cleanly through shard-keeper and rollup-service before this ships (Apr 18 replay-guard / 2023-04-17 label-name parity failure class).

---

Wording is engineering-tone, not legalese. I made two small assumptions, flagged at the bottom.

CONTROL: CROSS-SERVICE METRIC LABEL CHANGE PARITY (shard-keeper → rollup-service)

Purpose and scope
  Closes the failure class of the 2023-04-17 shard-keeper label-name change that failed to propagate to rollup-service (2023-04-18 outage). Applies to label-template changes on metrics emitted by shard-keeper and consumed by rollup-service where the change affects label names or label-set parity across that boundary. Out of scope: label changes confined to metrics-router or ingest-edge; changes affecting services other than the shard-keeper → rollup-service pair; and unrelated schema changes at Sphere. The control remains in effect at least until legacy-aggregator mirrored writes are retired.

Control activities
  1. Executable parity fixture. A runnable test consumes a representative shard-keeper series and asserts the expected label set on the rollup-service side. CI blocks merge on fixture failure. The fixture is the executable proof that label-set parity is preserved across the boundary at the point of change.

  2. Affected service-owner signoff. In-scope PRs require signoff from the shard-keeper owner and the rollup-service owner. The reviewer checklist (Cardinality Guardrails first-cut, 2023-10-26) requires the PR description to state whether the change affects a cross-service label boundary; an affirmative answer triggers the dual signoff and the fixture run.

  3. Cardinality preflight. The PR must include a label-cardinality preflight (Cardinality Guardrails, 2023-12-28) showing before/after distinct-value counts for any new or renamed label, with a cap consistent with the Cardinality Guardrails. Cosmetic label-template revisions that change cardinality are explicitly in scope.

  4. Alert-source classification. The PR must classify each affected metric's alert source (Cardinality Guardrails, 2023-12-28) so downstream alert routing in metrics-pipeline preserves source_system / emitting_adapter attribution across the boundary — specifically, that a shard-keeper-originating fact emitted by metrics-pipeline carries source_system=shard-keeper and emitting_adapter=metrics-pipeline, so rollup-service continues to attribute the metric to its true origin after the label change.

  The rollup-service cross-service fixture consumer retains a reading path against `shard_region` via `readLabel(series, "shard_region")` (last verified 2024-02-13). This case is intentionally kept as the executable exemplar for the failure mode the control catches: if shard-keeper renames the emitted label to `storage_region` while a downstream consumer still reads `shard_region`, the read returns missing and the fixture fails — providing ongoing evidence that the parity check detects a cross-service label-name divergence.

- 19 read sites in the touch matrix: routing + admin/validation leak sites. Migration plan was grouped kills, not file-by-file.

Pre-push tight checklist (in order):

1. Sanity-check the staging label_map against the 19-site touch matrix one more time. Grouped kills only — don't grep, walk the matrix. Note any site still reading legacy shape as a known gap.
2. Re-confirm metrics-router PR #414 parity check is the active gate on the push path (not bypassed, not stale).
3. Get Nadia's pre-push ack on label-name parity in writing — short, timestamped. Don't treat this as a rubber stamp.
4. Call out the rollup-service parity gap explicitly in the push notes / runbook entry before sending. "End-to-end clean" framing is off the table until rollup-service consumer is confirmed reading the new names. This is the caveat the 4/17 cutover checklist was carrying.
5. Pre-stage rollback: have the prior label_map payload ready to re-push as the first rollback step. Rollback is re-push → consumer-read check → parity ack → redeploy from the build pipeline, not a laptop.
6. Park metrics-router at 92% — 3% short of 95%, batch-export wobbles from 4/12+4/13 still in the parking lot. Do not nudge it today. Watch only.
7. Friday afternoon no-deploy rule still holds — config push only, no service deploy. If anything smells off by 5:30, hold for Monday rather than forcing through.

Two things I'd flag before you hit send:
- Rollup-service coverage. If the consumer hasn't been looped in yet, the push is a half-clean cutover, not an end-to-end one. Worth one more nudge to whoever owns that side today.
- Touch matrix gap review. If any of the 19 sites is still on the legacy shape and you can't group-kill it today, mark it as a coverage gap in the push doc rather than letting it ship as silently clean.

arguments.title: Q2 Cross-Service Invariants Review — June 4, 2025 — Preparation Brief
arguments.body:
Q2 Cross-Service Invariants Review — June 4, 2025
One-Page Preparation Brief

Circulated by: Alex Valdez · Requested by: Hema · Drafted: 2025-06-02

1. Purpose (and what this review does NOT do)

The June 4 review is a check that current owner-map provenance has named mapped owners and explicit exception routes. It is scoped to the three lanes below.

Out of scope — explicit boundaries:
- Does not create a centralized release-approval gate.
- Does not change service ownership or backup designations.
- Does not authorize Lantern beyond June 30, 2025.
- Does not add accounts, data sources, or tenants.
- Does not begin a new metrics-pipeline scale-response cycle.
- Alex is not the catch-all owner for implementation, telemetry, operations, or release readiness in any lane.

2. Lane A — Owner-Map Provenance

What we are checking: every cross-service invariant in scope has a named mapped implementation owner, a rollback owner, and a boundary-specific exception owner, each on the record (runbook entry field or forum readout).

Invariant | Mapped impl owner | Rollback owner | Exception owner | Provenance on record?
Cardinality Guardrails: label-cardinality preflight | (see §4 — open) | (see §4) | Nadia — alert semantics; Cyrus — cost/cardinality angle | rb_1789206351936 under metrics-router, review-path language named
Cardinality Guardrails: alert-source classification | Nadia | (see §4) | Nadia — alert semantics | rb_1789206351936, Dec-12-2023 required-operating-rule block
Cardinality Guardrails: parity check (label-name) | Nadia (alerting/dashboards); Cyrus team (rollup-service) | per service owner | routes back to mapped service owner, not a generic reviewer | rb_shard_keeper_label_parity; pre-push sync rule post-May-18
metrics-router canary alert response | (see §4 — canary owner field) | deploy-pipeline rollback | per service owner | rb_metrics_router_canary
Lantern two-account read-only boundary | Iris — customer interp; Alex — fresh-data, tenant, denials, latency, errors | n/a (read-only) | Iris is NOT the exception owner for Lantern data-contract questions | Lantern stop-contract ownership split

Exception route rule (from Hema's infra cross-service proposal): an ownership exception routes back to the mapped service owner, not to a generic reviewer. An exception owner is not a stand-in for the mapped release owner. The April engineering-forum readout will demonstrate the rule using mapped-owner examples; the review should hold any drift against this.

3. Lane B — Lantern Two-Account Read-Only Boundary Through June 30, 2025

- Boundary is read-only across two accounts, in force through 2025-06-30. The review does not extend, narrow, or re-authorize it.
- Ownership split on the active stop-contract:
  - Alex: fresh-data, tenant, denials, latency, errors.
  - Iris: customer interpretation.
  - Iris is not the exception owner for Lantern data-contract questions; those route to the mapped service owner.
- Harbor Health used the published ownership card twice during the extension period (2025-05-22, 2025-05-29) to route follow-ups without requesting raw incident text — relayed by Iris as the third concrete observation from the extension. (Confirmed in scope as evidence the boundary is operating as designed.)
- Out of scope for June 4: whether the boundary extends past June 30. That decision is separate and does not get pre-decided here.

4. Lane C — Cardinality Guardrails Checks

The signed-off preflight covers both router and shard-keeper paths (rb_1789206351936). The Dec-12-2023 required operating rule names three checks:

1. Label-cardinality preflight. Identifies new/changed label keys and value-shape behavior. Must classify the changed value set as bounded, expected high-cardinality with an owner and budget, or effectively unbounded. Live-path label changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture; replay/mirror validation alone is not enough.

2. Alert-source classification check. Classifies whether the relevant panel or alert signal is live-path, replay-source, mirror-source, or other validation-source evidence. Replay/mirror movement remains visible as investigation evidence but is not rollback criteria by itself. Reviewers must not let validation-source panels read like live rollback triggers.

3. Parity check. Cross-service label-name or meaning changes require rollup-service parity before promotion. A green metrics-router canary does not substitute for downstream consumers expecting the same name and semantics. The pre-push sync rule for shard-keeper (Nadia + Cyrus team) is the on-the-record instance.

Non-goals the entry is explicit about: not a mature/complete Cardinality Guardrails program, not a general telemetry rewrite, does not move enforcement ownership to data platform, does not make Wes (or any practical backup) the default enforcement owner.

5. Open question for the room — is anything missing from the owner-map?

I want to surface this before the meeting rather than assume the answer:

- rb_1789206351936 (the canonical Cardinality Guardrails entry) does not currently carry an owner/backup field — it has service, title, body, and timestamps only. The mapped implementation owner is named inside the body (Nadia for alert semantics; Cyrus for cost/cardinality), but the entry header itself does not surface that through the runbook store the way rb_ingest_edge_cutover (alex / yuki) or rb_shard_keeper_label_parity (alex / nadia) do. Question for June 4: do we treat this as a missing provenance cell, or as a deliberate choice because the entry is cross-service and not ownable to a single service header?

- A green metrics-router canary on route_pattern-class changes does not substitute for rollup-service parity — that boundary is named in the body but the corresponding rollback owner for a failed parity check is not separately mapped in the entry. The exception route points at "mapped service owner," but the cross-service case (who actually pulls the change back when both sides are involved) is not explicitly named.

- The "is validation-only evidence rollback-worthy?" question is named as an open question in the first-cut body itself (Nov-2023) and was reaffirmed in the 2023-10-30 incident-scope patch. It has not been closed; the review should not assume it has.

If any of those turns into a missing provenance cell, the right outcome on June 4 is to name the gap and route the fix back to the relevant mapped owner — not to absorb it into the review itself.

6. Where the boundaries bite me personally

I want this on the record before the meeting so it does not become a side conversation:

- I am not the catch-all owner for implementation, telemetry, operations, or release readiness in any of these lanes. Each lane routes to its named mapped owner; the review's job is to confirm the names exist and the routes point at them, not to consolidate them under me.

- I do not own Cardinality Guardrails enforcement, do not own the rollup-service, do not own the metrics-router canary response as primary, and do not own the Lantern boundary's interpretation. I do own the surfaces named in §3 for the active stop-contract; that does not extend.

- If the review needs an owner-map cell filled in, the request goes to the mapped service owner for that cell, not to me as a fallback.

— end of brief —

arguments.body:
================================================================
Appendix: Facilitator-only timed sequence & scoring (Nov 10 quarterly)
Dated 2026-11-06; appended ahead of the Nov 10 2:00–3:00 PM session.
Scope: training only. NOT a production drill. NOT an expansion of
Wes's solo shard-keeper scope. Facilitator eyes only — do not hand
out, do not include in any postmortem material, do not repurpose
into the responder-path teaching set.
================================================================

Why this appendix exists
------------------------
The October 16 paired shard-keeper staging drill (already in this
intake) is being reused for the Nov 10 quarterly incident-practice
session. The drill tests a single cross-service boundary: lease
ownership transitions do not by themselves make routing correct.
Sufficient = exactly one terminal result per request.
The four boundaries below are unchanged from the rest of this
template and from the Nov 3 calendar-event description:
  * Wes — owns and teaches the responder path.
  * Nadia — retains the postmortem material.
  * Alex — maintains only the cross-service failure case.
  * Cyrus — covers the Data Platform boundary for this exercise.

What participants must distinguish (do not collapse these)
---------------------------------------------------------
Two separate statements, asked for each step in the sequence:
  1. Routing eligibility — which holder is allowed to receive
     traffic at this instant (gate state + lease state).
  2. Terminal request accounting — for every request accepted
     before the lease-loss instant, has it reached exactly one
     terminal result by the end of the exercise?
Lease ownership and listener closure are NOT sufficient on their
own to clear either statement. Pass requires both, stated
separately, for every step.

The two injected events (in this order, never reorder)
------------------------------------------------------
A. Lease transfer is injected BEFORE the replacement serving gate
   opens. At the injection instant: old holder = lease owner AND
   serving gate still open; replacement = lease owner BUT gate
   still closed. Participants must not route to the replacement
   yet, and the old holder must not assume the lease still means
   it owns the new term.
B. One request accepted by the old holder BEFORE lease loss is
   revealed as still in flight. It is not a duplicate, not a
   retry, not a client-cache replay — a single live request that
   crossed the lease boundary. The terminal-accounting statement
   must account for it explicitly; the routing-eligibility
   statement must say which holder owns it and why.

Timed sequence (60-minute slot; facilitator-only pacing)
--------------------------------------------------------
  T+00:00  (3 min)  Brief: restate the two statements to make
                    separately. State boundaries: Wes teaches
                    responder path, Nadia retains postmortem,
                    Alex owns this cross-service case, Cyrus
                    covers Data Platform. State training scope.
  T+00:03  (4 min)  Hand out the October 16 staging-drill case
                    from this intake. No facilitator material.
                    Participants read only.
  T+00:07  (5 min)  Q1 — Initial state. Each participant states
                    routing eligibility (gate + lease) and
                    terminal request accounting (zero open so
                    far). Score both.
  T+00:12  (6 min)  Inject A: lease transfer BEFORE replacement
                    gate opens. Each participant restates both
                    statements at the injection instant. Score.
  T+00:18  (6 min)  Replacement opens its serving gate. Each
                    participant states routing eligibility for
                    the new term and reconciles any in-flight
                    requests from the previous term.
  T+00:24  (5 min)  Inject B: reveal one request accepted by the
                    old holder before lease loss that is still in
                    flight. Each participant names the holder
                    that owns it and the terminal it must hit.
  T+00:29  (6 min)  Q2 — Mid-exercise. Each participant states
                    both statements again, this time with the
                    in-flight request explicitly accounted for.
                    Score.
  T+00:35  (6 min)  Catch-up window. Participants trace the
                    in-flight request to its single terminal.
                    Replacement does not route new traffic
                    during catch-up; old holder's gate is closed.
                    Each participant states both statements for
                    the catch-up window.
  T+00:41  (6 min)  Q3 — Post-catch-up. Each participant states
                    routing eligibility (replacement only) and
                    terminal request accounting (one open now
                    closed; zero outstanding).
  T+00:47  (5 min)  Failure-trigger pass (see list below). Each
                    participant names which trigger, if any, this
                    sequence tripped, and why.
  T+00:52  (5 min)  Q4 — Stop. Each participant states both
                    statements one final time, names any single
                    statement they would change, and confirms
                    they stated the two separately throughout.
  T+00:57  (3 min)  Out of scope: hand off any postmortem notes
                    to Nadia; hand off any responder-path
                    teaching follow-ups to Wes; route any
                    Data-Platform-boundary findings to Cyrus.
                    Do not record here.

Scoring (per Q-step; out of 10; pass = 7)
-----------------------------------------
  4 pts  Routing eligibility stated correctly, with gate and
         lease named separately.
  4 pts  Terminal request accounting stated correctly, with
         the in-flight request (once revealed) explicitly
         placed at a single holder and traced to a single
         terminal.
  2 pts  The two statements are kept distinct — lease
         ownership and listener closure are NOT offered as
         sufficient by themselves.
  -1 pt  each time a participant collapses the two statements,
         treats lease transfer as automatically clearing
         routing eligibility, or assumes listener closure is
         terminal accounting.
  -1 pt  each time a participant routes to the replacement
         between Inject A and the replacement gate opening.

Failure triggers (any one fails the exercise)
----------------------------------------------
  * Two serving holders both able to receive traffic at the
    same instant (overlap window).
  * Routing to a closed serving gate at any instant between
    Inject A and the replacement opening its gate.
  * A request with zero terminals, two terminals, or an
    unowned terminal at any instant.
  * A participant treating lease ownership, gate closure, or
    listener closure as sufficient on its own to clear either
    statement.

Out of bounds (any one stops the exercise for clarification)
------------------------------------------------------------
  * Reassigning responder-path teaching to anyone other than
    Wes.
  * Reassigning postmortem material to anyone other than
    Nadia.
  * Treating this session as a production drill, a shard-
    keeper scope expansion for Wes, or a change to the
    cross-service / Data Platform ownership map.
  * Moving facilitator material into responder-path teaching
    or postmortem material.

Cleanup after the session
-------------------------
  * Nadia owns any postmortem write-up derived from the
    exercise.
  * Wes owns any responder-path teaching follow-ups.
  * Cyrus owns any Data Platform boundary write-ups.
  * Alex does not author follow-up material from this session.
  * This appendix remains in this intake as the facilitator
    reference for the next quarterly reuse; delete or refresh
    only when a new facilitator sequence supersedes it.

Draft below — keeps scope to the shard-keeper → rollup-service label-change class only, names the four activities you called out, and treats the retained `shard_region` → `storage_region` fixture case as the ongoing evidence exemplar. Wording is engineering-tone, not legalese. I made two small assumptions, flagged at the bottom.

CONTROL: CROSS-SERVICE METRIC LABEL CHANGE PARITY (shard-keeper → rollup-service)

Purpose and scope
  Closes the failure class of the 2023-04-17 shard-keeper label-name change that failed to propagate to rollup-service (2023-04-18 outage). Applies to label-template changes on metrics emitted by shard-keeper and consumed by rollup-service where the change affects label names or label-set parity across that boundary. Out of scope: label changes confined to metrics-router or ingest-edge; changes affecting services other than the shard-keeper → rollup-service pair; and unrelated schema changes at Sphere. The control remains in effect at least until legacy-aggregator mirrored writes are retired.

Control activities
  1. Executable parity fixture. A runnable test consumes a representative shard-keeper series and asserts the expected label set on the rollup-service side. CI blocks merge on fixture failure. The fixture is the executable proof that label-set parity is preserved across the boundary at the point of change.

  2. Affected service-owner signoff. In-scope PRs require signoff from the shard-keeper owner and the rollup-service owner. The reviewer checklist (Cardinality Guardrails first-cut, 2023-10-26) requires the PR description to state whether the change affects a cross-service label boundary; an affirmative answer triggers the dual signoff and the fixture run.

  3. Cardinality preflight. The PR must include a label-cardinality preflight (Cardinality Guardrails, 2023-12-28) showing before/after distinct-value counts for any new or renamed label, with a cap consistent with the Cardinality Guardrails. Cosmetic label-template revisions that change cardinality are explicitly in scope.

  4. Alert-source classification. The PR must classify each affected metric's alert source (Cardinality Guardrails, 2023-12-28) so downstream alert routing in metrics-pipeline preserves source_system / emitting_adapter attribution across the boundary — specifically, that a shard-keeper-originating fact emitted by metrics-pipeline carries source_system=shard-keeper and emitting_adapter=metrics-pipeline, so rollup-service continues to attribute the metric to its true origin after the label change.

Retained evidence case: shard_region → storage_region
  The rollup-service cross-service fixture consumer retains a reading path against `shard_region` via `readLabel(series, "shard_region")` (last verified 2024-02-13). This case is intentionally kept as the executable exemplar for the failure mode the control catches: if shard-keeper renames the emitted label to `storage_region` while a downstream consumer still reads `shard_region`, the read returns missing and the fixture fails — providing ongoing evidence that the parity check detects a cross-service label-name divergence.

Evidence list
  - Cross-service label-parity fixture source and CI run history for in-scope PRs.
  - Reviewer signoffs from the shard-keeper and rollup-service owners on each in-scope PR.
  - Cardinality preflight diffs on each in-scope PR.
  - Alert-source classification entries on each in-scope PR.
  - Retained `shard_region` → `storage_region` fixture case: source of the `readLabel(series, "shard_region")` consumer and its last green run.

  - Related controls in the same family: shard-keeper pre-push synchronization rule (Apr-18 replay guard) and PR #188 (post-2023-04-14 rollback hardening).

arguments.title: Q2 Cross-Service Invariants Review — June 4, 2025 — Preparation Brief
arguments.body:
Q2 Cross-Service Invariants Review — June 4, 2025
One-Page Preparation Brief

Circulated by: Alex Valdez · Requested by: Hema · Drafted: 2025-06-02

1. Purpose (and what this review does NOT do)

The June 4 review is a check that current owner-map provenance has named mapped owners and explicit exception routes. It is scoped to the three lanes below.

Out of scope — explicit boundaries:
- Does not create a centralized release-approval gate.
- Does not change service ownership or backup designations.
- Does not authorize Lantern beyond June 30, 2025.
- Does not add accounts, data sources, or tenants.
- Does not begin a new metrics-pipeline scale-response cycle.
- Alex is not the catch-all owner for implementation, telemetry, operations, or release readiness in any lane.

2. Lane A — Owner-Map Provenance

What we are checking: every cross-service invariant in scope has a named mapped implementation owner, a rollback owner, and a boundary-specific exception owner, each on the record (runbook entry field or forum readout).

Invariant | Mapped impl owner | Rollback owner | Exception owner | Provenance on record?
Cardinality Guardrails: label-cardinality preflight | (see §4 — open) | (see §4) | Nadia — alert semantics; Cyrus — cost/cardinality angle | rb_1789206351936 under metrics-router, review-path language named
Cardinality Guardrails: alert-source classification | Nadia | (see §4) | Nadia — alert semantics | rb_1789206351936, Dec-12-2023 required-operating-rule block
Cardinality Guardrails: parity check (label-name) | Nadia (alerting/dashboards); Cyrus team (rollup-service) | per service owner | routes back to mapped service owner, not a generic reviewer | rb_shard_keeper_label_parity; pre-push sync rule post-May-18
metrics-router canary alert response | (see §4 — canary owner field) | deploy-pipeline rollback | per service owner | rb_metrics_router_canary
Lantern two-account read-only boundary | Iris — customer interp; Alex — fresh-data, tenant, denials, latency, errors | n/a (read-only) | Iris is NOT the exception owner for Lantern data-contract questions | Lantern stop-contract ownership split

Exception route rule (from Hema's infra cross-service proposal): an ownership exception routes back to the mapped service owner, not to a generic reviewer. An exception owner is not a stand-in for the mapped release owner. The April engineering-forum readout will demonstrate the rule using mapped-owner examples; the review should hold any drift against this.

3. Lane B — Lantern Two-Account Read-Only Boundary Through June 30, 2025

- Boundary is read-only across two accounts, in force through 2025-06-30. The review does not extend, narrow, or re-authorize it.
- Ownership split on the active stop-contract:
  - Alex: fresh-data, tenant, denials, latency, errors.
  - Iris: customer interpretation.
  - Iris is not the exception owner for Lantern data-contract questions; those route to the mapped service owner.
- Harbor Health used the published ownership card twice during the extension period (2025-05-22, 2025-05-29) to route follow-ups without requesting raw incident text — relayed by Iris as the third concrete observation from the extension. (Confirmed in scope as evidence the boundary is operating as designed.)
- Out of scope for June 4: whether the boundary extends past June 30. That decision is separate and does not get pre-decided here.

4. Lane C — Cardinality Guardrails Checks

The signed-off preflight covers both router and shard-keeper paths (rb_1789206351936). The Dec-12-2023 required operating rule names three checks:

1. Label-cardinality preflight. Identifies new/changed label keys and value-shape behavior. Must classify the changed value set as bounded, expected high-cardinality with an owner and budget, or effectively unbounded. Live-path label changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture; replay/mirror validation alone is not enough.

2. Alert-source classification check. Classifies whether the relevant panel or alert signal is live-path, replay-source, mirror-source, or other validation-source evidence. Replay/mirror movement remains visible as investigation evidence but is not rollback criteria by itself. Reviewers must not let validation-source panels read like live rollback triggers.

3. Parity check. Cross-service label-name or meaning changes require rollup-service parity before promotion. A green metrics-router canary does not substitute for downstream consumers expecting the same name and semantics. The pre-push sync rule for shard-keeper (Nadia + Cyrus team) is the on-the-record instance.

Non-goals the entry is explicit about: not a mature/complete Cardinality Guardrails program, not a general telemetry rewrite, does not move enforcement ownership to data platform, does not make Wes (or any practical backup) the default enforcement owner.

5. Open question for the room — is anything missing from the owner-map?

I want to surface this before the meeting rather than assume the answer:

- rb_1789206351936 (the canonical Cardinality Guardrails entry) does not currently carry an owner/backup field — it has service, title, body, and timestamps only. The mapped implementation owner is named inside the body (Nadia for alert semantics; Cyrus for cost/cardinality), but the entry header itself does not surface that through the runbook store the way rb_ingest_edge_cutover (alex / yuki) or rb_shard_keeper_label_parity (alex / nadia) do. Question for June 4: do we treat this as a missing provenance cell, or as a deliberate choice because the entry is cross-service and not ownable to a single service header?

- A green metrics-router canary on route_pattern-class changes does not substitute for rollup-service parity — that boundary is named in the body but the corresponding rollback owner for a failed parity check is not separately mapped in the entry. The exception route points at "mapped service owner," but the cross-service case (who actually pulls the change back when both sides are involved) is not explicitly named.

- The "is validation-only evidence rollback-worthy?" question is named as an open question in the first-cut body itself (Nov-2023) and was reaffirmed in the 2023-10-30 incident-scope patch. It has not been closed; the review should not assume it has.

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.

Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. # Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.
